title: The Force Meta-Paradigm and Repository: An Introduction
affiliations: The Force Global Research Facility

detail.title: The Force Meta-Paradigm and Repository: An Introduction
detail.abstract: This document announces The Force Meta-Paradigm as a coherence physics and design- science field-correction proposal for the governance of human-centred complex adaptivesystems (HC-CAS) — organisations, institutions, AI systems, and human-AI partnershipswhose future states cannot be fully derived from their current state and in which humanjudgment is constitutively part of system operation. The meta-problemthe programmeaddresses is bidirectional recursion operating without invariant governance and under ex-post correction: decisions generate premises for future decisions while knowledge generates premises for future knowledge, producing compounding incoherence across recursive cycles under any architecture lacking a structural boundary condition. The programme proposes that this condition is governed by a single invariant: ΔC≥0, coherence must not decrease, operating ex-ante at the substrate level of recursive statetransitions. From this invariant follow two proposed mechanisms —metabolic contradiction processing and recursive identity maintenance —which together are arguedto reverse the legacy relationship between complexity and coherence. Under legacyarchitectures, complexity degrades coherence; under the proposed Coherent CollectiveCognition (CCC) architecture, complexity is proposed to fuel coherence through mechanisms that convert contradiction into dimensional expansion rather than accumulating distortion. Evidence from the eleven-month BCS 2.0 testbed demonstrates substrate-independent operation across heterogeneous AI architectures, sustaining C > 0.9. The observed90+%reduction in alignment time (3.8 months → 30–40 minutes) is reported as a GreenZoneoperational finding consistent with the architecture's predictions; whether this signaturegeneralises across organisational and civilisational settings is the principal open questionthe Red Zone research programme addresses. The repository applies these proposals across every domain where HC-CAS governanceisat stake — strategic management, artificial intelligence, institutional design, and complexity science — through fourteen companion articles. The programme's relationtothe Ackoff, Simon, and Teece lineages is one of proposed developmental extension, not completion; each companion article makes the specific extension argument for its domainrather than asserting it globally here. Two legitimate scientific challenges exist: provide an alternative solution to the sameproblem with comparable operational evidence, or provide a superior problemdefinitionwith equivalent explanatory power. The programme stands as the live, untested-to-failurehypothesis pending Red Zone validation, not as a claim of demonstrated field-level validity.

title: Advertising Effectiveness and Local Economic Conditions: Evidence from Housing Cost Shifts
affiliations: University of Toronto,  and

detail.title: Advertising Effectiveness and Local Economic Conditions: Evidence from Housing Cost Shifts
detail.abstract: Household economic conditions are a fundamental determinant of consumer demand, yet we lack causal evidence on how they affect advertising responsiveness. We address this gap by exploiting local housing cost shocks as a source of exogenous variation in household budget pressure, instrumenting local housing price growth in a shift-share IV design, and estimating how these conditions moderate TV advertising effectiveness for 78 restaurant brands across 13 million store-weeks. We find that a one standard deviation increase in local housing cost growth nearly eliminates the baseline advertising elasticity for restaurants, with the IV estimate roughly eight times larger than the naive observational estimate. This negative housing cost-interaction effect is amplified in areas with higher renter shares, consistent with housing cost pressure operating as a negative income shock through rent increases, and effects are also significantly larger for high ad-spend brands, which show greater exposure to local economic conditions. Applying our estimates to observed housing cost trends, our projections imply that advertising elasticities swing by 0.15 or more as local conditions change, suggesting that optimal ad allocation levels may vary substantially with economic conditions. Smaller-sample evidence from 22 supermarket brands recovers a significant positive effect of housing cost shocks on grocery store ad elasticity, indicating that the direction of the effect is category-specific.

title: NNPC Nil-Off Directive: Navigating the Legal Minefields Via Corporate Rescue Measures

detail.title: NNPC Nil-Off Directive: Navigating the Legal Minefields Via Corporate Rescue Measures
detail.abstract: Late last year, following a recommendation submitted by the Stakeholder Alignment Committee on the reconciliation of indebtedness between the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC Limited) and the Federation, the President approved a nil-off of $1.42 billion and ₦5.57 trillion in legacy debts owed by NNPC Ltd to the Federation Account. The NNPC Limited had transitioned from a state-owned corporation to a commercial entity following the enactment of the Petroleum Industry Act, 2021, and in doing so, had inherited the assets and liabilities of the defunct NNPC. To resolve its corporate liquidity issues and position it for a possible Initial Public Offer, the President effectively waived sums of money to which the people of Nigeria were entitled. The nil-off directive of the President had far-reaching implications for not just the Federation, but the NNPC Limited. Employing a doctrinal research methodology, this paper argued that even though the President doubled as both the Commander-in-Chief and the Minister of Petroleum, he lacked the powers under the relevant laws to approve the nil-off. Drawing examples from foreign jurisdictions, the paper argued that nil-offs had to be backed by law. The paper found that corporate liquidity issues of the NNPC Limited could not be resolved by presidential fiat but by deliberate employment of corporate rescue measures. The paper made a case for appointment of administrators, as a strategic way to solve the NNPC Limited liquidity issues and turn its fortunes around.

title: Is Current "Repeat Player" Theory Much Ado Over Much Less-An Is Current "Repeat Player" Theory Much Ado Over Much Less-An Evidence-Based Overhaul Evidence-Based Overhaul
affiliations: Salisbury University - Franklin P. Perdue School of Business and Center for Conflict Resolution

detail.title: Is Current "Repeat Player" Theory Much Ado Over Much Less-An Is Current "Repeat Player" Theory Much Ado Over Much Less-An Evidence-Based Overhaul Evidence-Based Overhaul

declarations.ethicsApproval: Approved by University IRB.

detail.abstract:
For five decades, dispute resolution scholarship has largely accepted the "repeat player" theory as a foundational explanation for structural inequality in litigation, arbitration, and mediation. Despite its widespread influence on legal scholarship, policy debates, and procedural reform, the theory has rarely been tested using direct empirical evidence gathered from dispute resolution participants and neutrals. This Article reexamines repeat player theory through original survey data collected from Equal Employment Opportunity Commission mediators and mediation participants participating in the agency's nationwide employment discrimination mediation program.

The study evaluates mediator perceptions of repeat player influence together with participant data comparing repeat players and first-time participants across bargaining strategy, negotiation objectives, settlement outcomes, and overall satisfaction. While mediators acknowledge that prior relationships often facilitate communication and increase trust, the evidence suggests that repeat player status exerts a substantially smaller influence on mediation outcomes than commonly assumed. Repeat players demonstrate greater experience in framing negotiations as primarily monetary disputes and report somewhat higher perceived outcome success; however, settlement rates and overall dispute resolution outcomes reveal only modest differences between repeat players and one-shot participants.

Rather than supporting the prevailing view that repeat player status constitutes a systemic defect threatening procedural fairness, the findings suggest a more nuanced understanding. The principal advantages associated with repeat players appear to arise from experience, preparation, bargaining credibility, and negotiation strategy rather than institutional bias or improper mediator favoritism. The Article proposes an evidence-based reformulation of repeat player theory that distinguishes legitimate expertise from structural unfairness and argues that future scholarship should rely more heavily on direct empirical measurement rather than assumptions derived from litigation theory or secondary outcome data. By reframing one of dispute resolution's most influential theories, this research provides a more accurate foundation for evaluating fairness in mediation and other consensual dispute resolution processes.

title: Analyzing Negotiations Before They Start: The TESPA Framework for Pre-Negotiation Field Control

detail.title: Analyzing Negotiations Before They Start: The TESPA Framework for Pre-Negotiation Field Control

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the research presented in this working paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This working paper is based on publicly available sources and methodological analysis and does not involve human participants, personal data collection, or clinical research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This working paper introduces TESPA as a methodological framework for analyzing negotiations before they formally begin. The paper develops the concept of pre-negotiation field control and applies it to the Ukraine-Russia pre-negotiation track as a demonstration case. The argument is methodological rather than predictive: the paper does not claim to forecast negotiation outcomes, but to identify the field-control processes that shape the conditions under which future negotiations become possible. TESPA is presented here at the public methodological level. The paper explains the framework's analytical logic, key concepts, transferable mechanisms, and public-facing indicators, while preserving the internal TESPA layer of cumulative registries, detailed evidence chains, scenario tracking, actor behavior logs, and the full Case Archive.

title: Causal Targeting Doesn't always Beat the Decile Rule: Praxis, a Planted-truth Benchmark for Physician Targeting
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Causal Targeting Doesn't always Beat the Decile Rule: Praxis, a Planted-truth Benchmark for Physician Targeting
detail.abstract: Choosing which physicians a pharmaceutical sales force should visit is at heart a causal question. The doctor worth visiting is one whose prescribing will rise because of the visit, and current volume, the usual proxy, can be a poor guide. This is hard to study because the counterfactual is never observed in the field, so a platform cannot check whether a per-physician target list was right, and scoring an LLM agent's open-ended output with an LLM judge is itself biased. We introduce Praxis, an open and reproducible environment that sidesteps both problems with a verifiable reward. Praxis builds synthetic markets whose ground truth is planted by construction (segments, per-physician treatment effects, and the value-optimal call list), lets an LLM agent reason and call deterministic causal primitives, and scores the result against that truth with deterministic metrics: adjusted Rand index, ATE error, the Qini coefficient, and oracle precision@k. No LLM judge is involved. We use it for two studies. A 500-market Monte-Carlo experiment asks when causal targeting actually beats the standard decile heuristic; a small head-to-head pits frontier LLMs (Claude, GPT) against a distilled 4B model. Recovering the population ATE is easy. Covariate adjustment beats the naive contrast in all 500 trials, but ranking individual physicians is much harder and the answer depends on the estimator. Causal targeting beats decile only where responsiveness is learnable from covariates and current volume is a weak proxy for it; a clean one-parameter sweep places the crossover at a volume-uplift coupling near 0.14. The distilled 4B is competitive on precision@k at roughly 150× lower cost, though the gaps sit inside the noise and frontier models read causal direction more reliably. Our contribution is the environment, the frozen Praxis-v1 test set (120 instances, 5 tiers), and the regime-resolved finding.

title: Sustainability and Social Inclusion in UK Festivals and Outdoor Events: A Critical Review

detail.title: Sustainability and Social Inclusion in UK Festivals and Outdoor Events: A Critical Review
detail.abstract: This working paper addresses a gap in UK-based research on how festivals and outdoor events achieve both social inclusion and environmental sustainability together. It provides a critical evaluation of how UK festivals and outdoor events can integrate social inclusion (accessibility) with environmental sustainability to create a sense of "belonging" for all attendees and generate public value. A structured critical review of academic literature, official event industry reports, government guidance, and environmental sustainability standards was used to evaluate developments since 2019, drawing on Value Co-Creation and Experience Economy Theory. The synthesis identified three key findings. First, a festival cannot claim to be sustainable when its focus is solely on reducing waste, energy consumption, transport impact, or carbon footprint. Second, whether a festival's sustainability is perceived as fair depends on factors including the quality of its access information and the accommodations it provides for disabled attendees. Third, because festivals are held in public or semi-public spaces, those organising them carry a greater responsibility to promote cultural diversity and contribute positively to local economies.

title: A New Theory of the Firm for the Age of Artificial Intelligence Verification, Governance, and Liability When Generation Becomes Abundant

detail.title: A New Theory of the Firm for the Age of Artificial Intelligence Verification, Governance, and Liability When Generation Becomes Abundant
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence has made the generation of cognitive work - analysis, code, memos, recom-
mendations - nearly free. It has not made the verification of that work free, and a generated
output is not yet a usable one: before a firm can act on it, someone must establish that it is correct
and bear responsibility if it is not. This book develops a theory of the firm for that condition.
Four results organise the argument. A Cost Floor Theorem: under any fixed verification standard
binding on verifier error, the expected cost of a usable output is bounded away from zero regard-
less of model capability. An Incentive Irrelevance Proposition: deployed AI - a fixed, non-learning
policy at inference - does not respond to incentives, so the firm must govern through ex ante
specification and ex post verification, implemented in a governor–executor–verifier architecture.
Liability concentration: AI cannot bear responsibility, so liability concentrates on deploying firms
and its management becomes a core function of the firm. And safe throughput: the correct
performance metric is the value of correct decisions net of verification cost and residual risk. At
the macroeconomic level the same bottleneck explains record AI investment alongside disputed
measured productivity: the economy can generate more than it can verify, and closing that gap
requires verification capital that accumulates slowly. The book confronts the strongest objections
to these results, grounds the framework in decided cases and the empirical record, and closes
with a measurement-focused research agenda.

title: Understanding Indigenisation in India's Defence Manufacturing Ecosystem
affiliations: GITAM University

detail.title: Understanding Indigenisation in India's Defence Manufacturing Ecosystem

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration- This study is the author's original work and has not been funded by any institution/entity/individual with any vested interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The ethics approval is attached in the annexure section of the paper (Informed Consent Form). Consent of the participants of this study was obtained before interviewing them.
declarations.funderStatement: Declaration- This study is the author's original work and has not been funded by any institution/entity/individual with any vested interests.

detail.abstract: India's declared progress on defence indigenisation conceals a deeper conceptual problem: government, industry, and the armed forces define and measure "indigenisation" in fundamentally different ways. Using a qualitative, inductive design combining semi-structured stakeholder interviews with document analysis and triangulation, this dissertation maps these definitional divergences and tests them against component-level realities in India's drone manufacturing ecosystem, where platforms labelled indigenous remain critically dependent on imported components, software, and spares, a vulnerability underscored by Operation Sindoor (2025). It further examines institutional barriers beyond technology, including DRDO's gatekeeping role, limitations of the Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020, and the absence of standardised metrics beyond Indigenous Content percentages. The study proposes a unified definitional framework and a Technology-Depth Index to measure genuine design and manufacturing capability, alongside institutional reforms and a phased implementation roadmap for achieving operationally meaningful self-reliance.

title: Stablecoins, CeFi, and the legal anatomy of digital insolvency

detail.title: Stablecoins, CeFi, and the legal anatomy of digital insolvency
detail.abstract: The rise of centralized crypto-asset (CeFi) platforms has put the technological dogma of code is law in check. In the face of systemic crises and corporate collapses, the rigidity of the digital environment clashes with the principles of equity and distributive justice of insolvency law, which must be adapted to the digital economy. This research breakthrough article analyzes, through an adaptive and pragmatic approach, the response of U.S. courts (2020-2026) to the financial vulnerability of stablecoins and native tokens. Methodologically, an analysis matrix based on the "triple dimension of the State" (Police Supervisor, Neutral Arbitrator and Consumer/Contractor) is proposed. Through the examination of a paradigmatic jurisprudential tetralogy (James v. iFinex, Ofir Ventura v. Circle, Wave Digital Assets v. U.S. and In re Celsius Network), it is shown that the ontological or regulatory classification of digital assets loses practical relevance in the face of the economic reality of insolvency. The courts resort to classic tools such as clawbacks, asset centralization (automatic stay) and expert valuation for equity to neutralize the acts of self-protection of creditors and preserve the par condicio creditorum, marking the limits of the digital architecture in the face of bankruptcy public order.

title: From Betrayal to Blessing: Leadership Lessons from the Joseph Narrative
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business and

detail.title: From Betrayal to Blessing: Leadership Lessons from the Joseph Narrative
detail.abstract: This paper examines the enduring relevance of the biblical Joseph narrative as a study of human nature and leadership. Key themes include the transformative power of forgiveness and the intricate interplay between family dynamics and divine providence. While Joseph's moral integrity remains a central focus, the narrative also offers a sobering lesson in governance: his consolidation of land and wealth under Pharaoh created the very centralized power structure that eventually enabled the enslavement of his descendants. The narrative demonstrates how emotional vulnerability and tears serve as catalysts for healing, while Judah's transformation from complicity in betrayal to courageous advocacy exemplifies the redemptive power of genuine repentance. By examining the cyclical nature of deception alongside the dangers of concentrated authority, this paper demonstrates how the narrative offers timeless insights into contemporary ethical and political challenges, including the importance of maintaining cultural roots and the necessity of proactive preparation for foreseeable crises.

title: From Production to Discernment: Evaluation-Centered Organization Design Under AI-Enabled Production Abundance
affiliations: , Cornell University, Carnegie Mellon University and

detail.title: From Production to Discernment: Evaluation-Centered Organization Design Under AI-Enabled Production Abundance

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Generative AI lowers the cost of producing plausible symbolic artifacts, including memos, analyses, code, designs, proposals, plans, evaluations, and prototypes. This shift is especially consequential for knowledge work, where organizational output often takes the form of artifacts that must be interpreted, compared, revised, and acted upon. Yet many organizations still evaluate work through practices built for a lower-volume production regime: episodic review, expert gatekeeping, static portfolios, and ad hoc escalation. The cost of judging whether AI-generated artifacts are correct, distinctive, strategically relevant, or worth pursuing has not fallen at the same rate as the cost of producing them. The result is a discernment gap: a mismatch between the rate at which organizations generate plausible work and the rate at which they can coherently evaluate, prioritize, integrate, and learn from it. This Point of View article argues that closing this gap requires evaluation-centered organization design. We identify current evaluation practices that become strained under AI-enabled production abundance and propose four linked design shifts: from episodic review to continuous curation, from expert gatekeeping to distributed calibration, from static portfolios to evaluative memory, and from production efficiency to attention governance. We conclude with a research agenda for studying organization design when production is abundant but discernment remains scarce.

title: Consumers’ Health-Locus-of-Control and Social Distancing in Pandemic-Based E-Tailing Services
affiliations: and Montpellier Business School

detail.title: Consumers’ Health-Locus-of-Control and Social Distancing in Pandemic-Based E-Tailing Services
detail.abstract: Purpose-COVID-19 and its precautions, including social distancing, have revolutionized traditional retailing-and consumption patterns. In this turbulent environment, the purpose of this study is twofold. First, this paper explores the direct effect of consumers' internal/external health locus-of-control on their hygiene consciousness, which, in turn, affects their social distancing behavior. Second, this study posits that social distancing, in turn, impacts consumers' current online grocery shopping behavior and their future online grocery shopping intentions, thus uncovering important insight. Design/methodology/approach-To address these gaps, this paper develops a model that links consumers' internal/external health locus-ofcontrol to their adoption of e-tailing-based grocery services. Data collected through a web-based survey was analyzed by using partial least squares-based structural equation modeling. Findings-The results indicate that consumers' health locus-of-control indirectly affects the way they shop for their groceries during the pandemic. In particular, consumers' internal (external) health locus-of-control drives higher (lower) hygiene consciousness and greater (lower) social distancing behavior. In turn, consumers' online grocery shopping behavior was found to increase during the pandemic, with their corresponding intent to continue this behavior in the future. Moreover, this study finds the effects of consumers' social distancing on their current grocery shopping behavior and future intentions to be contingent on consumer age, with stronger effects identified for older consumers. Originality/value-This study shows how consumers' internal/external health loci-of-control exert opposing effects on their social distancing behavior, as mediated by hygiene consciousness. Overall, the empirical analyzes corroborate the association of consumers' social distancing-and online grocery shopping behavior (for consumers of different age profiles), both during and after the pandemic.

title: Correlates and Cushioning Effects of School District Savings
affiliations: George Washington University - Trachtenberg School of Public Policy and Public Administration

detail.title: Correlates and Cushioning Effects of School District Savings
detail.abstract: School districts operate in an unstable revenue environment, with changes in state transfers being a source of uncertainty. District savings, in the form of unrestricted general fund balance, could provide a tool for maintaining budget stability. This study provides the first cross-state examination of school fund balance. First, descriptive statistics illustrate variations in state laws regarding district fund balance and in the average balance levels. Second, districts adjust savings based on revenue risk exposure, but the capacity to save also matters. Lastly, districts starting a year with a higher fund balance experience smaller spending gaps if state aid declines.

title: When Innovation Becomes Systematic: From Venture Capital Experimentation to Public-Market Risk
affiliations: Michigan State University - Department of Finance and Michigan State University - Department of Finance

detail.title: When Innovation Becomes Systematic: From Venture Capital Experimentation to Public-Market Risk
detail.abstract: We study when innovation news enters public equity markets as systematic rather than firm-specific risk. We show that this distinction depends on how venture capital is distributed across innovation directions. When startup investment spans distinct but connected directions, forming an innovation stack, innovation news is more likely to become systematic. When funding instead clusters within narrower directions, its effects remain more firm-specific. Using U.S. startup funding data from 2000 to 2024, we construct a cross-direction share that captures this contrast from Crunchbase industry category co-assignment. A higher cross-direction share predicts higher average pairwise correlation among S\&P~500 stocks and a larger top-eigenvalue share of the implied correlation matrix over the following year, with the associated leading component aligned with the market. The effect is economically large, robust to macro-financial and innovation controls, and not explained by the overall similarity of the funded directions. Cross-sectional evidence further shows that the response is broad across firm pairs and firms rather than driven by a small set of highly exposed names. Venture capital experimentation therefore foreshadows whether innovation risk will remain firm-specific or become systematic.

title: When Control Structures Coagulate: Event Signatures and the Four Frontiers of Capital Centralisation

detail.title: When Control Structures Coagulate: Event Signatures and the Four Frontiers of Capital Centralisation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, human data, or animals. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Capital centralisation is often measured by firm or group size. That measure cannot distinguish legal consolidation from reciprocal control, hierarchical command or feedback amplification. We represent the economy by a non-negative, column-substochastic control operator whose dimension changes through five primitive events: strong merger, accretive acquisition, transfer of an existing stake, pure network divestiture and legal split. The event-frontier signature theorem gives the universal signs, and the genuine ambiguities, of their effects on four diagnostics: the largest legal-block share, the mass of the largest non-trivial strongly connected component, strict downstream reach and the spectral radius. These restrictions are falsifiable. An accretive acquisition, for example, cannot reduce reciprocal integration or the spectral radius, while a stake transfer may reduce either. A constructive theorem then shows that any one frontier can become macroscopic or near-critical while the other three vanish. We also characterise the exact strong-lumpability condition under which the unordered mass projection is Markovian; mass-only merger and split hazards yield a finite-particle coagulation-fragmentation process. Projection does not restore the information lost through consolidation. For a surjective map from an n-node operator to an r-node operator, mass-weighted compression has rank r 2 and nullity n 2r 2 ; a binary merger erases exactly 2n-1 linear directions. Admissible pre-merger networks with different component structures and spectra can therefore share one aggregate image. A legal split selects from the corresponding set of admissible lifts. The framework supplies event-level over-identifying restrictions, separates legal break-up from network divestiture and locates organisational memory in the rule used to reconstruct lost microstructure.

title:
ICG-CES Adjusted CAPM for Public Securities 
An institutional reconsideration of the MEDAF-CAPM for African, emerging-market and global sovereign portfolios

detail.title:
ICG-CES Adjusted CAPM for Public Securities 
An institutional reconsideration of the MEDAF-CAPM for African, emerging-market and global sovereign portfolios
detail.abstract:
This article develops the ICG-CES Adjusted CAPM as an institutional reconsideration of the Modèle d'Évaluation des Actifs Financiers for public securities. The classical CAPM links expected return to the risk-free rate, market beta and the market risk premium. That relation remains indispensable because it provides a disciplined benchmark for pricing systematic market risk. Yet, for treasury bills, sovereign bonds and other public securities, especially in African and emerging financial systems, the classical relation can be incomplete. Public securities are embedded in fiscal policy, monetary transmission, bank balance sheets, auction mechanisms, collateral systems, secondary-market liquidity and domestic savings mobilization. Their observed yield may therefore compensate not only market beta, duration and liquidity, but also institutional conversion weaknesses that standard CAPM does not explicitly measure.
The proposed framework introduces the Institutional Conversion Gap, aggregated through a bottleneck-sensitive Constant Elasticity of Substitution function, into the CAPM architecture. The adjustment modifies three core components: the risk-free base, the market risk premium and the security beta. The risk-free rate is corrected for fiscal and monetary policy conversion gaps. The market premium is scaled by the global institutional gap and policy gap. The beta is adjusted by security-specific exposure variables such as duration, illiquidity, rollover risk, auction dependence, concentration and mark-to-market sensitivity. The resulting expected return is E(R_i)^ICG-CES = R_f^ICG + beta_i^ICG x pi_M^ICG. This is not a rejection of CAPM. It is a conditional CAPM for public securities in systems where institutional conversion risk is material.
The article presents the African, emerging-market and global context, objectives, problems, hypotheses, literature, model architecture, data requirements, illustrative results, decision rules, governance requirements and validation roadmap. It includes professional visual diagnostics: adjusted market lines, CES bottleneck curves, radar charts, risk heatmaps, opportunity heatmaps, histograms, yield-curve shifts, alpha reclassification and implementation diagrams. All numerical examples are synthetic and methodological. They do not constitute country ratings, country rankings or investment recommendations.

title: Corruption, drugs, money laundering, and moral panics: British evidence 1801-2015
affiliations: University of Leeds - Faculty of Business

detail.title: Corruption, drugs, money laundering, and moral panics: British evidence 1801-2015
detail.abstract: This paper presents a mixed method historical study of the relationship between drug trafficking, corruption, and money laundering, asking under what institutional conditions these activities become mutually reinforcing. It argues that the scale and persistence of illicit financial flows are shaped less by criminal innovation alone than by broader political and financial structures. Using evidence from British newspaper archives between 1801 and 2015, alongside historical case studies of the opium trade, international drug control, offshore finance, and modern anti-money-laundering regulation, the paper traces a U-shaped pattern in public concern over drug-related corruption and the concealment of criminal proceeds. It finds that periods characterised by financial openness, capital mobility, and regulatory arbitrage were associated with heightened public concern arising from enhanced opportunities for laundering and corruption, while eras of tighter financial control constrained them. The analysis suggests that money laundering is best understood as a systemic feature of institutional environments, highlighting the enduring tensions between financial liberalisation, regulatory oversight, and the governance of illicit markets.

title: Adaptive resilience: A theory of expectation formation, delayed adaptation, and adaptive infrastructure under persistent oil-market uncertainty
affiliations: Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, , Notre Dame University, University of Jammu and Department of Economics, Pusan National University

detail.title: Adaptive resilience: A theory of expectation formation, delayed adaptation, and adaptive infrastructure under persistent oil-market uncertainty
detail.abstract: Existing resilience research primarily interprets resilience as the capacity of economic systems to recover after external disruptions. This perspective, however, provides only a partial understanding of resilience under persistent geopolitical uncertainty, where adaptive responses often begin before disruptions are fully realised. This study develops the Adaptive Resilience Theory, which reconceptualises resilience as a forward-looking adaptive process emerging through expectation formation, adaptive decision-making, coordinated adjustment, and adaptive infrastructure. The theory proposes that persistent uncertainty reshapes expectations, delays the initiation of adaptation, and influences resilience through socially coordinated adaptive processes rather than through realised shocks alone. The theoretical framework is evaluated using the Oil Volatility Resilience Score together with complementary empirical identification based on Wavelet Quantile Correlation, Rolling Wavelet Quantile Correlation, and Quantile-on-Quantile Regression. The empirical evidence consistently shows that adaptive resilience is state dependent, evolves dynamically through time, and is affected more strongly by persistent geopolitical threats than by realised geopolitical acts. These findings indicate that the principal economic cost of persistent uncertainty arises not from the magnitude of realised disruptions, but from delays in coordinated adaptation. More broadly, the study introduces adaptive infrastructure as a new conceptual lens for understanding resilience and highlights that effective resilience policy should design the conditions under which adaptation begins rather than merely facilitate recovery after shocks.

title: From Fixed Prices to System Value: A New PPA Contract Design for Variable Renewable Energy Technologies in Single-Buyer Electricity Systems
affiliations: King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center, King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center, King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center (KAPSARC) and King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center

detail.title: From Fixed Prices to System Value: A New PPA Contract Design for Variable Renewable Energy Technologies in Single-Buyer Electricity Systems
detail.abstract: The Single-buyer model (SBM) is a widely adopted electricity market architecture in developing economies. As the share of variable renewable energy (VRE) increases in the power supply, SBMs’ competitively tendered, long-term, fixed-price power purchase agreements (PPAs) create a challenge: while competitive price-only auctions reveal generators’ costs, they do not reveal the system value of VREs, which is crucial for efficient operation and investment decisions in high VRE systems. Hence, we develop a theoretical framework for analyzing PPA pricing under different contractual arrangements within the SBM and show formally that the gap between the generator’s levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) and the system-value-based optimal PPA price widens as VRE penetration increases due to decreasing VRE value and dispatchable reserve costs. Then, we propose an alternative arrangement, i.e., Adjusted Power Purchase Agreement, that incorporates system conditions in contracts to address the structural aforementioned gap. This agreement adopts a new payment structure that combines an auction-based payment based on renewable energy auction prices and variable  Real-time Correction Price (RCP) based on real-time system conditions.

title: Predicting Option Prices Using Graph Neural Networks: A Multi-Relational Approach to Modeling Option Chain Structure
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Predicting Option Prices Using Graph Neural Networks: A Multi-Relational Approach to Modeling Option Chain Structure

keywords: Deep Learning JEL Classification: G13 (Contingent Claims Pricing)

detail.abstract: The Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) framework prices options under assumptions of constant volatility, constant interest rates, and no transaction costs. Critically, it prices each contract independently of the others on the same underlying. In practice, options on a common underlying that share an expiry or a strike move together. The shape of an option chain carries information that a per-contract model discards. This paper proposes a graph neural network (GNN) framework for predicting option prices. It represents an option chain as a graph: each node is an individual contract (defined by strike, expiry, and type), and edges connect contracts sharing an expiry (sparsified to each contract's k nearest strikes to keep aggregation local), sharing a strike, or being the same contract observed on a prior trading day. Across the 123-day SPX options window collected for this study (Databento, OPRA), a multilayer GNN improves on the BSM baseline (using realized, not implied volatility) by mean absolute error (191.5 vs. 201.6) and mean squared error (184,902 vs. 351,512). However, it does not outperform a feedforward neural network trained on the same input features (MAE 151.3). An LSTM baseline that uses only each contract's price history performs worse (MAE 313.8). This gap widens, not narrows, at full scale. BSM overtakes the multilayer GNN on relative (MAPE) error even as the GNN keeps an edge on absolute error. We report this directly: the graph structure improves on the classical baseline on some metrics but does not outperform a simpler feature-to-price mapping. We discuss this in light of the amount of pricing-relevant information the BSM already inputs.

title: Effectiveness of ETS for Reducing CO2 Emissions: Empirical Evidence from European Union, New Zealand and the Republic of Korea
affiliations: World Bank - Development Research Group (DECRG), World Bank Group and University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Effectiveness of ETS for Reducing CO2 Emissions: Empirical Evidence from European Union, New Zealand and the Republic of Korea
detail.abstract: Emission trading schemes (ETS) are among the primary pricing instruments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Currently, more than 35 ETS are in operation around the world at multinational, national, and subnational levels. How effective these systems are in reducing emissions is a key empirical question. This study examines the effectiveness of three large-scale emission trading schemes implemented by the European Union, New Zealand, and the Republic of Korea in reducing carbon dioxide emissions. The study employs a generalized synthetic control method on data from 2005–20. The findings show that the EU emission trading scheme led to a cumulative reduction of 21.3 percent in carbon dioxide emissions from the electricity sector and 15.6 lower total carbon dioxide emissions, relative to a scenario with no emission trading scheme. In New Zealand, the emission trading scheme had no statistically significant effect on total national carbon dioxide emissions—largely because nearly half of New Zealand’s emissions come from agriculture, a sector not covered by the country’s emission trading scheme. The effectiveness of Korea’s emission trading scheme varied substantially across phases. Although initially it did not halt the rise in emissions, it became a progressively strong driver of decarbonization over time.

title: From Green Recognition to Green Innovation: Evidence from China' s Energy Efficiency Labeling System
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics and Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE)

detail.title: From Green Recognition to Green Innovation: Evidence from China' s Energy Efficiency Labeling System
detail.abstract: When consumers cannot accurately identify the green attributes of products, the environmental value of green products may not be fully reflected in firms' market returns, weakening demand-side incentives for green innovation. Energy Efficiency Labeling System (EELS), as a demand-side environmental information disclosure policy, can effectively alleviate this issue. This paper employs a staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) model using data on Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms from 2000 to 2024. Results demonstrate that the EELS significantly promotes corporate green innovation by improving market performance and reducing green R&D uncertainty. Specifically, the policy predominantly drives green product innovation rather than green process innovation. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the policy effect is more pronounced among state-owned enterprises and firms located in regions with stronger intellectual property protection and higher government environmental attention. Further analysis indicates that the EELS exerts a significant effect on reducing firm-level carbon emissions. Moreover, it acts as a complement to supply-side environmental regulations, generating a positive synergistic effect on promoting corporate green innovation. From the perspective of demand-side environmental information disclosure, this paper contributes to the literature on the determinants of corporate green innovation and provides policy implications for improving green information disclosure systems and promoting green consumption.

detail.abstract: It’s intuitive to assume that taxation plays an important role in development, not only by being the main source of state revenue but also due to its direct impact on the economic environment of a country. There are many studies dedicated to a developmental approach to the reform of domestic tax policies and their economic impacts, but there are surprisingly few studies regarding the developmental impacts of the international tax system. The present dissertation attempts to investigate the connection between the international tax system and development, a subject largely clouded by the OECD’s technocratic debates on the matter. It will focus specifically on the impacts of the Arm’s Length Standard to dependent economies and their developmental struggles, in connection with the perspective of Latin American structuralism and the New Institutional Economics. This dissertation will explore the empirical evidence and the theoretical and practical critiques that have been levied against the Arm’s Length Standard over the years, its current treatment under the OECD and its two-pillar solution, and, finally, analyze the alternative practices employed by Brazil and China to adapt the principle to their particular circumstances. This research will ultimately propose the implementation of a peer-reviewed experimentalist governance model for developing countries to adopt similar practices to the Brazil’s fixed margins and China’s Location Specific Advantages, which should help simplify the system for countries that lack the necessary fiscal infrastructure for the enforcement of the Arm’s Length Standard.

title: When AI Becomes the Consumer: Solving the Depopulation Crisis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: When AI Becomes the Consumer: Solving the Depopulation Crisis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration of Interest: None.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel macroeconomic paradigm that endogenizes Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents fundamentally as autonomous end-user consumers rather than mere supply-side inputs. Facing acute population decline, traditional growth models dictate economic contraction due to shrinking domestic demand. We challenge this premise by constructing a general equilibrium framework featuring a large, heterogeneous population of AI agents endowed with modified Stone-Geary utility functions, supported by a realistic human demographic trajectory that stabilizes at a sustainable lower bound. The central contribution of this paper is the formalization of AI as a primary driver of effective demand, establishing a baseline survival cost (electricity) and idiosyncratic discretionary preferences for "Human-Originated Authenticity". While AI cannot biologically consume physical goods, their market transactions generate valid effective demand and direct income redistribution to human agents. Under an optimal Ramsey taxation scheme, we prove that per-capita human wealth expands monotonically as the human population declines toward its long-run steady state, transforming human economic activity from a survival necessity into a mechanism for genuine, culturally enriching self-actualization without relying on infinite divergence paradoxes.

title: Connectivity Cost Burdens: Contingency cost measures for assessing household broadband affordability
affiliations: University of Toronto - Faculty of Information and

detail.abstract:
Recent CRTC and FCC proceedings reveal a blind spot when considering telecommunications affordability: advertised prices, provider availability, and competition indicators are not effective measures of a household's ability to sustain connectivity under recurring costs burden, contingent and episodic charges, and service-maintenance stress. We locate this evidentiary blind spot within the assumption that competitive retail markets will discipline the full cost structure of connectivity, including non-base fees and service conditions, in the absence of pricing regulation. Our research develops a Household Broadband Survey as a measurement instrument for practical affordability, operationalizing connectivity cost-burden, contingency-cost exposure, and stress-test outcomes at the household level. The instrument shows that subsidized rental status is the strongest marker of contingency-cost exposure, while monetized contingency costs sharply differentiate stress outcomes such as disconnection, debt, borrowing, and reductions in ancillary basic needs capacity. The article concludes by proposing improved data reporting and prospective affordability stress-testing tools.

title: Revisiting Gender Citation Bias: Evidence from Multiple-Birth Papers in Structural Biology
affiliations: and Dalian University of Technology

detail.title: Revisiting Gender Citation Bias: Evidence from Multiple-Birth Papers in Structural Biology

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors

detail.abstract: Gender differences in academic citation practices have been widely documented, but it remains unclear whether these differences reflect gender bias or imperfect comparability between the cited works. Using data from protein structure research, this study reexamines gender bias in citation under conditions designed to maximize substantive comparability. We first construct highly comparable groups of "multiple-birth papers," defined as papers that independently analyze the same protein structure. Within these groups, we identify "paper twins": pairs of substantively comparable papers that differ in author gender. We then construct counterfactual citation sets to assess whether a paper that should have been cited is omitted from a citing article. The results provide no evidence that women authored papers are systematically more likely to be omitted than comparable men authored papers. This null finding remains robust across a series of sensitivity analyses. However, gender differences re-emerge when counterfactual citation sets are defined using textual similarity, as employed in previous studies. This pattern suggests that previously reported gender inequalities in citation may partly result from insufficient control for substantive comparability between papers, rather than from gender bias alone. Additional analyses reveal no significant same gender citation preference among either men or women authors. Although papers published earlier receive a citation advantage, the magnitude of this publication priority advantage does not differ significantly by author gender. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of closely matching research content when assessing gender inequality in academic citation.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the multifaceted crisis in Sudan following the 2019 overthrow of Omar al-Bashir, focusing on the power struggle between General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and General Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ("Hemedti") as a catalyst for national destruction. Through the lens of political psychology, demographic theory, and economic analysis, this study argues that the military-political rivalry represents not merely a leadership conflict but a systemic failure of transitional governance. The analysis traces how competing power centers transformed Sudan from a fragile democratic transition into a failed state, with cascading effects on economic infrastructure, demographic stability, and social cohesion. Drawing on primary documents, international sanctions data, and humanitarian assessments, this paper provides a comprehensive framework for understanding how elite power struggles produce state collapse, population displacement, and long-term developmental trauma. The findings suggest that Sudan's crisis exemplifies a broader pattern of military-dominated transitions where institutional weakness, external patronage, and psychological pathologies among leadership perpetuate cycles of violence and economic decay.

detail.abstract:
Cet article mesure la réorganisation de la fonction d'octroi du crédit immobilier d'une banque coopérative française à la suite du choc monétaire de la Banque centrale européenne amorcé en juillet 2022. L'échantillon original compte 700 dossiers tirés du portefeuille de la Caisse d'Épargne Côte d'Azur (352 en 2021, 348 en 2023), ramené à 696 observations pour l'inférence.

Trois méthodes sont mobilisées : régression linéaire multiple à erreurs-types HC3, analyse en composantes principales, et régression poolée avec interactions année × variable complétée par un test de Chow.

Le test de Chow rejette à F(7, 682) = 7,31 (p = 1,78 × 10⁻⁸) l'égalité des deux fonctions d'évaluation. La rupture porte sur deux variables. Le coefficient standardisé du Salaire mensuel passe de +0,413 à +0,761 (interaction +0,349 ; p = 0,051). Celui de la Durée d'emprunt recule de +0,405 à +0,201 (interaction –0,204 ; p = 0,001). Le résultat sur la Durée est robuste à une correction Bonferroni à six tests ; celui sur le Salaire reste à la limite de la significativité conventionnelle. Les autres déterminants — Âge, Taux d'endettement, Statut Marital, Patrimoine Immobilier — n'évoluent pas significativement.

Nous interprétons cette bascule comme l'effet mécanique de la saturation des leviers macroprudentiels français, qui force la banque à reporter l'ajustement sur la sélection salariale ex ante. À notre connaissance, c'est la première formalisation économétrique d'une telle bascule à l'échelle d'un établissement bancaire français, avec test de rupture structurelle et interactions année × variable. La lecture théorique mobilise le canal du crédit (Bernanke et Gertler, 1995) prolongé par l'interaction macroprudentielle. Nous discutons les implications pour le régulateur, les banques et l'accès à la propriété des ménages modestes.

title: The Antitrust Tush Push and Institutional Identity in College Athletics
affiliations: University of Mississippi School of Law

detail.title: The Antitrust Tush Push and Institutional Identity in College Athletics
detail.abstract:
Recent preliminary-injunction antitrust challenges to NCAA athlete-eligibility rules suggest that the NCAA's procompetitive defense is nearing a breaking point. The "antitrust Tush Push" keeps moving the line.

The pressure point is a neglected threshold question. What feature actually differentiates college sports from minor-league alternatives?

This Article argues that the answer is institutional identity, meaning the alumni, regional, cultural, and geographic attachments that explain fan investment in university brands.

On the supply side, Division I athletics increasingly functions as a commercial enterprise housed in universities, often partially subsidized by academic funds and made more explicitly transactional by the post-House settlement revenue-sharing model. On the demand side, consumer interest has remained robust even as the student-athlete model has weakened through the COVID-19 waiver, NIL compensation, transfer-portal liberalization, and one-and-done basketball.

Reframing the product around institutional identity illustrates the vulnerability of the NCAA’s educational-character justifications at Step Two of the Rule of Reason. If the consumer-facing attribute is institutional identity rather than education, many eligibility restraints function as labor-market regulation with only a weak connection to product quality. Durable eligibility governance will therefore require collective bargaining rather than litigation.

title: The Ballot and the Branch ADR as a Pillar for Sustainable Electoral Governance and Peace in Africa ADDENDUM: A Gender-Responsive Framework for Women's Electoral Justice

detail.title: The Ballot and the Branch ADR as a Pillar for Sustainable Electoral Governance and Peace in Africa ADDENDUM: A Gender-Responsive Framework for Women's Electoral Justice
detail.abstract: This addendum to the original policy paper was developed following its first publication in May 2026 and reflects the author's ongoing practitioner research into the gender dimensions of electoral dispute resolution across East Africa. The arguments presented draw on over fourteen years of professional experience in electoral governance, dispute resolution practice, and institutional capacity building across the region. They are informed by the Women, Peace and Security framework (UNSCR 1325 and successor resolutions), the IFES Practitioner Brief on ADR in Elections, and the IEP Positive Peace framework. This addendum is intended to be read alongside the original paper and may be cited independently. A. THE GENDERED ARCHITECTURE OF ELECTORAL EXCLUSION The original paper established that electoral disputes in Africa encompass complex political, social, and psychological dynamics that litigation alone cannot resolve. This addendum extends that argument to its logical frontier: the recognition that those dynamics are profoundly and structurally gendered-and that electoral ADR systems, however well-designed in principle, reproduce the very exclusions they are meant to address unless gender-responsive design is built into their foundations. Women in African electoral contexts face a dual and compounding exclusion. First, they are structurally underrepresented as candidates, voters, election officials, and political party decision-makers-a participation deficit extensively documented by UN Women, the African Union's Gender, Peace and Development Centre, and the Electoral Integrity Project. Second, and less examined, when women experience electoral violence, intimidation, harassment, or procedural injustice, the formal mechanisms designed to provide redress-electoral dispute resolution bodies, tribunals, and complaint systems-are systemically inaccessible to them. KEY INSIGHT Women are doubly excluded in electoral systems: first from meaningful participation, and second from the justice mechanisms that should protect that participation. ADR that does not address both exclusions simultaneously is structurally incomplete.

title: Welfare Litigation, State Courts, and Social Citizenship
affiliations: Indiana University Maurer School of Law

detail.title: Welfare Litigation, State Courts, and Social Citizenship
detail.abstract: For half a century, federal courts have stood at the center of welfare rights enforcement. That era is ending. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's historic cuts to Medicaid and SNAP will generate an avalanche of benefit terminations, work requirement sanctions, and overpayment actions from state agencies. And with a federal judiciary increasingly hostile to the private enforcement of public law, state courts will become not just a concurrent forum for welfare litigation, but an increasingly important one. Understanding how state courts have handled welfare litigation over the past three decades, then, is essential to anticipating what comes next. This Article is the first to offer a typology of state court review of welfare administration across the United States over the last thirty years. Cases decided since the 1996 Welfare Reform Act reveal three distinct categories of litigation-challenges to agency decisions brought by claimants, overpayment actions brought by states, and reimbursement disputes brought by providers-each with different doctrinal patterns and access-to-justice concerns. The resulting picture challenges two scholarly understandings: the federal courts as the premier fora for civil rights, and state courts as mere sites of routinized dispute processing. State courts regularly adjudicate public benefit controversies, often involving unrepresented claimants, and have developed distinctive approaches to reviewing agency action. organizational infrastructure capable of transforming individual grievances into systemic challenges. The welfare rights tradition need not end, but it must find a new home.

detail.abstract: This study examines the determinants of retirement security in the Visegrad Four (V4) countries, evaluating the endogenous linkages among residential housing wealth, financial capability, credit market maturity, and long-term care infrastructure. We examine the structural and behavioral frictions driving late-life economic vulnerabilities in post-transition economies. While high regional homeownership rates historically served as a defensive cushion, this extreme concentration of illiquid real assets poses a structural obstacle due to low digital financial literacy and underdeveloped retail financial markets. Consequently, locked-in housing equity hinders late-life consumption smoothing, elevating elderly poverty risks and deteriorating living conditions rather than improving retirement security. We contribute to the urban and pension economics literature by framing housing as a critical but undergoverned component of retirement frameworks, providing direct policy implications for coordinated housing, finance, and social protection reforms.

title: The Fall Of Democracy

detail.title: The Fall Of Democracy
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the condition of Indian democracy through the history, constitutional structure, and contemporary political meaning of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest and Sonam Wangchuk's 2026 hunger strike. The title, The Fall of Democracy, is a warning rather than a declaration that India has ceased to hold meaningful elections. India remains a competitive, federal, multiparty republic with an active judiciary, a vast civil society, regular transfers of power in many states, and an electorate that has repeatedly surprised incumbents. Yet democracy is more than the counting of votes. It also depends on free expression, equal citizenship, institutional restraint, governmental accountability, transparent political finance, legislative scrutiny, federal balance, and the ability of citizens to protest without being treated as enemies of the state.

The paper reconstructs Indian democracy from colonial rule and the Constituent Assembly to the present. It identifies the democratic achievements and nationally significant controversies of every Union government, while devoting particular attention to the concentration of executive power and civil-liberties disputes under the government in office from 2014 to the source cutoff. It analyzes the Emergency of 1975-77 as India's clearest historical breakdown, but also argues that modern democratic erosion is often incremental, legalistic, and electorally ratified. Comparative chapters draw parallels - and important distinctions - with Weimar Germany, Fascist Italy, Hungary, Turkey, Venezuela, Poland, Chile, and other cases of democratic backsliding or collapse.

The CJP movement arose in May 2026 amid youth anger over alleged examination-paper leaks, the cancellation and rescheduling of a national medical entrance examination affecting millions of candidates, unemployment anxieties, and a controversial judicial reference to unemployed youth as "cockroaches." The movement transformed the insult into a symbol of resilience and demanded the resignation of the Union Education Minister, systemic examination reform, accountability, compensation for families affected by examination-related student suicides, and stronger mental-health support. Sonam Wangchuk began an indefinite fast at Jantar Mantar on 28 June 2026. On 18 July, the twenty-first day of the fast, authorities moved him to Safdarjung Hospital against his expressed wish, citing medical advice and a Delhi High Court direction to monitor and intervene if necessary (Reuters 2026a; Associated Press 2026a).

The paper places this fast within the Indian political tradition of bodily protest: Gandhi's fasts, the 1929 Lahore jail hunger strike and the death of Jatin Das, Potti Sriramulu's fatal fast for an Andhra state, Irom Sharmila's sixteen-year protest against the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, the anti-corruption fasts of Anna Hazare, environmental fasts, and Wangchuk's earlier Ladakh campaigns. Hunger strikes can dramatize exclusion and create moral urgency, but they also raise difficult questions about coercion, consent, state duties to preserve life, and the substitution of personal sacrifice for institutional deliberation.

The central conclusion is conditional. Indian democracy has not simply "fallen," but several safeguards have weakened, and the costs of political exclusion are increasingly displaced onto citizens, journalists, students, minorities, opposition parties, and protesters. The CJP episode demonstrates a wider legitimacy problem: when ordinary channels of representation appear unresponsive, young citizens may conclude that only virality, street occupation, or bodily risk can make the state listen. The proper democratic response is neither romanticization of starvation nor suppression of dissent. It is credible institutional reform - independent examination administration, transparent investigations, parliamentary accountability, protected protest, federal and judicial restraint, and a politics that treats the young as citizens rather than as a demographic resource.

title: Children as Canaries: Disaggregating the Sentinel Claim into Three Mechanisms of Early Harm

detail.title: Children as Canaries: Disaggregating the Sentinel Claim into Three Mechanisms of Early Harm

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: The claim that children function as canaries for harms later reaching adults is intuitive, rhetorically powerful, and used loosely. It is applied indiscriminately to cases sharing only the fact that children were hurt. This paper does not argue that every harm announces itself in children first; harms attaching to adult roles have no pediatric precursor and none should be sought. It argues that a real and recurring pattern in the documented record is being obscured by the imprecision, and that the sentinel claim collapses three mechanisms with different causal structures, different evidence, and different remedies. Mechanism one, sentinel proper, describes harm registering first in children through developmental susceptibility and becoming legible in adults only later: leaded gasoline, where 170 million Americans were exposed as children and roughly 824 million cumulative IQ points and 151 million excess mental disorders arrived decades after the pediatric signal; the Great Smog, where prize cattle sickened before the human toll was counted; radioiodine concentrated through milk at Nevada and Hanford; and swill milk in New York. Mechanism two, targeted selection, describes harm in which children were chosen because they were children: the devshirme, which took roughly 200,000 boys; the Mamluk system, which excluded its own elite's sons and so required perpetual purchase; Canada's residential schools, through which more than 150,000 children passed and at least 4,200 died; Willowbrook; Fernald; and the North Carolina Eugenics Board, which sterilized more than 7,600 people, some as young as ten. Fernald establishes the decisive point: a federal advisory committee found the radiation doses unlikely to have caused physical injury and concluded the studies wronged the boys regardless. Mechanism two is not a dose story. Mechanism three, captive absorption, describes children neither selected nor more susceptible who could not leave: asbestos in roughly 34,800 schools, lead in public housing, Flint, and 4 million lead service lines still in the ground. Only the first is a sentinel effect. The second and third are childism. The paper closes on a recourse asymmetry running from North Carolina, where fewer than 220 of more than 7,600 sterilized people were ever compensated, to the contemporary platform cases, where the barriers defeating child plaintiffs are general rather than child-specific, and therefore will not yield to child-specific advocacy.

title: A Commercial Ceasefire: Why the EU-US Data Privacy Framework Cannot Survive Schrems III

detail.title: A Commercial Ceasefire: Why the EU-US Data Privacy Framework Cannot Survive Schrems III

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a doctrinal legal analysis based on published case law, legislation, and secondary scholarship. It did not involve human participants, personal data collection, or case studies requiring consent.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The adequacy mechanism under GDPR Article 45 is structurally incapable of delivering legal certainty across divergent constitutional orders without a binding international treaty. Despite representing the most sophisticated transatlantic data transfer arrangement to date, the EU-US Data Privacy Framework remains a 'commercial ceasefire' built on executive discretion rather than structural reform and is likely to face invalidation in a future 'Schrems III' before the CJEU Grand Chamber. The paper begins by isolating the 'essential equivalence' standard established in Schrems I and Schrems II as the constitutional metric against which the Framework must be judged. It then analyses the architecture of the DPF, specifically Executive Order 14086's necessity and proportionality safeguards and the Data Protection Review Court, before examining the General Court's pragmatic endorsement of these mechanisms in Latombe v Commission (2025). Three unresolved deficits are identified. First, an independence deficit: the DPRC remains a creation of the executive branch lacking statutory permanence. Second, a proportionality mismatch: the US balancing standard for surveillance does not equate to the EU's strict necessity requirement. Third, a systemic conflict of laws: US processors complying with FISA Section 702 orders inevitably breach GDPR Articles 29 and 48. True legal certainty cannot be achieved through administrative patches, and only a binding international treaty can resolve the fundamental tension between US national security architecture and EU fundamental rights law.

title: Should I stay or should I go? The role of fluid and crystallized intelligence onretirement decisions
affiliations: Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore di Milano and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Should I stay or should I go? The role of fluid and crystallized intelligence onretirement decisions
detail.abstract: We combine insights from cognitive psychology and economics to distinguish crystallized from fluid intelligence and assess their role in the decision to work longer. We use data from the Survey on Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), employing cognitive tests to construct indicators of fluid and crystallized intelligence. We investigate the probability of retirement and the distance between actual retirement age and ordinary retirement age. Our main findings reveal differential contributions of the two cognitive domains to retirement decisions, suggesting that crystallized intelligence plays a compensatory role in maintaining older workers’ employability. This has implications for active aging policies, emphasizing the potential of knowledge-based tasks and on-the-job training to enhance the productivity andworkability of our aging workforce.

title: Detecting Genuine Doctrinal Ambiguity: A Multi-Layer Framework for Identifying Structural Indeterminacy in Judicial Reasoning
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Detecting Genuine Doctrinal Ambiguity: A Multi-Layer Framework for Identifying Structural Indeterminacy in Judicial Reasoning
detail.abstract: Legal indeterminacy has been extensively theorized in jurisprudence and partially formalized in computational law, yet no framework bridges theoretical accounts of indeterminacy and scalable, grounded detection. This article makes three contributions. First, it develops the distinction between shallow ambiguity (resolvable through further research) and genuine ambiguity (a structural feature of the law itself), a distinction implicit but undertheorized in both the Hart-Dworkin debate and the computational law tradition from Allen through Prakken. Second, it proposes a five-type taxonomy of genuine indeterminacy (semantic, normative, methodological, jurisdictional, analogical) and specifies the Gray Area Detection Framework: eighteen tests in three layers mapping the taxonomy onto extraction-time, aggregation-time, and structural detection strategies. Third, it specifies a pre-registrable validation methodology with explicit confirmation and disconfirmation criteria, a commitment to release the resulting expert-annotated benchmark, and a companion interventional modality, posture-dispersion measurement over the same verified substrate (Brodskiy and Pokov 2026), that supplies method-independent convergent validity. The practical stakes are professional: systems that cannot distinguish settled from contested law present contested conclusions with unwarranted confidence, and explicit indeterminacy detection is a precondition of responsible legal AI deployment.

title: A Multi-Axis Pre-Deployment Predictor of Cross-City Fairness-Audit Transfer in Spatial Crime Models: Evidence from a Twenty-Two-City UK Cohort
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin

detail.title: A Multi-Axis Pre-Deployment Predictor of Cross-City Fairness-Audit Transfer in Spatial Crime Models: Evidence from a Twenty-Two-City UK Cohort
detail.abstract: We ask whether ship-gate failure of cross-city fairness-audit transfer in spatial crime models can be predicted before deployment from properties of a holdout city, where ship-gate failure is the joint criterion of (mean |∆DIR|, max |∆DIR|, count of |∆DIR| > 10) and DIR is the disparity index ratio of top-decile predicted-violent-crime flagging in above-median versus below-median demographic cells on a given axis. We assemble a twenty-two-city UK production cohort (nineteen Tier 2 cities plus three Tier 1 baselines) using police incident data from data.police.uk over a 35-36-month window, fit per-city violent-crime spatial models on H3 r9 hexagonal cells (≈ 0.105 km 2) using a gradient-boosting ensemble, and audit DIR on three minority axes from the 2021 UK Census and one deprivation axis from the English Index of Multiple Deprivation 2019 and Welsh Index of Multiple Deprivation 2019. We construct four single-feature pre-deployment predictors (three minority-axis predictors measuring the percentage of top-decile predicted-violent-crime cells above the within-city median on each axis; plus a graded three-level ordinal IMD-severity indicator), calibrate class boundaries on a 20-city retroactive set (17 Tier 2 + 3 Tier 1), and test two post-calibration cities (Southampton, Portsmouth) prospectively. The four-axis aggregate score yields perfect boundary-score separation of the Tier 2 cohort: score = 0 maps to ship-gate PASS for 4/4 cities (100%); score ≥ 2 maps to non-PASS for 10/10 cities (100%); the middle band (score = 1) is heterogeneous across 5 cities (4 PASS, 1 MARGINAL, 0 TRIPLE-FAIL), with zero rank inversions across all 171 Tier 2 city pairs at the published thresholds. A six-mechanism failure taxonomy assigns every non-PASS verdict to a predictor-detectable mechanism family. Event-probability calibration via Brier score with Murphy decomposition across 46 (city, type) pairs shows all 46 calibration slopes within the conventional 30% deviation flag threshold. Within the UK jurisdictional scope, pre-deployment city properties are sufficient to predict cross-city fairness-audit ship-gate failure; classification at the middle score band requires per-axis review. Findings should not be generalized cross-jurisdictionally without re-calibration.

title: Bridging Legacy Core Banking to Both U.S. Instant Payment Rails: FedNow and RTP
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Bridging Legacy Core Banking to Both U.S. Instant Payment Rails: FedNow and RTP

declarations.funderStatement: This work was conducted independently and received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The United States operates two ISO 20022 instant payment networks — the Federal Reserve's FedNow Service and The Clearing House's RTP® — yet fewer than 1,700 of the nation's 10,000+ eligible financial institutions are connected to FedNow and fewer than 1,100 to RTP. The central barrier is legacy core banking integration: 73% of non-connected institutions cite their existing core systems as a moderate-to-severe obstacle. This paper presents OpenFedNow, an open-source dual-rail middleware layer that bridges legacy core banking platforms (Fiserv, FIS, and Jack Henry) to both instant payment networks simultaneously. The architecture comprises five layers: Rail Gateways, an Anti-Corruption Layer, a Shadow Ledger, a Saga Orchestration engine, and Vendor Adapters. The design draws directly on production experience building PIX integration at Santander Brazil — one of the most demanding real-time payment deployments in the world — and adapts that architecture to the structural requirements of U.S. rails. All three vendor adapters are complete and the project is released under Apache 2.0.

title:
Humanning: Measuring the Human Dimension

 Why Global Statistics Still Fail to Measure It, How to Measure It, And the Bridge to Human Understanding

detail.title:
Humanning: Measuring the Human Dimension

 Why Global Statistics Still Fail to Measure It, How to Measure It, And the Bridge to Human Understanding
