declarations.declarationOfInterest: PD has provided consulting advice, unrelated to the present work, to Novo Nordisk Research & Development UK Limited. FM and SW have no competing interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: FM is supported by the Clarendon Fund Scholarship in partnership with the Brasenose Clarendon Award and Department of Population Health Studentship. SW is supported by the Oxford NIHR Biomedical Research Centre.

detail.abstract:
INTRODUCTION:

Health technology assessment (HTA) compares an intervention’s incremental costs and health effects, implicitly assuming all costs are interchangeable (“a cost is a cost”). However, policy developments in multiple jurisdictions suggest that policymakers place additional value on spending for on-patent drugs/therapies (“product costs”) compared to other spending such as staff time, generic drugs, or administration costs (“non-product costs”). This is operationalised by applying higher cost-effectiveness thresholds to products. This study examines how HTA should assess value when policymakers have preferences over both population health and products spending.

 

METHODS:

We developed a theoretical framework that formalises policymaker objectives as a trade-off between population health and the additional perceived value assigned to product spending. Using several examples, we assessed whether alternative formulations of cost-effectiveness metrics consistently implement these objectives.

 

RESULTS:

Conventional HTA methods can misvalue interventions depending on their mix of product and non-product costs. We derive a more consistent approach that applies separate thresholds to product and non-product costs. This framework increases the value attributed to high-price interventions which reduce non-product costs, such as curative gene therapies.

 

CONCLUSIONS:

The proposed framework provides a transparent and consistent approach to value assessment, with implications for which types of products are developed by industry and reimbursed by payers.

title: What's Important Under the Hood? Decomposing Sequential Risk Taking with Feedback through Behavioral Structural Modeling
affiliations: , University of Basel, Faculty of Psychology, University of Basel, University of Basel and University of Basel

detail.title: What's Important Under the Hood? Decomposing Sequential Risk Taking with Feedback through Behavioral Structural Modeling
detail.abstract: Understanding sequential risk-taking with feedback, and how people deviate from rational benchmarks, has led to many behavioral finance models, without converging on a unifying theory. We propose to first shift the analysis from models to their constituent parts, that is, mechanisms. Second, we systematically compare the most common mechanisms against each other. We find that they all improve predictive accuracy relative to a Bayesian benchmark, but inertia and asymmetric updating explain most of the variation, while risk or loss aversion contributes little once learning is modeled. Better trading performance is associated with greater risk tolerance and near-Bayesian learning rates.

title: Eliciting social norms and norm shifts under extreme weather conditions: Coordination game experiments with Swedish farmers Working Paper
affiliations: University of Trento, German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) Halle-Jena-Leipzig and Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (SLU)

detail.title: Eliciting social norms and norm shifts under extreme weather conditions: Coordination game experiments with Swedish farmers Working Paper

declarations.funderStatement: Jens Rommel and Julian Sagebiel are grateful for funding received from the Swedish Research Council for Sustainable Development (FORMAS) for the project “Building resilience for Swedish food production under increasing risk of extreme weather” under registration number 2019-00993.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether extreme weather conditions strenghten or erode social norms that support pro-environmental behaviors among Swedish farmers. We conceptualize norms as shared beliefs about socially appropriate and inappropriate behaviors and elicit them through incentivized coordination game experiments with over 400 farmers. Participants ranked behaviors across irrigation, pesticide use, and manure spreading scenarios, with treatments varying between normal and extreme weather year framing. Results show shared norms with little polarization, and we find no evidence that framing behaviors under extreme weather conditions affects these norms. Our findings do not suggest norm changes and illustrate the value of incentivized framed field experiments for studying how environmental stressors interact with social norms.

title: Build the Judge Before the Strategy: A Reproducible Retail Backtesting Platform and a Five-Study Negative-Results Program on ASX/US Equities

detail.title: Build the Judge Before the Strategy: A Reproducible Retail Backtesting Platform and a Five-Study Negative-Results Program on ASX/US Equities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. The research was conducted independently, and the author has no financial relationship with any organization that could have influenced the design, analysis, or conclusions of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study. The research uses publicly available financial market data and does not involve human participants, personal data collection, clinical research, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was conducted independently by the author using publicly available and commercially accessible financial data sources.

detail.abstract: We describe Project-Drift, a solo-researcher, reproducible backtesting platform for long-only equity strategies, and report the results of a five-study, six-candidate pre-registered evaluation program run on it against ASX and US equities. The platform's central design commitment is that the evaluation machinery-a bitemporal point-in-time (PIT) data store, a structurally enforced features/labels leakage boundary, a walk-forward simulator with a costed and fairly constructed benchmark, and pre-registered Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) and Probability-of-Backtest-Overfitting (PBO) gates-was built and frozen before any strategy return was computed. Four candidate strategies were evaluated against this fixed judge to a return-based verdict: (1) cross-sectional momentum with a trend overlay, (2) a franking-credit dividend-capture trade, (3) US insider cluster-buying, and (4) S&P/ASX 200 index-addition reconstitution. Two further candidates (LIC/LIT discount-to-NTA, post-earnings-announcement drift), reported together as a fifth study, were blocked at the data-feasibility stage by vendor data-access limits before any return could be computed. All six candidates resolve negative or blocked: no candidate clears its pre-registered promotion bar, and none is presently under active evaluation. We report the headline numbers for each study together with the concrete software and measurement bugs that pre-registration, mutation-tested gates, and adversarial review caught along the way, including a first-pass insider-cluster result of +871.5% mean return that a data-alignment bug had manufactured, which fell to a statistically indistinguishable-5.2% after three independent fixes (N = 2,110 paired events). The contribution of this paper is accordingly not the discovery of a profitable trading rule, but a demonstration that a pre-registered, reproducible evaluation framework can reject several plausible retail strategies while simultaneously detecting multiple implementation errors that would otherwise have produced false positives. We argue that five rejections from one disciplined evaluation harness are informative in aggregate, not merely five failures, and that the harness and the discipline, not any single strategy, are the durable output of this project.

title: The Study of Jesuit, Catholic Legal Education: An Idea and a Program

detail.title: The Study of Jesuit, Catholic Legal Education: An Idea and a Program
detail.abstract: The Society of Jesus has been among the most important influences on Catholic legal education in the United States and around the world. Yet, focused scholarly attention to its history has been relatively scarce. This symposium in Jesuit Educational Quarterly therefore features ten research articles and reflective essays on the Society’s relationship to the law and legal education. And, to introduce this symposium, this editorial reflects briefly on how scholars might approach the future study of Jesuit, Catholic legal education.

title: From Data to Decisions: Connecting Evidence, Science, and Policy
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - College of Agricultural Sciences, Department of Agricultural Economics and Rural Sociology

detail.title: From Data to Decisions: Connecting Evidence, Science, and Policy
detail.abstract: Data, facts, and evidence underpin effective policy, yet political pressures, declining survey capacity, and the weaponization of information are eroding the foundations of trusted statistics. Economics can inform policy but cannot resolve the political, distributional, and communication challenges that shape real-world decisions. The value of public data depends on reliability, integrity, and quality, and the loss of Federal data collections leaves policy advisors "flying blind" while non-Federal (private, regional, think tanks, Non-Governmental Organizations) alternatives fill the void with uneven standards. Sustaining an evidence-based future requires reimagining data systems, strengthening statistical institutions, and building public-private partnerships that preserve trust, credibility, and access for citizens as well as stakeholders. It also calls for democratizing science by widening access to data, methods, and interpretive authority so evidence remains a public good capable of informing credible, resilient public decisions.

title: The Plague and the Protectorate: Empirical Evidence Fields and Materialist Metrics of the Early Islamic Polity
affiliations: University of Toledo

detail.title: The Plague and the Protectorate: Empirical Evidence Fields and Materialist Metrics of the Early Islamic Polity
detail.abstract: This technical note provides a simplified, evidence-based data framework for the early origins of Islam by replacing traditional and predatory "protection racket" narratives with a model of primary state-building and institutional economics. We demonstrate that the rapid stabilization of the early Caliphate was a rational response to the massive governance vacuum left by the Byzantine-Sasanian War and 7th-century pandemic shocks—specifically the devastating Plague of Shīrawayh (627–628 CE). Analyzing twenty-one distinct data exhibits, this paper charts a clear two-stage evolution of the early state: first, the Southern (Hijazi) political core lowered transaction costs and expanded its coalition by co-opting the highly developed theological, liturgical, and scribal infrastructures of the Northern (Syro-Mesopotamian) monotheistic substrate; second, the landmark monetary, administrative, and architectural transformations of 691–692 CE formalized this fluid movement into a strict, state-enforced imperial code of conduct. Ultimately, the surviving material, papyrological, and numismatic evidence shows that early Islam succeeded because it provided a superior, highly resilient institutional solution to the systemic regional collapse of late antiquity.

title: When Tariffs Bite: The Short-Run vs Long-Run Welfare Effects of Trade Wars
affiliations: University of Sussex Business School

detail.title: When Tariffs Bite: The Short-Run vs Long-Run Welfare Effects of Trade Wars
detail.abstract: This paper estimates short-run and long-run sector-specific trade elasticities using a panel of 170 countries and 22 manufacturing sectors over 1995-2022, and incorporates them in a multi-country, multi-sector framework calibrated for 77 countries. Counterfactual experiments evaluate how the welfare effects of tariff shocks vary with the nature of the shock, the time horizon, and the presence or absence of retaliation. The distinction between short-run and long-run elasticities affects the relative magnitude, rather than uniformly the direction, of the welfare response: under unilateral tariffs, trading partners' losses diminish over time as they redirect trade toward alternative markets, whereas under multilateral escalation net losses grow larger in the long run because the terms-of-trade and tariff revenue gains that partly cushion the impact effect erode faster than real-wage losses recover, leaving no untaxed suppliers to redirect toward.

title: The Hegemon's Fingerprint: Currency Role, Duration, and Reversibility in Central Bank Intervention

detail.title: The Hegemon's Fingerprint: Currency Role, Duration, and Reversibility in Central Bank Intervention
detail.abstract: A companion paper documents that Federal Reserve balance-sheet expansion coincides with a persistent reorganisation of foreign-exchange information architecture: the variance share of the first principal component across USD pairs rises from 40% to 65% and passes a difference-indifferences test against non-USD crosses. This paper asks what kind of fingerprint that is, of intervention in general or of intervention in the system's funding currency, how it depends on duration, and whether it reverses. Five tests on sixteen FX pairs at hourly resolution, 2014-2026, give a consistent answer. The ECB's pandemic programme, contemporaneous and of comparable scale, moves euro-leg concentration +3 percentage points against +32 for the dollar. The earlier €2.6 trillion Asset Purchase Programme leaves it flat. Across eight central banks expanding by 16-33% of GDP, response is unrelated to dose; the dollar sits roughly six standard deviations above the dose-response line fitted to the other seven. Blitz-shaped yen interventions revert fully within two weeks in five of six events. Under quantitative tightening, dollar-leg concentration decays at roughly 3.5 percentage points per year, pricing a year of maintenance at roughly three and a half years of recovery. The fingerprint is duration-dependent, slowly reversible, and appears only on the funding rail.

title: Initiative and Responsive: Auction Market Theory at the Signed Tape

detail.title: Initiative and Responsive: Auction Market Theory at the Signed Tape
detail.abstract: Auction Market Theory's central constructs, initiative activity that extends price and responsive activity that absorbs it, have lived for four decades as practitioner discourse, untested on signed order flow because aggressor-tagged data sits behind exchange licensing. This paper tests them on a practitioner archive of 624 recorded futures sessions (2018-2023, eight CME/CBOT instruments, 11,484,323 book messages, 1,774,079 trade prints), subjected first to a layer-wise authentication protocol that the data only partially survives. The restingdepth layer is shown to be vendor-reconstructed, invariant through the March 2020 Treasury seizure that licensed data shows collapsing, and is retired from evidence. The trade layer authenticates: aggressor-signed flow predicts contemporaneous price change at median correlation +0.50 across 545 sessions, positive in 99% of them. On the authenticated layer, the magnitude-direction separation holds on true aggressor marks (|flow| autocorrelation +0.275 against sign autocorrelation-0.097), an eighth domain for the invariant. Responsive absorption is locational: flow pushing into the session extreme earns sign-adjusted continuation of-0.232 ± 0.077, while identical flow mid-range earns +0.003, and the footprint folklore that absorption is an event property is null unconditionally. The constructs behave as the theory says, where the theory is read carefully.

title: Thermo-Structural Performance of SMA-reinforced Elliptical and Von Kármán Nose Cones for Reusable Sounding Rockets

detail.title: Thermo-Structural Performance of SMA-reinforced Elliptical and Von Kármán Nose Cones for Reusable Sounding Rockets
detail.abstract: As aerospace and reusable rocketry forms the backbone of the novel Space Era, nose cone geometry and material heavily influence aerodynamic efficiency and reusability, especially for reusable sounding rockets. Traditionally, research has studied material recovery and aerodynamic performance separately, leading to concrete, but incompatible results and recommendations for rocket design. This study presents a Python-based thermo-structural simulation comparing elliptical and von Kármán nose cones reinforced with Shape Memory Alloy (SMA) material, specifically Nitinol. The analysis integrates a TEXUS rocket-based trajectory, aerodynamic heating using the Sutton-Graves correlation, thermodynamic heating (conduction and radiation), and temperature-dependent SMA behavior. A novel performance metric, Shape Recovery Efficiency (SRE), quantifies recoverable deformation after ascent and descent.Results show that the von Kármán nose cone achieved a higher SRE (70.35%) than the elliptical design (59.95%), indicating greater recoverable deformation under equivalent conditions. Aerodynamic studies have previously revealed that the elliptical shape performs better in subsonic regimes, while the von Kármán profile minimizes supersonic wave drag. This framework provides an integrated aerodynamic, thermal, and mechanical modeling approach and demonstrates the potential of SMA-reinforced von Kármán nose cones for adaptive, reusable aerospace systems, despite its comparatively inferior performance in subsonic regimes.

title: The Welfare Implications of Manipulation under Stable Mechanisms
affiliations: Nanjing Audit University

detail.title: The Welfare Implications of Manipulation under Stable Mechanisms
detail.abstract: This paper studies how a profitable report changes assignments and welfare under a stable mechanism. We first show that the set of matched agents is unchanged. The new outcome reallocates their partners through disjoint trading cycles, and within each cycle, all agents on one side move in the same welfare direction, while agents on the other side move in the opposite direction. We then introduce Similarity: after a profitable report, a mechanism does not select a stable outcome if another stable outcome can restore some changed agents to their original partners without creating any new changes. Both versions of deferred acceptance satisfy Similarity, but DA is not the only stable mechanism with this property. Our main welfare result shows that harm to an agent on the manipulator's side requires a false aspiration-the report treats a truly worse affected alternative as if it were better than the achieved partner. Finally, we show that a change involving more than one trading cycle requires an Ergin-type cyclic preference profile.

title: Explanations May Not Travel, Positions Can: A Grammar for Comparable, Cumulative, and Extendable Public Sector Evaluation
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Explanations May Not Travel, Positions Can: A Grammar for Comparable, Cumulative, and Extendable Public Sector Evaluation
detail.abstract: Public sector evaluations often diverge, and explanations developed in one institutional, cultural, or governance context frequently fail to travel to another. Contextual accounts alone do not explain why evaluative explanations struggle to transfer across settings. This study identifies a positional governance mechanism behind this difficulty: evaluative elements-purpose, observation, adequacy, and exemption-are organized differently across settings, and without a positional logic that makes these elements explicit, conclusions such as a "4.0, good" rating remain opaque and difficult to compare, accumulate, or transfer. Drawing on Ostrom's positional decomposition logic as a methodological precedent (Crawford and Ostrom 1995), the study develops a positional configuration-Goal, Proxy, Criteria, and Veto (GPCV)-that identifies four analytical positions in evaluations and decomposes evaluative elements accordingly. Applying GPCV to two published cases reveals a conditional governance mechanism: when P and C are shared across actors, G divergence is absorbed and produces mediating effects; when P and C are imposed from above, G divergence is amplified and produces governance paradoxes. Veto positions function as boundary conditions that specify when otherwise valid evaluative conclusions no longer apply, shaping how positional configurations generate governance outcomes. This conditional mechanism travels across settings because it is specified in positional rather than contextual terms. The study makes four contributions. First, it reconceptualizes difficult-to-accumulate evaluative patterns as arising from positional misalignment rather than contextual or conceptual differences alone. Second, it provides a positional vocabulary-Goal, Proxy, Criteria, and Veto-that disentangles often conflated evaluative elements. Third, it identifies a governance mechanism that makes evaluative configurations comparable, explanations cumulative, and research extendable across traditions and contexts. Fourth, it refines the positional decomposition logic implicit in Ostrom's institutional analysis by applying the same structural operation to evaluative settings.

title: Hypervolume-Based Returns-to-Scope Measure
affiliations: National Taiwan University and University of Chicago

detail.title: Hypervolume-Based Returns-to-Scope Measure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This article does not contain any studies with human participants or animals performed by any of the authors.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was partially funded by Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST111-2628-E-002-019-MY3), Taiwan.

detail.abstract: Economies of scope refer to the cost advantages that a business achieves by producing a variety of products or services together rather than producing each one separately. The cost savings could arise because shared resources, technologies, or processes can be used across multiple products or services. Particularly, given the same inputs, returns to scope (RTSco) measures the change of productivity resulting from the joint production of multiple outputs compared to producing them separately. This study proposes a global normalized hypervolume (GHV) for RTSco estimation, which employs free disposal hull (FDH) to estimate the hypervolume under the frontier. Our method enables a more novel application of hypervolume, allowing for direct and consistent comparisons of RTSco across both convex and non-convex production frontiers in multiple-output scenarios. By leveraging the area under the frontier (AUF) and GHV metrics, we quantify the positive or negative RTSco with improved accuracy and consistency. Through simulation experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed method more effectively identifies RTSco on both convex and non-convex frontiers compared to other existing benchmarks. This achievement facilitates productivity and efficiency analysis, and provides additional managerial insights of RTSco besides to returns to scale.

title: Scoring vs. Ranking in Cold-Start Fraud Detection: A Premature Top K Rate Metric for Uncertainty-Aware Queue Placement

detail.title: Scoring vs. Ranking in Cold-Start Fraud Detection: A Premature Top K Rate Metric for Uncertainty-Aware Queue Placement
detail.abstract:
Fraud detection systems typically treat the cold-start problem as a scoring task: estimating the risk associated with an entity that has little or no transaction history. We argue that this framing overlooks a second problem with important operational consequences: where that entity should be placed within a capacity-constrained review queue. Because Top-K review slots are limited, a highly uncertain score can displace a well-supported one even when their estimated risks are similar.

We distinguish this ranking problem from the scoring problem and show that commonly used ranking metrics, particularly Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG), are largely insensitive to it. Across four placement strategies evaluated on both a controlled synthetic dataset and the IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection dataset (590,540 transactions across 13,553 cards), NDCG@K remains above 0.998 despite substantial differences in queue behavior.

To capture the failure mode that NDCG overlooks, we introduce Premature Top-K Rate (PTKR), a metric that measures how often highly uncertain entities occupy Top-K review slots they would not receive if ranked by their true risk. We compare a conventional score-based ranking strategy with two uncertainty-aware alternatives: a Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) adjustment and a rule-based holding-band (Tiered) approach, together with a random-placement baseline. In the synthetic experiment, naive ranking reaches a peak PTKR of 29.6%, compared with 1.9% for LCB and 0.0% for Tiered, while reducing NDCG by only about 0.0001. The same qualitative pattern appears in the IEEE-CIS experiment despite the much lower prevalence of high-risk cold entities.

These results suggest that scoring and ranking should be treated as separate problems in cold-start fraud detection. PTKR is intended to complement, rather than replace, existing ranking metrics in systems that already maintain uncertainty estimates.

title: Phantom Abatement Loop: Corporate Offsets, Public Project Pipelines, and the Financialization of Unverified Climate Outcomes

detail.title: Phantom Abatement Loop: Corporate Offsets, Public Project Pipelines, and the Financialization of Unverified Climate Outcomes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founder and Chief Architect of ENHANCE Institute / ENHANCE Inc., which developed the structural audit frameworks and datasets referenced in this paper and may in the future provide structural audit, training, or advisory services related to climate project integrity, transition finance, and pre-finance structural audit. No external sponsor, client, project developer, financial institution, public agency, or carbon-market participant commissioned, funded, reviewed, or approved this study. This paper does not propose ENHANCE Institute as the designated provider of Pre-Finance Structural Audit functions; the institutional criteria discussed in the paper are intended to apply to any qualified independent entity. The author declares no other personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the research.This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author at ENHANCE Institute / ENHANCE Inc. using publicly available institutional documents, climate finance disclosures, and author-developed structural audit datasets.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patients, interviews, surveys, experiments, personal data, or confidential institutional data. The analysis is based on publicly available documents, institutional reports, climate finance disclosures, and a stylized structural case illustration. The Producer A illustration is not a case study of any specific company or institution. Ethics approval and informed consent were therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author at ENHANCE Institute / ENHANCE Inc. using publicly available institutional documents, climate finance disclosures, and author-developed structural audit datasets.

detail.abstract:
This paper identifies and structurally defines the Phantom Abatement Loop — a self-reinforcing market mechanism in which corporate transition pressure is converted into offset demand, offset demand into project finance, project finance into reported abatement claims, and unverified abatement claims back into perceived transition progress. We argue that this loop is not an incidental market failure, but an endogenous outcome of three simultaneously operating forces: financed emissions disclosure pressure, the systemic protection of hard-to-abate emitters, and the expansion of publicly-legitimized climate project pipelines whose structural integrity is rarely tested at the level required for financial reliance.
The loop’s operative mechanism is not the direct reduction of financed emissions through offset accounting. Current financed-emissions methodologies do not generally allow external offsets to be deducted from attributed borrower emissions. Rather, the mechanism operates through the use of offset-based transition narratives to justify continued credit extension and additional liquidity provision to high-emission borrowers. When abatement claims enter credit assessment processes as qualitative signals of transition effort, rather than as verified physical outcomes, lending decisions may extend institutional exposure without delivering the emissions reductions that nominally justify them.
Drawing on ENHANCE Institute’s structural audit of 101 GGGI climate project disclosures, which produced an average structural integrity score of 0.41/1.00 under the ToC:f(x)™ framework, and its portfolio-level analysis of 352 GCF-approved projects, this paper provides preliminary empirical grounding for the supply-side risk embedded in the loop, while recognizing that the underlying structural audit methodology and project-level dataset remain subject to external replication and peer review. Many projects likely to populate future corporate offset pipelines are designed under ODA and development finance logics that do not necessarily require the causal closure, physical verifiability, or MRV precision necessary for credible abatement attribution. The gap between what such projects claim and what their causal architecture can deliver is therefore structural, not incidental.
We further identify the conditions under which the loop escalates into systemic financial risk: when unverified abatement claims are financialized as the underlying assets of carbon-linked structured products, performance-based instruments, transition finance facilities, or offset-backed credit decisions. At that point, project failure is no longer confined to the corporate balance sheet or lending portfolio. It may propagate through financial markets as mispriced climate risk.
The paper concludes that carbon abatement claims are not self-verifying. When they enter credit markets, they must be treated as conditional, structure-dependent, and auditable. We propose Pre-Finance Structural Audit as the necessary institutional response — functionally analogous to credit assessment prior to capital allocation — and identify the structural conditions such an audit function must satisfy before abatement claims are used as the basis for lending, investment, disclosure, or financial product design.

title: Supply Chain Common Analyst Network and Firm Digital Transformation
affiliations: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics,  and

detail.title: Supply Chain Common Analyst Network and Firm Digital Transformation
detail.abstract: Drawing on social network theory from an information perspective, we investigate how supply chain common analyst networks-where a focal firm and its customers share a common analyst-affect the focal firm's digital transformation. Using a large dataset of customer-supplier relationships, we find that the supply chain common analysts significantly enhance the digital transformation of focal firms. We argue that this positive effect arises from the improved focal firms' understanding of the customer needs through more effective and trustworthy information flow between the firm and its customers, facilitated by the common analyst. Furthermore, our results show that the positive impact of supply chain common analysts is weaker when analysts have lower motivation, such as in contexts of high environmental dynamism. Conversely, the effect is stronger when common analysts possess greater capability, as reflected in their historical forecasting accuracy. Our study contributes to the operations management literature on the role of supply chain relationships and extends understanding of the role of common analysts in shaping firm outcomes within supply chain networks.

title: Women's Empowerment and Environmental Efficiency in Smallholder Rice Production: Evidence from Bangladesh

detail.title: Women's Empowerment and Environmental Efficiency in Smallholder Rice Production: Evidence from Bangladesh
detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between women's empowerment and environmental efficiency using a directional distance function within a by-production DEA framework and a Simar-Wilson two-stage regression. We also report associated patterns in technical efficiency as part of the joint production process. Results show that overall empowerment is positively and significantly associated with environmental efficiency, but only weakly linked to technical efficiency. Domain-specific analysis reveals that empowerment in income, resources, and leadership domain enhances environmental efficiency. However, empowerment in the production domain is negatively associated, likely reflecting structural resource constraints and distress-led delegation of poorly resourced plots. The findings underscore that empowerment pathways are heterogeneous. Policies that strengthen women's decision-making capacity alongside equitable resource access may promote more climate-responsive and environmentally efficient smallholder systems.

title: Shadow Data in Higher Education: A Socio-technical Framework for Governing Unused and Under-managed Third-party Digital Assets
affiliations: Coastline Community College and Coastline College

detail.title: Shadow Data in Higher Education: A Socio-technical Framework for Governing Unused and Under-managed Third-party Digital Assets
detail.abstract: Higher education institutions operate through dense ecosystems of learning management systems, advising platforms, student success tools, remote proctoring services, customer relationship management applications, cloud productivity suites, tutoring platforms, library systems, assessment tools, vendor dashboards, and artificial intelligence services. These systems generate and retain large amounts of data that may be technically available to an institution but remain unused, inaccessible, low trust, weakly governed, or outside routine institutional stewardship. This article develops shadow data as a theoretical construct for higher education. Shadow data is defined as data generated, collected, stored, exported, integrated, or made available through institutional or third-party digital systems but not meaningfully accessed, analyzed, governed, or used because of quality, relevance, ownership, access, interoperability, privacy, ethical, contractual, or capacity constraints. The article distinguishes shadow data from dark data, shadow information technology, shadow artificial intelligence, data exhaust, and governed institutional data. It integrates sociotechnical systems theory, information governance, institutional theory, platformization, contextual integrity, learning analytics ethics, and responsible artificial intelligence governance to explain why shadow data emerges and why it matters. The article proposes a typology, conceptual model, theoretical propositions, practitioner checklist, and research agenda. It argues that shadow data is not only a technical backlog. It is a governance, privacy, equity, institutional effectiveness, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence readiness issue that requires lifecycle stewardship, vendor accountability, transparent data classification, and cross-functional institutional ownership.

title: The Digital Dead Hand and Autonomous Strategic Depth: The Paradox of Algorithmic Hegemony and Turkish Foreign Policy

detail.title: The Digital Dead Hand and Autonomous Strategic Depth: The Paradox of Algorithmic Hegemony and Turkish Foreign Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This study examines how Turkey’s process of integrating autonomous military systems and artificial intelligence serves as a model of “algorithmic neutrality” and “technical resistance” for the Global South against the West’s algorithmic hegemony. The research analyzes the potential systemic risks arising from this technological hegemony, including the deployment of “black box” decision-making systems, standardization crises within NATO (the Alliance Paradox), and the elimination of human-involved mechanisms in the field of diplomatic relations. The central argument posits that countries' individual efforts at technological sovereignty possess a destructive potential capable of triggering an uncontrolled escalation in conflict zones, which would ultimately create a “Digital Dead Hand” asymmetry and increase the risk of an “Algorithmic Petrov Event” in international relations.

title: Shadow AI in Higher Education: A Socio-technical Framework for Governing Unauthorized Employee use of Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: Coastline Community College and Coastline College

detail.title: Shadow AI in Higher Education: A Socio-technical Framework for Governing Unauthorized Employee use of Artificial Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There was no finances involved

declarations.funderStatement: The research was not funded

detail.abstract: Shadow AI-the use of artificial intelligence tools by employees without institutional approval, procurement review, or datagovernance oversight-is emerging rapidly across higher education as generative AI adoption outpaces institutional policy. This article argues that shadow AI is not principally a compliance failure but a socio-technical governance gap that appears when employee adoption advances faster than an institution's policy, procurement, training, cybersecurity review, and data-governance infrastructure. Drawing on the shadow information technology literature and contemporary research on artificial intelligence governance in higher education, the article advances a conceptual framework, The Shadow AI Adoption-Governance Gap Model, comprising seven dimensions: employee need and use pressure, institutional enablement gap, policy and governance ambiguity, risk awareness and data sensitivity, shadow AI behavior, institutional outcomes, and governance response. The framework is examined against an original 2026 survey of employees at a single two-year public college (50 valid respondents; an 18.9% response rate). Respondents reported high self-assessed AI literacy (98.0% understood basic AI concepts) and strong demand for additional training (84.0%), yet preferred external consumer tools-ChatGPT (72.0%), Google Gemini, Claude, and Microsoft Copilot-none of which were the institution's three sanctioned platforms. Interpreted through the model, this pattern points less to low risk awareness than to institutional enablement gaps and policy ambiguity. The article offers risk-tiered governance recommendations and a practitioner readiness checklist, arguing that institutions should move employees from hidden AI use toward transparent, supported, and ethically governed practice. Because the survey is single-institution and self-reported, the findings are interpretive rather than confirmatory.

title: Having Backbone: Regime Dependence in SABR Tenor Interpolation

detail.title: Having Backbone: Regime Dependence in SABR Tenor Interpolation
detail.abstract: The construction of a continuous implied volatility surface from SABR smiles calibrated at a discrete set of market tenors requires the interpolation of those smiles to non-pillar maturities, a problem for which the literature offers several competing methods but no systematic comparative assessment. In this paper we provide such an assessment, benchmarking parameter-space interpolation in piecewise-constant, linear, cubic-spline, and exponential-polynomial form against total-variance interpolation with subsequent recalibration and Gaussian-process regression of the parameter term structures, evaluating each method on the accuracy of recovered implied volatilities and on the static-arbitrage consistency of the interpolated slices. The assessment is conducted across two simulated data-generating processes - one model-consistent and one drawn from the rough volatility literature - and its predictions are checked for consistency against market-observed volatility surfaces. The central findings of this paper are that: once the data-generating process departs from the SABR family, surface-space and probabilistic methods dominate across every regime; the backbone elasticity $\beta$ is of second-order importance to the choice of method; and that the classical exponential-polynomial parametrisation is found throughout to be the least robust to model misspecification and the most prone to calendar-spread violations.

title: Causal Separation, Conditional Risk, and Projected Markowitz Portfolios
affiliations: University of Reading

detail.title: Causal Separation, Conditional Risk, and Projected Markowitz Portfolios
detail.abstract: We formalize a single structural condition on a portfolio problem, causal separation: conditional on the realized path of a declared set of drivers through the investment horizon, asset returns are mutually independent. From this condition we derive the complete static portfolio theory it induces. Separation forces a diagonal-plus-low-rank conditional covariance through an exact tower decomposition, with the low-rank block identified as the response to driver innovations, and the constrained mean-variance problem admits a closed-form projected Markowitz solution in which the classical information matrix is replaced by its projection onto the constraint-compatible subspace. We prove uniqueness of the minimal sufficient separator as an information set; invariance of all derived objects under separator equivalence and reparametrization of the driver state; a conditional efficient-frontier theorem; a Hansen-Jagannathan bound whose gap to the unconstrained bound is an exact quadratic form in the shadow prices of the constraint geometry; a conditioning bound showing that separation regularizes estimation through the idiosyncratic variance floor; an exact two-stage solver whose cost is linear in the number of assets; and exact first-order sensitivity bounds under approximate separation at a certified tolerance. The causal content of the framework is stated and proved rather than assumed: under an explicit structural margin the common causes form a separator, observational data identify their realized information and nothing more, causal and correlational separators of equal fit are distinguished by interventions on non-parents, and an unexplained common cause leaves a quantifiable floor on the dependence diagnostic, so latent confounding is detected rather than absorbed. Seven reproducible experiments validate the theory, with five structural identities holding at machine precision, and quantify its practical content: out-of-sample estimation risk against sample, shrinkage and principal-component covariances, robustness under injected residual dependence, invariance under an intervention that collapses a correlational alternative, and computational scaling to thousands of assets.

title: When Appearance Replaces Proof: Artificial-Intelligence-Assisted Evidence in Indonesian Criminal Procedure

detail.title: When Appearance Replaces Proof: Artificial-Intelligence-Assisted Evidence in Indonesian Criminal Procedure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is normative legal research (doctrinal study) that does not involve human or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: With the aid of artificial intelligence, a document can be accused of being forged so convincingly that the accusation spreads and comes to appear commonly known, as in the widely publicized case concerning an alleged forged diploma. Conversely, artificial intelligence can create something that appears to be recorded although it never happened, as in the deepfake-content case tried by the Semarang District Court. Two events running in opposite directions, one fragility. This article names it trust in appearance (appearance-trust), and shows that it occupies two neighbouring provisions in Indonesian criminal procedure: notorious facts (fakta notoire) under Article 184(2) of the 1981 Criminal Procedure Code in conjunction with Article 235(2) of Law No. 20 of 2025, which trusts what is commonly known, and electronic evidence under Article 235(3) to (5) of the same law, which trusts what is recorded. The age of artificial intelligence undermines both at once. So long as procedural law lacks objective criteria to test AI-assisted claims about the authenticity or the notoriety of a piece of evidence, cases are decided on impression - and a decision resting on impression can oppress the truthful as harshly as it acquits the guilty. This normative legal research diagnoses that fragility and shows that appearance can be disciplined into a tested test through objective criteria traceable to their source, as has already been demonstrated in the doctrine of notorious facts, while pointing toward a direction for regulating AI-assisted evidence.

title: Deep Learning for Dynamic Programming with Recursive Utility
affiliations: Peking University - HSBC School of Business and

detail.title: Deep Learning for Dynamic Programming with Recursive Utility

declarations.funderStatement: The research is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 72573011).

detail.abstract: We propose the first deep learning algorithm, the Certainty Equivalent Learning (CEL) algorithm, for solving high-dimensional discrete-time dynamic programming problems with recursive utility. Dynamic programming with recursive utility is numerically challenging because the recursive utility does not have an explicit representation and the Bellman equation contains a certainty equivalent that is difficult to evaluate. The CEL algorithm learns this certainty equivalent value directly with neural networks and jointly approximates value functions, policy functions, and certainty equivalent functions. The CEL algorithm is mesh-free and simulation-based, allowing high-dimensional state and control spaces, and does not rely on Euler equations, first-order conditions, or differentiability of the state transition function. The CEL algorithm also works for dynamic programming problems with expected utility as expected utility is a special case of recursive utility. We apply the CEL to discounted linear exponential quadratic Gaussian control, small-noise robust control, Epstein-Zin DSGE, and multivariate strategic asset allocation problems. Compared with closed-form and VFI-based benchmarks, the CEL delivers accurate value and policy approximations, remains effective in high-dimensional problems, achieves accuracy comparable to VFI in the small-noise robust-control case, and produces out-of-sample Bellman errors and Euler or first-order residuals that are in the range from 1.0e-4 to 1.0e−3 for most problems.

title: Welkin Foods Case: Supreme Court Resets India’s Commodity Classification for Taxation Laws
affiliations: Supreme Court of India

detail.title: Welkin Foods Case: Supreme Court Resets India’s Commodity Classification for Taxation Laws
detail.abstract: In its recent decision the Supreme Court of India has examined the applicable rules governing classification of goods – both statutory stipulations and judicial principles – to contextualise their extent and inter se application. The decision pivots the hitherto prevailing understanding of the interpretative principles to determine the commodity classification and thus it is critical to appreciate the contours of the decision which has a direct bearing on application of Indian taxation laws, particularly Customs and GST.

title: An Islamic Finance Eurozone Headquarters in Ireland—Is Enough Done to Ensure that Middle East Investment Streams through the International Financial Services Centre in Ireland?

detail.title: An Islamic Finance Eurozone Headquarters in Ireland—Is Enough Done to Ensure that Middle East Investment Streams through the International Financial Services Centre in Ireland?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Faiza Ismail, 'An Islamic Finance Eurozone Headquarters in Ireland—Is Enough Done to Ensure that Middle East Investment Streams through the International Financial Services Centre in Ireland?' (2013) 20(1) Commercial Law Practitioner 7

detail.abstract: This article evaluates Ireland's strategy for positioning itself as a Eurozone headquarters for Islamic finance, in the context of the country's broader efforts to attract foreign direct investment following the 2008 financial crisis and subsequent EU-IMF bailout programme. The article is structured in three parts. Part A outlines the objectives set by Ireland's Department of Finance for developing an Islamic finance industry domestically — including attracting Middle Eastern investment, offering ethical investment alternatives, and serving Ireland's Muslim population — and examines the Finance Act 2010's introduction of "Specified Financial Transactions" to provide equal tax treatment for Islamic finance products such as Murabaha, Mudaraba, Musharaka, Sukuk, and Takaful. Part B benchmarks Ireland's regulatory approach against that of the United Kingdom, which has emerged as the leading Western hub for Islamic finance, highlighting persistent gaps in Ireland's framework — particularly the absence of stamp duty relief for credit transactions (unlike the UK's Finance Act 2003) and unresolved legal uncertainty regarding the interpretation of Sharia-governed contracts in Irish courts, illustrated by reference to the English case of Beximco Pharmaceuticals Ltd v Shamil Bank of Bahrain EC. Part C offers policy recommendations, including a comprehensive review of Ireland's tax regime modeled on comparable reviews conducted in the UK, Australia, and Hong Kong; stronger institutional networking with Gulf state financial authorities; public awareness campaigns targeting market participants; and increased investment in academic research on Islamic finance at Irish universities. The article concludes that while Ireland has taken meaningful first steps, more decisive government action is required to realize its ambition of becoming a genuine gateway for Middle Eastern investment into the Eurozone.

title: The Ethics of Migration in the Long Run
affiliations: Université Paris Cité

detail.title: The Ethics of Migration in the Long Run
detail.abstract: In the contemporary ethics of immigration, the "conventional view" is often assumed to be restrictionist: the claim that states have a moral right to control immigration. But has this view always been considered "conventional"? A review of major political theories on human mobility and political power, from the 16th to the18th century, suggests not. The restrictionist view on immigration was far from being the "conventional view." Instead, freedom of movement was supported across a wide range of political theories, both rights-based and consequentialist. During the 16th-17th centuries, denying innocent people their freedom of movement was seen as an injustice, an unjustified hostility, and therefore a potential justification for retaliating with war. In the 17th-18th centuries, sovereigns were commonly advised to attract immigrants and discourage emigration. Consequentialist arguments drawn from mercantilism, physiocracy, and classical economics often favoured liberal mobility policies. The rediscovery of this intellectual history challenges the assumption that immigration control is the natural or default starting point for normative debate. It demonstrates both that restrictionism is a historically contingent and relatively recent position, and that freedom of movement is a topic that has been strikingly neglected in contemporary political theory.

title: Eradication of Money Laundering: A Reality or a Dream?

detail.title: Eradication of Money Laundering: A Reality or a Dream?

contentType.other: It is a work in process

detail.abstract: Switzerland's compliance with FATF's recommendations cost it, well-established privacy laws which were developed to facilitate an offshore center (OFC) whereas Pakistan had to deal with enormous economic losses and reputational damage to ensure compliance with FATF's recommendations. Interestingly neither Switzerland nor Pakistan can present any empirical data that would act as evidence of completely eradicating money laundering from their financial system. FATF's efforts to curb money laundering globally are undoubtedly extraordinary, however, their effectiveness requires empirical data particularly in the context of grey listed countries that have been penalized and released based on a system that has not been able to prove successful.

title: Duopoly Model with Asymmetric Buyer Distribution
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Duopoly Model with Asymmetric Buyer Distribution
detail.abstract: We introduce asymmetric buyer distribution into a traditional duopoly model to study its impact on equilibria both in price-setting competition and quantity-setting competition. We show that non-negative output constraints become binding when products are close enough substitutes and buyer distribution is asymmetric enough. When these constraints are binding, a rival firm with less than 50% buyer distribution effectively exists the market and monopoly profit is accrued to the surviving firm. Since pricesetting competition is more intense than quantity-setting competition, the market exit occurs with less asymmetric buyer distribution in price-setting competition than in quantity-setting competition. Therefore, the reversal of usual profit ranking can arise in the sense that the surviving firm in price competition earns monopoly profit in price-setting competition while the same firm earns much less duopoly profit in quantity-setting competition. Moreover, three distinct limit equilibria are identified in price-setting competition with perfect substitutes and symmetric buyer distribution. These results highlight an important role played by buyer distribution.

title: Unknown Buyer Distribution between Two Markets, Choice of Price or Quantity in Monopoly
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Unknown Buyer Distribution between Two Markets, Choice of Price or Quantity in Monopoly
detail.abstract: In manufactured durable product markets, sellers regularly launch multiple grades/trims within the same product category to capture a wider range of buyers. In such a situation, a seller needs to evaluate to what extent buyers would be distributed among multiple grades of the product. Suppose a monopolist chooses either price or quantity of all grades simultaneously subject to incomplete information about unknown distribution of buyers. We find that the equilibrium profit is strictly higher in price-setting mode than in quantity-setting mode as long as the buyer distribution remains unknown ex ante. In addition, a price-setting monopolist's profit is unaffected in the presence of uncertainty but a quantitysetting monopolist's profit decreases as the degree of uncertainty rises. In the limit case of maximal uncertainty where one grade capturing 100% share of buyers or 0% share of buyers, a quantitysetting monopolist earns zero expected profit but a price-setting monopolist earns positive expected profit. These results arise because a quantity-setting monopolist's price elasticity approaches to infinity while a price-setting monopolist's price elasticity remains constant.

title: Longitudinal Capitation: A Mechanism Design to Cure Asymmetric Information and Strategic Gaming Applied to Medicare Managed Care

detail.title: Longitudinal Capitation: A Mechanism Design to Cure Asymmetric Information and Strategic Gaming Applied to Medicare Managed Care

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: No Ethical Considerations.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Traditional capitated health insurance contracts suffer from acute information asymmetry, incentivizing strategic diagnostic upcoding and rent-seeking over genuine clinical care management. This paper utilizes a mechanism design framework to model optimal plan behavior under a novel contract structure: Longitudinal Capitation. We introduce a multidimensional, zero-sum, market-clearing progression metric paired with a utilization financial shield. The mechanism formally reverses the information asymmetry. Solving the joint optimization problem proves that a single regulatory lever simultaneously eliminates excess coding intensity and expands clinical management effort to achieve the first-best social optimum. Converting risk adjustment into a dynamic progression vector aligns corporate solvency with verifiable disease velocity decrease. This design collapses the traditional multitasking principal-agent conflict, eliminating systemic data gaming while protecting fiscal sustainability.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the discount rate applicable to the calculation of the economic benefit of noncompliance — known in Peru as beneficio ilícito or Factor B — in environmental administrative fines imposed by the Agency for Environmental Assessment and Enforcement (OEFA). It argues that the rate used to capitalize avoided or deferred compliance costs must reflect both the economic logic of the benefit calculation and the legal constraints governing administrative sanctions. Although OEFA’s penalty methodology was historically influenced by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s BEN model and by technical documents that point to the weighted average cost of capital (WACC), OEFA has applied sectoral opportunity cost rates associated with the cost of equity. This paper argues that WACC is generally a more reasonable benchmark for for-profit companies because it reflects the actual structure of corporate financing, including both debt and equity. It also argues that, where reliable information is available, the discount rate should be tailored to the regulated entity or to the specific business unit in which the violation occurred, and that sectoral rates must be updated to reflect current economic conditions. The analysis is grounded in the principles of reasonableness, material truth, less burdensome administrative action, and adequate reasoning.

title: Leaving the Shell behind: Strategic Offloading and Reputation Whitewashing by Fund Managers
affiliations: Beijing Normal University (BNU),  and Beijing Normal University (BNU)

detail.title: Leaving the Shell behind: Strategic Offloading and Reputation Whitewashing by Fund Managers
detail.abstract: We study reputation management by mutual fund managers who simultaneously manage multiple funds and strategically resign from poorly performing ones while retaining other products. We provide empirical evidence of this strategic offloading, showing that managers with both star and dog funds are significantly more likely to offload underperforming products than other managers. This behavior selectively improves managers' observed aggregate performance and attracts substantial capital inflows. However, these inflows are followed by a significant deterioration in future performance. We show that strategic offloading weakens the traditional "performance-flow" mechanism by decoupling observed performance from true managerial ability. The effectiveness of this strategy stems from investors' limited attention, memory bias, and more broadly biased beliefs about managerial ability, which cause investors to focus on managers' current product sets while neglecting offloaded poor performers. Overall, our findings uncover a novel agency conflict in which fund managers strategically exploit investor belief distortions to expand fund scale at the expense of investor performance.

title: The Economic Returns to Business Master’s Degrees and Heterogeneity Across Undergraduate Majors
affiliations: Purdue University

detail.title: The Economic Returns to Business Master’s Degrees and Heterogeneity Across Undergraduate Majors

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: Deidentified data
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: Graduate business schools in the United States often offer programmes for both the master of business administration (MBA) degree and master's degrees in specialized business fields (non-MBA); yet little evidence exists on how the economic returns of these options compare or how the earnings premiums they offer vary across undergraduate majors. Using nationally representative data from the 2019 National Survey of College Graduates, we estimate earnings differentials associated with the MBA and non-MBA business degrees while allowing returns to vary by undergraduate major. We make two contributions. First, we distinguish between MBA and non-MBA degrees in a single modelling framework and show that MBAs are associated with larger average earnings premiums. Second, we document substantial heterogeneity across undergraduate majors: graduates from lower-earning fields tend to experience larger relative gains than those in higher-earning fields like engineering and technology. We then test potential mechanisms and find that business master's degree holders are significantly more likely to work in managerial positions, at larger firms, and in for-profit sectors. These findings highlight an important distinction between MBA and non-MBA business programmes and suggest that the economic returns to these degrees depends on students' undergraduate major.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the legal and financial consequences of valuing mine post-closure measures under a perpetuity scenario in Peru. Supreme Decree No. 006-2025-EM amended the Regulation for Mine Closure and removed the prior possibility of entrusting the State with the continuation of certain post-closure measures after issuance of the final closure certificate. Under the current framework, the mining titleholder remains responsible for post-closure until physical, geochemical, and hydrological stability is demonstrated and the Final Closure Certificate is obtained. The paper argues that, as a result, the full cost of post-closure measures — including measures projected for more than thirty years and therefore treated as perpetual under the regulation — must be incorporated into the Mine Closure Plan budget and covered by the corresponding environmental guarantee. It further analyzes the financial implications of valuing perpetuities with nominal inflation and discount rates published by the Ministry of Energy and Mines, the problem that arises when inflation exceeds the discount rate, and the possibility of using a defined-horizon annuity or a constant-value methodology when standard perpetuity formulas would produce an indefinite or economically unreasonable present value. The analysis is grounded in legality, reasonableness, financial assurance, and the need for technically robust methodologies in mine closure regulation.

affiliations: Harvard Business School
