detail.abstract: This paper interprets Hikma’s activation of “actively” from § 271(b) in a series of four Supreme Court inducement decisions from 2005–2015, proposes a three-factor test for what constitutes encouragement, and tests it on a survey of Federal Circuit decisions.

title: Through the Hidden States: Synthetic Latent Supervision for Cold-start Financial Prediction
affiliations: Middle East Technical University

detail.title: Through the Hidden States: Synthetic Latent Supervision for Cold-start Financial Prediction
detail.abstract: Financial prediction has a cold-start problem: a newly listed asset trades actively from its first minute, and a structural break resets an established asset to the same condition-a dense, information-rich tape but only a handful of trustworthy forecast labels. We target this cold-start regime (𝑏 ≲ 10 target labels) directly. Our approach, market decompression, separates the two tasks a direct learner must solve with one small budget: it first learns to recover a hidden market state from the tape, supervised by instrumented synthetic worlds where that state is directly observed, and only then fits a small forecast head on real labels. The paper makes four contributions. First, a supervision-privilege identity isolates the mechanism: decompression improves log-risk when privileged information transferred by the synthetic prior exceeds the representation bottleneck. Second, we introduce the transfer field 𝐹 𝑅 𝑏 (𝜃)-the expected log-risk improvement of decompression over a matched direct forecaster as a function of source-world parameters 𝜃-and its positive-transfer envelope, the positive level set that separates useful from harmful synthetic supervision. Third, a computable predictive layer turns the field into a deployment tool: posterior transfer probability, an effective label-equivalence estimator, envelope-volume statistics, and a retrospective validation showing the surrogate posterior predicted which candidates would confirm. Fourth, a raw-label-equivalent recovery law yields six falsifiable predictions, and all six are confirmed. In controlled synthetic markets, decompression improves normalized MSE by 7-9% at five labels. On real BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT, and SOLUSDT markets, independent frozen confirmation-fully disjoint from discoveryidentifies priors delivering 6.3% and 7.2% pooled MSE reductions at five labels (one-sided 𝑝 = 0.021, robust to conservative basket-level testing), confirms predicted negative transfer from mismatched priors, and establishes that transfer fields are marketspecific: the field, not any single prior, is the portable object.

title: Data-Driven Predictive Maintenance Model Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Continuous Process Industries: A Case Study of Coal Power Plant Paiton
affiliations: , Institut Teknologi Sepuluh Nopember and Sepuluh Nopember Institute of Technology

detail.title: Data-Driven Predictive Maintenance Model Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Continuous Process Industries: A Case Study of Coal Power Plant Paiton
detail.abstract: This study addresses the critical challenge of implementing effective predictive maintenance (PdM) strategies in continuous process industries, specifically focusing on power generation facilities. Despite the routine implementation of PdM activities, functional failures continue to occur unexpectedly in industrial equipment. Using historical Computerized Maintenance Management System (CMMS) data spanning 5.5 years (2017-2022) from PT PJB CPP Paiton Unit 9, East Java, Indonesia, this research develops data-driven PdM models using Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) techniques. The study analyzes Circulating Water Pump-A (CWP-A) equipment with 229 work orders, implementing data preprocessing, semantic similarity analysis using LSTM and S-BERT, curve-fitting analysis, and multiple ML/DL classification models including LSTM, Random Forest, and Decision Tree. Results demonstrate that LSTM-based semantic similarity analysis successfully identifies 14 correlated functional failures (66.67% of total failures), despite 16 routine PdM activities. The developed LSTM classification model achieves 100% accuracy across four data split scenarios, while Random Forest attains near 100% accuracy and Decision Tree achieves 87.5% accuracy. Weibull analysis reveals equipment reliability of 76.80% with MTTF of 2299.69 hours, following a Weibull 3-parameter distribution with Decreasing Failure Rate (DFR). The recommended maintenance frequency is optimized from routine intervals to every 26 days between overhauls. This research contributes to bridging the gap between routine PdM implementation and actual failure prevention in continuous process industries, providing actionable insights for industrial reliability improvement.

title: Revisiting Five Decades of African Regional Integration: Has Globalization Overstated the Trade Effects of Regional Trade Agreements?

detail.title: Revisiting Five Decades of African Regional Integration: Has Globalization Overstated the Trade Effects of Regional Trade Agreements?

declarations.funderStatement: The author received no funding for this research

detail.abstract: This paper reexamines the trade effects of African Regional Trade Agreements (RTAs) through the broader lens of globalization. Existing studies generally attribute Africa's trade expansion to regional integration while assuming that the trade-impeding effects of international borders and geography remain constant over time. Using a structural gravity model estimated by Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood (PPML) on a panel of 122 countries covering 1960-2021, this paper allows the effects of international borders and effective distance to evolve, thereby separating the contribution of regional integration from broader globalization forces. The results show that RTAs increased intra-African trade by approximately 670% when border and geographic frictions are assumed constant. However, once these frictions are allowed to vary over time, the estimated long-run effect falls to about 260%, indicating that a substantial share of Africa's trade growth reflects declining border frictions and reduced effective distance rather than regional integration alone. The analysis also uncovers significant trade diversion after accounting for globalization and shows that the estimated RTA effects are robust to alternative data intervals and sample periods. Moreover, the analysis found a smaller trade effect in the post-WTO period than in the pre-WTO period, suggesting that accelerating globalization has reduced the incremental contribution of RTAs to trade growth. These findings demonstrate that conventional gravity models systematically overstate the trade effects of African RTAs by conflating regional integration with broader globalization-induced reductions in trade frictions.

title: Conceptualising an Integrity or Fourth Branch of Government in Aotearoa New Zealand: Promoting Probity in Governance and Safeguarding Constitutional Democracy
affiliations: Victoria University of Wellington, Te Herenga Waka - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Conceptualising an Integrity or Fourth Branch of Government in Aotearoa New Zealand: Promoting Probity in Governance and Safeguarding Constitutional Democracy
detail.abstract: In this paper, I explore the concept of an ‘integrity’ or ‘fourth’ branch of government in Aotearoa New Zealand and its role in promoting the health of the nation’s constitutional democracy. The notion of a fourth branch of government capturing institutions, other than the judicial branch, charged with ensuring integrity and probity by other branches has emerged in comparative constitutional and other scholarship. This paper builds on this work and conceptualises the nature and shape of an integrity or fourth branch in New Zealand in the light of its distinctive constitutional framework and traditions. I draw together the conceptual framing of a fourth or integrity branch and these distinctive constitutional settings in order to imagine how this relatively novel branch might be realised in New Zealand. I conclude this paper by explaining the virtue of realising this institutional collective as a branch of government — conceptually as part of our constitutional imagination and understanding of the anatomy of systems of democracy,  practically in its promotion of the health of our constitutional democracy and institutionally in the operation and reform of the integrity bodies included within it.

title: Resistance to Assimilation: Land Claims as a Proxy to Indigeneity and Sovereignty Between Lesotho and South Africa

detail.title: Resistance to Assimilation: Land Claims as a Proxy to Indigeneity and Sovereignty Between Lesotho and South Africa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interests
declarations.funderStatement: The current study did not recieve any external funding

detail.abstract: The interests and political shift in Lesotho, particularly in relation to the identity of Basotho and what it means to resist assimilation into South Africa contributes to the discourse and underlying nuances of the land claims rhetoric. The perspective that it is only economic factors which bear greater meaning to this discourse necessitates the emergence of a new conceptual approach to the idea of land claims in relation to Basotho. It is thus in this line of view that this essay seeks to contribute that there is a conceptual disjuncture in regard to this discourse.

title: Three Strikes Against Political Antitrust
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - School of Law and Princeton University - Princeton School of Public and International Affairs

detail.title: Three Strikes Against Political Antitrust
detail.abstract: In recent years, there have been numerous calls to expand antitrust law beyond the sphere of economics and use it to address the democratic harms that flow from economic concentration and inequality. We agree that concentration and inequality may have adverse consequences for democratic governance, but we offer three reasons to be cautious about using antitrust law as a remedy. First, the nature of democratic harms and their relation to market concentration is not well understood. The most direct hypothesized relationships between economic and political concentration have not withstood empirical scrutiny, and other invocations of democratic harms remain elusive. Second, based on what social scientists know about the political role of business, antitrust law does not seem well equipped to address political harms. The focus on corporate titans reveals a blind spot about the political influence of other businesses, which the anti-bigness thrust of political antitrust will leave untouched or even enhance. Finally, far from putting the law in service of a common vision of democratic governance, incorporating political goals into antitrust would empower politicians of different parties and ideological persuasions to use the law as a tool to advance their narrow political agendas.

title: Mandatory Reconsideration ‘By Another Name’? Re-Determination in the Scottish Social Security System
affiliations: School of Law, University of Glasgow

detail.title: Mandatory Reconsideration ‘By Another Name’? Re-Determination in the Scottish Social Security System
detail.abstract: A prominent feature of the modern United Kingdom social security system is what is described as ‘mandatory reconsideration’, whereby a person wishing to appeal a range of benefits decisions must first request that the decision in question is reconsidered by the decision-maker, and possibly revised as a result. Though the requirement of such mandatory reconsideration has been widely criticised, a similar scheme has been adopted within the system of devolved social security constructed in Scotland after 2016, under the name of ‘mandatory re-determination’. This article considers the UK approach to the matter, before turning to the Scottish equivalent and its evolution in the years since the (partial) devolution of social security. It considers, in particular, the compatibility of the requirement of ‘mandatory re-determination’ with the idea that the devolved system of social security in Scotland represents a fundamental break from the key characteristics of modern social security at the UK level. It argues that the available evidence suggests that despite important differences between them, mandatory re-determination replicates at least some of the problems identified in the system of mandatory reconsideration.

title: The Riemann-Polya  Density as a Γ(2) Mixture
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Riemann-Polya  Density as a Γ(2) Mixture
detail.abstract: The Riemann–P´olya kernel decomposes, cell by cell on the half-line, as a mixture of Gamma(2, λ) densities ue−λu, the building block being e −ku = R ∞ k ue−λu dλ. Two facts make this the natural representation. By Steutel’s conjecture (Kristiansen, 1994) a positive mixture of Γ(α) laws is infinitely divisible exactly when α ∈ (0, 2], so Γ(2) is the threshold shape at which positivity of the mixing measure alone secures infinite divisibility. And that mixing measure is positive: our main result proves it, through the observation that 1−ym m(1−y) (with y = n−1 n ) is the mean of the first m powers of y, which turns an apparently signed alternating series into a monotone Leibniz series. Equivalently each cell kernel is completely monotone after division by u, and is a positive superposition of Gumbel densities. We then recast the problem through the square-root substitution, working throughout with the measure M rather than with gamma variables. The function H(s) = ξ( 1 2 + √ s) has all zeros on (−∞, 0) iff RH, and its reciprocal H(0)/H(s) is the Laplace transform of a generalized gamma convolution (GGC), equivalently one with a positive Thorin measure, exactly when RH holds. The identity 1 − cos θ = 2 sin2 ( θ 2 ) converts the oscillatory L´evy density of the critical strip into a signdefinite integral into which the proved positivity feeds; the squaring map identifies the degenerate bilateral P´olya-frequency problem for the even kernel with the tractable one-sided GGC problem for H; and the Nevanlinna–Pick criterion reduces RH to a single classical statement: the Pick function H′ /H has no poles off its cut (−∞, 0]. This is a working note, not a proof. The cell-wise positivity is proved and the reduction is exact; moreover the correctly assembled global density is explicit, Ψ(u) = 1 2 e −u/4 − e u/4ψ(e u ) with ψ the Jacobi theta, and its mixing measure is again positive. But positivity of a Γ(2) mixture is infinite divisibility, whereas reality of all the zeros is total positivity (PF∞), preserved under convolution and not under mixing, equivalently, the Stieltjes property of H′ /H, the no-off-cut-pole condition. Bridging that gap, from a positive mixture to total positivity, is equivalent to RH and is not carried out here.

title: Conditional and Marginal SNP-heritability to Leverage Ancestral and Environmental Diversity
affiliations: University of California San Diego Halıcıoğlu Data Science Institute, Israel Institute of Technology and University of California San Diego Halıcıoğlu Data Science Institute

detail.title: Conditional and Marginal SNP-heritability to Leverage Ancestral and Environmental Diversity
detail.abstract: SNP-heritability is defined as the fraction of variance of a trait that is explained by the SNPs in a genome-wide association study. Several methodologies have been proposed to estimate this quantity. More recent methods aim to do so with ancestrally diverse datasets and yet obtain a single heritability for an entire dataset, which we refer to as marginal heritability. However, the different underlying subpopulations that compose a genetically diverse dataset might have different environmental and genetic exposures, and thus may have different heritabilities. In order to address this, we propose a conditional SNP-heritability approach that allows to estimate multiple SNP-heritabilities on a dataset corresponding to different ancestral compositions and environmental exposures. We take a careful statistical approach, including estimation of conditional genetic and environmental variances, and calculation of standard errors via a combination of the delta method with bootstrapping. We validate our method via extensive simulations. We then apply it to an ancestrally  and socio-economically diverse dataset of 6623 subjects aged around 9 to 11 from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, and illustrate how the SNP-heritability of intelligence scores can change due to differing extrinsic variances in different socio-economic groups, which coincides with previous work in the literature. This conditional estimation approach can be a valuable tool for understanding differences in risks across subpopulations. Our work here improves on existing methodology and allows us to leverage the heterogeneity of the data to obtain more granular insights.

title: Judicial Review of Prosecutorial Power in Nepal
affiliations: Far Western University

detail.title: Judicial Review of Prosecutorial Power in Nepal

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study utilizes purely doctrinal legal research methodologies, analyzing publicly available statutory frameworks, constitutional provisions, and judicial precedents. It does not involve any human participants, patients, or field-based clinical trials, and therefore did not require formal institutional bioethics committee approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was conducted entirely using self-funded personal resources and institutional access provided by the university.

detail.abstract:
Article 158 of the Constitution of Nepal vests the Attorney General with the final authority to decide whether a criminal case shall be instituted on behalf of the Government. The word final has supplied successive officeholders with a constitutional shelter that, on its face, looks beyond the reach of judicial review. The reality is less tidy. The Supreme Court has, across a quarter-century of writ petitions, traced the outer limits of that finality and produced a body of jurisprudence that oscillates between strong deference and assertive intervention. This dissertation maps whether the existing case law can be assembled into a principled standard of review.

The study is doctrinal. It reads the constitutional text alongside the Muluki Criminal Procedure Code, the Government Cases Act, the Government Attorneys Rules, the Code of Conduct for Government Attorneys, and the National Prosecution Policy. It then examines reported decisions of the Supreme Court of Nepal jurisprudence within the comparative experience.

Three findings emerge. First, the framework supplies clear constitutional and statutory anchors for review, principally Articles 133, 20, 21, and 22 read with sections 31, 32, and 116 of the Muluki Criminal Procedure Code. Second, the Court has developed an eight-part doctrine a core rule of deference; four  exceptions covering victim access to justice, transitional-justice obstruction of investigation, and reviewability of pardon and amnesty for jus cogens violations; a procedural scaffolding on evidentiary sufficiency and reverse burdens; the use of structural mandamus; and the delegation doctrine that preserves the professional autonomy of subordinate government attorneys. Third, the architecture is under-theorised rather than under-powered; the recent clean-chit, mass-withdrawal, and attempted legislative-relaxation episodes show that gaps remain in its consolidation and application.

The dissertation concludes that the Article 158 finality is structural, not immunising; that the Court possesses the doctrinal vocabulary to consolidate a coherent standard of review along the lines of the Matalulu test received in comparative Commonwealth practice; and that a calibrated package of constitutional, statutory, administrative, and doctrinal reforms is required to translate that potential into ordinary practice. Recommendations are addressed to the constituent authority, Parliament, the Office of the Attorney General, the Supreme Court, the Nepal Bar, and civil society.

title: Measuring Capital Elasticity: A Framework for Bank Capital Planning Under Basel III Finalization

detail.title: Measuring Capital Elasticity: A Framework for Bank Capital Planning Under Basel III Finalization
detail.abstract: Basel III finalization is narrowing opportunities for capital optimization through internal models and increasing the importance of standardized capital constraints in bank capital planning. As traditional optimization levers decline in strategic value, capital planning needs to place greater weight on whether capital can still be adjusted or repositioned under a more rule-based regulatory regime. This article introduces the Strategic Capital Elasticity Framework (SCEF) to evaluate where capital remains flexible, where it is constrained, and where it may become difficult to move. The framework decomposes capital elasticity into four components: model elasticity, portfolio elasticity, product elasticity, and client elasticity. It then applies these components through a Capital Elasticity Score (CES) and a Structural Lock-in Test to identify where capital is difficult to reprice, restructure, reduce, or redeploy. These tools help senior management, boards, and relevant risk or capital committees distinguish between capital that is merely large and capital that is not readily adjustable. The article argues that capital planning should incorporate not only capital adequacy, risk-weighted asset attribution, and stress resilience, but also practical adjustability of capital. The framework has implications for risk appetite, balance sheet allocation, pricing discipline, capital deployment decisions, and supervisory assessment of systemic effects.

title: A Universal Sufficient Statistic for Health Financing Policy

detail.title: A Universal Sufficient Statistic for Health Financing Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available, de-identified secondary data from the World Bank Microdata Library, WHO Global Health Expenditure Database, and published replication files. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Micro studies of health interventions report substantial returns while macro studies find null effects. This paper identifies a financing burden channel: out-of-pocket expenditure depletes complementary inputs, attenuating productivity gains. We estimate a neutralization threshold of 11.16 percent of household income. This threshold is validated across Nigeria, Kenya, and the United States using distinct identification strategies; all yield estimates between 10.6 and 11.2 percent (p=1.000 for equality). The framework predicts coefficients from seven influential studies with correlation-0.94. Globally, 78 percent of countries exceed the threshold. Health financing reform is prerequisite for capturing returns that health investments are designed to deliver.

title: Text-based Environmental Shocks and Sovereign Risk
affiliations: Central South University, Central South University, Central South University, University of Liverpool - Management School (ULMS) and University of Portsmouth

detail.title: Text-based Environmental Shocks and Sovereign Risk
detail.abstract: The impact of broad environmental issues on sovereign risk remains less understood. We apply machine learning methods to extract country-level environmental shocks from global news articles. We document that non-climate shocks, such as those related to energy, natural capital, and pollution, robustly predict wider CDS spreads. This positive predictive relationship is associated with multiple types of environmental events, displays significant heterogeneity across regions and economic conditions, and persists over long horizons without reversal, reflecting adjustments in both sovereign default risk and investor risk compensation. In addition, we show that environmental shocks predict worsening macroeconomic conditions and that their impact is amplified by global attention to environmental issues. Our results are robust to various machine learning and textual analysis approaches.

title: BBCH-Based Codification of Vegetative and Reproductive Phenology in European Pear cultivars (Pyrus communis L.) under Sub-Himalayan Conditions of India
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: BBCH-Based Codification of Vegetative and Reproductive Phenology in European Pear cultivars (Pyrus communis L.) under Sub-Himalayan Conditions of India
detail.abstract: This study showed the phenological growth stages of four European exotic pear cultivars (Early Desire, Lucas, William Bartlett and Conference) according to the BBCH General Scale (Meier, 2001). The BBCH scale provides a uniform coding system for phenologically similar growth stages of all monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plant species Hack et al. (1992). It uses clear and easily recognizable morphological characteristics to describe phenological developmental stages, dividing the complete developmental cycle of plants into 10 distinguishable phases. Based on this scale, European pear phenology showed 8 of the 10 principal growth stages (0–9): bud development, leaf development, shoot development, inflorescence emergence, flowering, fruit development, fruit maturity and senescence. A schematic representation of the chronological progression of vegetative and reproductive growth stages also shown. Phenological studies are essential for orchard management and for alerting growers of environmental changes since the phenological stages of pears are greatly impacted by environmental circumstances, which in turn affect the crop yield and quality. For varietal characterization and the proper timing of orchard management (such as pruning, pollination techniques, fertilizer management, irrigation, disease and pest management, etc.), accurate phenological stage identification is crucial.

title: Inference Based on Scale, Label, and Economic Restrictions
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, Emory University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Inference Based on Scale, Label, and Economic Restrictions
detail.abstract: The results of nearly one hundred prominent studies in empirical macroeconomics have been called into question by Baumeister and Hamilton (2018). We show that their concern about distributional asymmetry for a typical question of interest under a uniform prior with respect to the Haar measure is actually driven by an unacknowledged sign restriction. We also demonstrate that such a prior induces symmetric prior distributions over individual impulse responses conditional on the reduced-form parameters, or more generally when the prior over the reduced-form covariance matrix rules out correlation among the residuals, as in the typical implementation of the Minnesota prior. Furthermore, we provide a theory for avoiding the pitfalls of Baumeister and Hamilton's critique. Key to our theory is a proposition establishing that any restriction can be decomposed into three types: scale, label, and economic. We use this theory to develop an algorithm for inference based on the unit modulus normalization that tackles a practical problem commonly faced by users of Bayesian SVAR methods. JEL classification: C11, C32.

title: Tick Size, Exchange Fees, and Market Quality: Evidence from a Bundled Regulatory Transition
affiliations: State University of New York at Buffalo - School of Management, University at Buffalo (SUNY) - School of Management and State University of New York at Buffalo - School of Management

detail.title: Tick Size, Exchange Fees, and Market Quality: Evidence from a Bundled Regulatory Transition
detail.abstract: We examine how tick-size rules and exchange fee schedules affect market quality using the regulatory discontinuity at the $1 price threshold. When stock prices fall below $1, the minimum tick size declines from $0.01 to $0.0001, while many exchanges simultaneously eliminate or reduce maker rebates. Finer pricing narrows spreads, reduces displayed depth, and intensifies price competition, but these effects vary across exchange fee regimes. Liquidity providers partially offset lower rebates by widening spreads but cannot fully recover lost rebate income. Our findings suggest that tick-size rules and exchange fee schedules are complementary components of market design.

title: Value of Machine Learning in Mutual Fund Trades
affiliations: University of Illinois at Chicago - Department of Finance, University of Nottingham, UK and University of Leicester

detail.title: Value of Machine Learning in Mutual Fund Trades
detail.abstract: We examine the ability of an artificial neural network (ANN) to learn from the investment decisions of mutual fund managers. Our findings suggest that an ANN can utilize mutual fund holdings disclosures, firm characteristics, and macroeconomic variables to learn fund managers’ stock trading strategies and deliver desirable performance. We also find that fund managers have critical skills that artificial intelligence (AI) cannot replicate. Funds with higher levels of “non-AI” skills consistently generate significantly higher alphas for at least two quarters after these skills are identified. Such non-AI skills persist over time. Funds likely exhibit higher non-AI skill levels if they have more assets under management, charge higher fees, and do not invest primarily in large-cap stocks.

title: Climate Policy Uncertainty and Financial Transmission Evidence from U.S. Credit Markets

detail.title: Climate Policy Uncertainty and Financial Transmission Evidence from U.S. Credit Markets
detail.abstract: Climate policy uncertainty (CPU) has reached record levels amid repeated policy reversals, yet its financial transmission remains poorly understood. Using the narrative identification strategy of Gavriilidis et al. (2026), I document three findings. First, CPU shocks tighten credit markets: the excess bond premium and GZ spread rise by 5–8 basis points, high-yield spreads widen by 15–25 basis points, and commercial and industrial loans fall by 1–2%, with bank lending standards explaining the short-run contraction. Second, the effects are strongly state dependent. Under tight financial conditions, CPU shocks generate much larger investment declines and sharper increases in risk premia and corporate spreads than under loose conditions. Third, firm-level evidence shows larger investment declines among climate-exposed firms, while leveraged firms face higher bond yields and weaker bond market access. The results reveal a financial amplification channel with implications for transition policy, central bank communication, and climate stress testing.

title: Firms' responses to the covid-19 crisis: strategies, financial leverage, public support. The case of Italy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and National Institute of Statistics (Istat)

detail.title: Firms' responses to the covid-19 crisis: strategies, financial leverage, public support. The case of Italy
detail.abstract: This paper examines how firm-level strategic responses to the COVID-19 shock shaped capital structure dynamics among Italian firms, and how the two main public support instruments, debt moratoria and state guarantees, interacted with those responses. By integrating multiple statistical data sources and using an innovative classification of firms' reaction strategies, we find that strategic profiles do not independently determine the level of leverage; rather, they condition the channels through which policy support affects firms' financing decisions. Moratoria functioned primarily as a liquidity stabiliser for defensive firms, while guarantees were disproportionately associated with leverage-financed intangible investment among proactive firms. This instrument-specific duality reveals a structural bias in untargeted crisis support instruments that risks amplifying pre-existing productivity asymmetries. The results carry concrete implications for the design of crisis-response tools that simultaneously address short-term liquidity needs and long-term structural objectives.

title: Bank Intermediation Costs and Monetary Policy Transmission: A Decomposition Across EU Member States

detail.title: Bank Intermediation Costs and Monetary Policy Transmission: A Decomposition Across EU Member States
detail.abstract: We ask how much of the euro-area lending-deposit spread reflects structural bank pricing rather than sovereign risk and term premia, and what explains the persistent cross-country differences. We construct a Cost of Bank Intermediation (CBI) measure from harmonised ECB data over January 2017--December 2025, decomposed for household deposits and NFC loans. During the 2022--2024 tightening, the deposit-side CBI rose by nearly 400 basis points while lending margins compressed only moderately, shifting the burden onto household savers. Heterogeneity is large and persistent: deposit margins peak in the euro-area periphery, lending margins in the Baltic and Eastern members. Because the measure nets out sovereign and term-premium compensation but retains operating, capital, and competition costs, we read it as an upper bound on the policy-addressable component, not a direct measure of inefficiency; its cross-country pattern is consistent with, though cannot establish, a role for limited competition.

title: AI Deceleration (or Acceleration) by Taxation
affiliations: Washington University School of Law and University of Wisconsin Law School

detail.title: AI Deceleration (or Acceleration) by Taxation
detail.abstract:
Even the chief executives of America’s leading AI companies cannot agree on whether their products will substitute for or complement human labor. Yet most policy proposals, from data center bans to bonus depreciation for AI hardware, commit policymakers ex ante to just one view of how AI will integrate with workers. By extending a leading macroeconomic model of worker automation, we show that any fixed policy is unacceptably fragile: an AI tax calibrated to a world in which AI on net substitutes for human labor produces large welfare losses in a world in which AI is a net complement, and vice versa.

We propose an adaptive Pigouvian rule that responds to observed wage dynamics by taxing automation when real wages fall and subsidizing it when they rise. We show that this rule is the unique policy in our comparison set with positive welfare gains in both worlds, and it exhibits other attractive qualities that are emphasized in the policy robustness literature. From a coalition-building perspective, it is the only policy mechanism that both AI decelerationists and accelerationists should commit to ex ante. We propose implementing this adaptive rule through a two-pronged reform: (1) equalize the existing capital-labor tax wedge, and (2) enact a national AI-usage sales tax whose rate (which may be negative) is indexed to AI-induced unemployment (or change in real wages) by an independent labor-market body.

title: Bayesian Fairness
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, George Mason University and

detail.title: Bayesian Fairness
detail.abstract: We argue that algorithmic unfairness is, at its core, a missing-covariate problem. A predictor discriminates on a protected attribute A precisely when a legitimate but unobserved covariate U has been omitted, so that the fitted score retains predictive dependence on A as a surrogate for the information that U would have supplied. This reframing does three things. First, it maps the three canonical group-fairness criteria-independence (demographic parity), separation (equalized odds), and sufficiency (calibration)-onto conditional-independence statements that fail under an identifiable missing-data mechanism, placing fairness inside Rubin's MCAR/MAR/MNAR taxonomy and the potential-outcomes account of counterfactual fairness. Second, it re-reads the Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan and Chouldechova impossibility results as an over-identification failure: when base rates genuinely differ, the identifying restrictions imposed by competing fairness criteria are mutually incompatible, exactly as incompatible moment conditions over-determine a missing-data model. Third, it delivers a constructive Bayesian remedy: impute the missing covariate and deploy the posterior-predictive score. We frame fair prediction as Lindley (1968) decision-theoretic variable selection under Rubin (1976) missingness, giving the protected attribute an explicit shadow price; we derive a closed-form omitted-variable expression for the unaware model's sufficiency gap; and, using Pólya-Gamma augmentation for computation and the horseshoe prior for selecting proxy channels, we show on a credit-scoring example that imputing U with the protected attribute as an auxiliary variable restores sufficiency to within Monte Carlo error of an oracle that observes U , while also improving accuracy by de-noising the proxy. Because the imputation model is misspecified whenever the missingness is not at random, we close with a quasi-Bayes / Gibbs-posterior update that targets consistent fair-model selection where ordinary Bayes need not.

title: Who's Afraid of Copyright and AI?
affiliations: University of North Carolina School of Law

detail.title: Who's Afraid of Copyright and AI?
detail.abstract:
Copyright and AI need not be a copyright no man’s land. Recent decisions by the Copyright Office have gotten so much media attention that many creators are unsure if they can secure copyright protection if they use AI as a creative tool. The proposed creative control paradigm can help us all tackle the challenge of determining when works created with the assistance of AI are copyrightable. Instead of   relying on long-established nuanced precedent for protecting works generated with new technology, the Copyright Office asserts that any content generated with assistance from AI tools is unprotectable. This position is radically inconsistent with foundational copyright precedent. Copyright authorship and originality principles have long permitted ownership of content made using content generated by cutting edge technology or the assistance of other creators.


Copyright authorship doctrine permits authors to own content created with such tools or by contributors who are not co-authors. If an author can own copyrights in content created collaboratively with a non-author creator or another mechanical tool, why can’t that author own a work created using an AI platform? The work-for-hire doctrine permits non-human companies to own content they direct their employees to create. It is inconsistent to permit nonhumans to own content created by humans but refuse to allow humans to own content they direct machines to create. Derivative works are protectable even when they are based on preexisting public domain content. Why can’t a photographer own a copyright in a work if AI was used to create the first draft? No clear principle indicates why content generated by AI should be treated so differently from other works that contain unprotectable elements. When an author satisfies the originality and authorship standards, but the work cannot be disaggregated from their first AI generated draft, the creative contributions should be copyrightable despite the use of unprotectible building blocks, comparable to words in a language or colors in a palette. In an era when AI is so prevalent, artists may not even be aware of all the applications that incorporate it. When everyone from software engineers to artists, filmmakers to writers, and translators to composers are using AI, everyone needs clarity about who can protect what.


In addition to being unclear and inconsistent with settled copyright doctrine, the Office’s position is creating bizarre incentives. Telling the truth about the creative process could jeopardize copyright protection, especially for authors without access to copyright counsel. By asserting that the use of generative AI defeats copyrightability absent detailed disclaimers, the Copyright Office may be incentivizing applicants to lie about their creative process or abandon efforts of registration if they used AI as a creative tool. For these reasons, the current position of the Copyright Office on the protectability of AI-generated works should be clarified in a way that is consistent with foundational copyright doctrine. Instead of refusing to engage with the creative possibilities and limitations of AI, courts and the Copyright Office could apply a creative control paradigm to meet the challenge of discerning when works generated with the assistance of AI should be protected.

detail.abstract: Carbon share budgeting is increasingly used to translate global climate targets into entity-level carbon budgets and benchmarks for corporate decarbonization. However, commonly used fair-share approaches often yield highly dispersed initial budget estimates and exhibit strong baseline dependence, which can materially affect the assessment of forward-looking decarbonization pathways. We introduce SmoothShare, a new carbon share budgeting method that builds on the fair-share framework while addressing these limitations. SmoothShare includes a robust calibration mechanism that reflects heterogeneity in emission sources and provides a procedure for entities with missing data. We illustrate the method by assigning carbon budgets to companies in the MSCI All Country World Index. The proposed framework supports more stable and comparable budget allocations across firms, enabling more reliable evaluation of decarbonization trajectories.

detail.abstract:
Biodiversity loss is a long-horizon, fat-tail risk to the productive capacity of whole national economies, and the financial system has only recently begun to see it. The response over the past decade has been substantial: nature has been threaded into corporate and financial disclosure through frameworks such as the TNFD, into measurement and management standards such as ISO 17298, and into a growing family of instruments from biodiversity credits to debt-for-nature swaps and sustainability-linked bonds. This paper addresses a narrow, complementary question that opens once the lens shifts from single to double materiality: from protecting returns against biodiversity loss to protecting the natural capital those returns ultimately rest on. 

That shift challenges an assumption much of the investment industry has been built on: that relative size is the primary proxy for importance. The larger the balance sheet or the position, the more it is assumed to matter. Once the objective includes pricing a public-good externality and not only a return, what matters is the intensity of a participant's transmission into outcomes, not the size of its balance sheet. Notably, the leveraged investors who use credit-default swaps (CDS) to hedge can be a meaningful share of the flows that set sovereign borrowing costs, so a deeper, hedgeable CDS rail can move a sovereign’s cost of capital through that channel; Section 6 sets out who these pricesetters are and what frees each to act. 

This is also where the choice of market infrastructure comes into view. Where finance has reached for a market mechanism to price nature, it has largely extended the infrastructure built for carbon, which in turn drew on the rails of commodity markets. A commodity rail is built to price a fungible unit of consumable value changing hands over time. Biodiversity loss is not a missing unit; it is a slow, compounding fat-tail risk to a sovereign's solvency, which is the kind of risk credit markets are designed to insure against. The instrument built for it already exists. We argue the credit-default swap, pointed deliberately and bounded by design, can translate a verified national biodiversity signal into the cost of sovereign capital, working through a mechanism that already moves capital at very large scale. We offer this as a complement to the disclosure, measurement and market-building work already underway.

The economic premise, that nature loss already moves sovereign creditworthiness, rests on an established body of research, most recently corroborated by peer-reviewed work (Agarwala et al., 2026). Our focus is the question that evidence leaves open: through what market mechanism a sovereign can most credibly be incentivised for stewardship. We set out the design and its single-todouble-materiality logic, locate it among adjacent instruments, state the pricing logic and confront the small-sample detectability problem, specify a pilot hosted by a multilateral development bank with explicit scale-up and sunset logic, and set out the principal risks and objections.

title: BayesXAI: Horseshoe Priors for Explainable AI
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, George Mason University and

detail.title: BayesXAI: Horseshoe Priors for Explainable AI
detail.abstract: We develop BayesXAI, a Bayesian framework for Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) grounded in model-free variable selection via the horseshoe prior. Existing approaches-SHAP, LIME, and integrated gradients-produce point estimates of feature importance with no principled uncertainty quantification. We recast XAI as a sparse Bayesian regression problem: given oracle queries to a black-box model f , we learn a posterior distribution over feature importance coefficients using the horseshoe prior of Carvalho et al. (2010). The horseshoe's near-Cauchy tails prevent excessive shrinkage of large signals; its pole at zero achieves automatic, continuous spike-and-slab-like sparsification. We prove posterior contraction at the minimax rate s 0 log(p/s 0)/n for s 0-sparse explanations (Theorem 1) and establish horseshoe predictive minimaxity via the GLX framework (Theorem 2; Polson et al. 2025e). Bayesian hypothesis tests for feature relevance exploit the moderate-deviation Bayes factor approximation. We compare BayesXAI with SHAP, LIME, integrated gradients, ALE, Anchors, and counterfactual methods, providing an honest regime map of when the horseshoe wins and when it does not. Experiments on synthetic sparse benchmarks show signal recovery of 0.96 at FDR 0.02, versus 0.74 / 0.19 for kernel SHAP. A complete Python implementation is provide.

title: Too Much Finance: Mechanisms That Harm Growth and Policy Implications
affiliations: Birkbeck, University of London, Birkbeck, University of London and Heriot-Watt University

detail.title: Too Much Finance: Mechanisms That Harm Growth and Policy Implications
detail.abstract: The mechanisms for the financial sector to harm growth arise through short-termism of financial markets. This leads to the misallocation of resources in the private sector, leading to financial crises and damage to growth. However, harm to growth comes not only from financial crises, but also from the failure of short-termist financial markets to facilitate public investment in long-term, growth-enhancing projects. While the literature has discussed the first channel extensively, it is largely silent on the second one. Our contribution is to develop a formal model to clarify how investment reticence of governments can arise from the fear of financial crises. A central conclusion is that in the presence of a large financial sector, the fear of market turmoil can damage growth even in the absence of an actual crisis episode. We discuss policy responses to both mechanisms.

title: Heterogeneous beliefs with Uninsurable Income
affiliations: National University of Singapore and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Heterogeneous beliefs with Uninsurable Income
detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes the general equilibrium of a pure-exchange economy in which agents with uninsurable income trade a dividend-paying stock and borrow from or lend to each other. Agents are heterogeneous in risk aversion, time preferences and beliefs about the growth rates of both the dividend and all agents' incomes. We derive in closed form the equilibrium interest rate, stock price, and agent consumption and investment policies.

Key findings include: a positive correlation between optimists' income and dividend growth lowers the interest rate; beliefs on hedgeable risks and those on unhedgeable incomes are aggregated differently in equilibrium; agents with atypical beliefs possess high subjective utility while facing potentially unbounded negative expected utility under the objective probability measure.

title: The Structural Directive: Vindicating The High Purpose of the Antitrust Laws
affiliations: Open Markets Institute

detail.title: The Structural Directive: Vindicating The High Purpose of the Antitrust Laws
detail.abstract:
After more than a decade of vigorous advocacy by policy analysts, journalists, and legal scholars, federal and state enforcers finally found the political will to initiate numerous antitrust enforcement actions under Section 2 of the Sherman Act—the antitrust provision proscribing unfair monopolization. During the first Trump and Biden administrations, multiple enforcement actions were brought against the world’s largest corporations, some of which are currently navigating the litigation process. Yet, lawsuits are neither the objective nor the measure of success; remedies are. Remedies are the heart, body, and soul of litigation. No enforcement action is consequential without meaningful relief.

With this generational influx of enforcement, antitrust in the United States is at an inflection point. Over the last two decades, federal judges have not had to seriously contemplate or implement structural antitrust remedies. Structural remedies are those that permanently dismantle a corporation’s dominant control and alter the market architecture itself by divesting assets or breaking up firms. The last structural relief issued by a court was in 1982 with the breakup of telecommunications giant AT&T Judges’ experience with structural antitrust remedies has become atrophied, demanding a return to first principles. Judges and enforcers must recenter effective remedies as the core of antitrust law and resist the urge to issue or seek favorable judgments that merely identify violations and restrain the conduct at issue.

To give effect to the “high purpose” of the antitrust laws, judges must adhere to what I call the “structural directive.” The structural directive is the binding doctrinal principle that obligates lower courts to impose the requested structural relief on liable parties—as opposed to merely permitting courts to do so—if the plaintiff requests the remedy and the request is reasonable.

They represent a node within a broader, state-proximate architecture in which organised crime, rival intelligence services, and competing geopolitical strategies have become entangled in ways that European security institutions have not yet found coherent answers to. detail.abstract: This paper examines Ijarah as a Sharia-compliant leasing structure and its potential application in a modern Islamic financial product for the Dutch market. It explains the doctrinal foundations of Ijarah in the Qur’an, Sunnah, and classical Islamic jurisprudence, highlighting the core distinction between ownership of an asset and the lessee’s lawful right to use its benefit. The paper compares the treatment of Ijarah across the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi‘i, and Hanbali schools, showing how each balances contractual certainty, commercial flexibility, custom, and avoidance of uncertainty. It argues that Ijarah differs fundamentally from interest-based lending because the financier earns rental income from providing access to a real asset rather than charging for the use of money. Building on this foundation, the paper positions Ijarah as a transparent, asset-based financing model suitable for retail households and SME owner-operators in the Netherlands, with potential for wider EU-ready design.

title: Trade Arrangements Between Pakistan and EU/UK

detail.title: Trade Arrangements Between Pakistan and EU/UK
detail.abstract: This brief outlines the features of the EU's Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+) and the UK's post-Brexit Developing Countries Trading Scheme (DCTS), both of which give Pakistan preferential, tariff-free access to European and British markets respectively. It weighs these advantages against notable drawbacks — including export caps and demanding compliance requirements tied to international conventions — and argues that Pakistan should instead pursue full Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) with the EU and UK to secure more durable, equal-footing trade relationships and improve the quality and volume of its exports.

title: Murābaḥah Penalty Clause is Ribā in Disguise! The Penalty Clause Questions the Deep-rooted Preference for Literal Interpretation over Substantial Interpretation of Ribā

detail.title: Murābaḥah Penalty Clause is Ribā in Disguise! The Penalty Clause Questions the Deep-rooted Preference for Literal Interpretation over Substantial Interpretation of Ribā
detail.abstract: Following the literal interpretation of ribā, jurists have agreed that muḍārabah and mušārakah are legitimate modes of financing. As both arrangements are highly risky to manage in practice, murābaḥah has been introduced as an alternate mode of financing. Despite its extraordinary success, murābaḥah has led to moral hazard in the form of frequent delays in payments and defaults for which Islamic scholars have introduced a penalty clause as discouragement. Examination of the murābaḥah penalty clause instrument suggests that it is ribā, prohibited when interpreted literally. Moreover, the penalty clause has never been enforced in Pakistani courts. This article suggests that the literal interpretation based on the objectives of Sharīʿah (substantial interpretation) will prevent loopholes such as the abuse of the murābaḥah instrument and consequently the penalty clause as well and will lead to substantial compliance with the principles of Islamic finance.

title: Social Media Disputes, Toxicity and Spillovers
affiliations: Peking University - Guanghua School of Management, Peking University - Guanghua School of Management, Peking University - Guanghua School of Management, Department of Applied Economics and University of Connecticut

detail.title: Social Media Disputes, Toxicity and Spillovers
detail.abstract: Online disputes are pervasive on social media, yet their effects on user welfare remain largely unexplored. We study fan-group disputes on Weibo, a leading social media platform in China, using 8.9 million posts from 30,516 users. Exploiting plausibly exogenous dispute shocks in a stacked difference-indifferences design, we show that disputes sharply increase toxic expression and late-night posting, with implications for both mental and physical well-being. The effects are especially pronounced among younger users, women, and opinion leaders. Mechanism evidence is consistent with identity reinforcement: disputes increase out-group-directed toxicity and support for the focal celebrity through consumption-related posting. We further document spillovers across topics and over time, showing that the harms of online disputes extend beyond the original conflict to the broader online discourse environment.

title: The Sharpe Ratio within the ARMA-GARCH Framework
affiliations: Finance and Risk Engineering, NYU Tandon School of Engineering

detail.title: The Sharpe Ratio within the ARMA-GARCH Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The Sharpe ratio (SR) being the risk-adjusted asset return has been a major portfolio performance measure widely used by practitioners. In classical finance, risk is associated with price volatility that is usually estimated using the standard deviation (SD) of asset returns. This implies that returns are assumed to be independent, identically distributed, and Normal. There have been several analytical studies devoted to autocorrelations and volatility clustering (GARCH) in asset returns that highlighted importance of these effects for obtaining the adequate SR estimates. In this work, we offer a computational approach for calculating SR using the optimal ARMA-GARCH models that account for both autocorrelations and GARCH effects. First, for each given data sample, we use MLE-based derivations of the optimal ARMA-GARCH models with different flavors. Then, we compare the accuracy of these models out of sample using their forecasts of the 21 trading-day returns. Finally, we use the volatility (sigma) of the most accurate out-of-sample model for calculating SR. As an example of this approach, we discuss the AIC-based and BIC-based optimal ARMA-GARCH and ARMA-GJR-GARCH models for the S&P 500 returns in all one-year periods within 2000-2024. We found that the ARMA-GARCH sigma can be notably higher than SD in the samples with pronounced autocorrelations, which results in the corresponding changes in the SR values.

title: Regime-aware Risk-sensitive Reinforcement Learning for Trading: A Controlled Study of CVaR-constrained Policy Optimization under Distribution Shift

detail.title: Regime-aware Risk-sensitive Reinforcement Learning for Trading: A Controlled Study of CVaR-constrained Policy Optimization under Distribution Shift
detail.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) agents trained to maximize expected return can adopt positions whose downside risk is unacceptable in financial applications, where rare crisis regimes drive most large losses. We present a controlled study of risksensitive policy optimization for trading in which the data-generating process is known, so that the effect of the risk objective can be isolated from confounders such as deep function approximators and noisy historical data. We introduce a reproducible regime-switching market simulator with fat-tailed (Student-t) crisis dynamics, and compare three agents that share an identical proximal policy optimization (PPO) update: a risk-neutral baseline, a Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR)-constrained agent following the CVaR-PPO/CPPO formulation, and a mean-variance agent. All three risk mechanisms are expressed through a single trajectory-level advantage augmentation, making the comparison exact. Across five random seeds, the CVaR agent reduces the 5% tail loss of annual return from 34.0% to 28.0% and the mean maximum drawdown from 18.9% to 16.2% while sacrificing only 0.5 percentage points of mean annual return; sweeping the riskaversion coefficient traces a monotone risk-return frontier. A regime-conditional analysis shows that the benefit comes from cutting gross exposure specifically during high-volatility crisis periods. We further find that CVaR attains a better return-for-downside tradeoff than mean-variance, which by penalizing symmetric variance also sacrifices upside. Code and full experimental configuration are released for reproducibility.

title: India's Government e-Marketplace (GeM): Architecture, Outcomes, and a Replication Framework for the Global South

detail.abstract: Public procurement, which constitutes between 15 and 20 percent of GDP in most developing countries, remains one of the most corruption-prone and inefficiency-laden functions of government in the Global South. Fragmented legal frameworks, opaque tendering processes, limited supplier access, and weak audit trails collectively cost developing economies hundreds of billions of dollars annually in leakages, overpricing, and foregone market participation by small businesses. India's Government e-Marketplace (GeM), launched in August 2016, offers a compelling and evidencebacked alternative. Within a decade, it has become the world's largest single-government procurement platform by order volume, transacting ₹18.4 lakh crore cumulatively and ₹5 lakh crore in FY 2025–26 alone, while simultaneously positioning Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs), womenled businesses, SC/ST entrepreneurs, and startups as primary beneficiaries of government demand. This brief examines GeM's architecture, its distinguishing design features, its measurable outcomes, and the institutional preconditions that made it possible. It then assesses the replication potential for Global South countries and proposes a structured framework for South-South cooperation through which India can share not just the platform, but the governance logic that makes it work. The analysis draws on publicly available GeM transaction data, World Bank assessments, and the author's practitioner experience in digital governance across multiple Government of India institutions.

title: Financial Reporting Regulation, Market Power, and Welfare
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad

detail.title: Financial Reporting Regulation, Market Power, and Welfare
detail.abstract: How does financial reporting regulation affect welfare? We present a novel outcome of financial reporting regulation: it can generate cross-sectional markup dispersion with considerable welfare effects, despite having no influence on the average firm. The cross-sectional markup dispersion has an impact on the misallocation of capital. Using a generalized difference-in-differences design centered around the Sarbanes Oxley Act, 2002 (SOX), we demonstrate that there is a reallocation of market power from young life cycle firms to mature firms, as measured by price-marginal cost markup. Young life cycle firms' markup decreases as mature firms' markup increases. There is a comparable redistribution of economic outputs. After regulation, high markup firms—which were already more mature and productive—have been able to increase both their productivity and intangible assets. However, compared to mature firms, the costs have risen disproportionately for younger firms. Cross-sectional markup dispersion reduces misallocation, as assessed by a decrease in the industry-level dispersion of Marginal Revenue Product of Capital (MRPK). Additionally, the regulation causes a labor reallocation from young to mature firms. The results uncover a distinct allocative role for transparency regulation that operates not through the average firm but through the cross-sectional market power dispersion it induces with significant welfare implications - improving eﬀiciency while generating sharp distributional consequences that fall on the young, innovation-intensive firms central to long-run growth.

title: Letting the Reins Loose: Central Bank Stock Purchases and Corporate Governance
affiliations: ,  and Meisei University

detail.title: Letting the Reins Loose: Central Bank Stock Purchases and Corporate Governance
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the effect of the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) equity purchases via exchangetraded funds (ETFs) on firm-level corporate governance. As part of its unconventional monetary easing policy, the BOJ became one of the world's largest institutional shareholders, raising concerns about the governance implications of passive central bank ownership. Using a panel of Japanese listed firms from 2006-2023, we construct a composite governance index and employ a Difference-inDifferences framework with continuous treatment intensity. Our baseline estimates indicate that a 1% increase in the BOJ's effective ownership share is associated with a decline in the governance index of approximately 0.7 points, with the effects concentrated in shareholder structure and board accountability. These findings suggest a trade-off: while central bank equity purchases stabilize markets, they can weaken corporate discipline.

title: Labor, Investment and Financing Decisions with Diffusion and Jump Ambiguity
affiliations: Hunan University - School of Finance and Statistics, Hunan University - School of Finance and Statistics and Jishou University

detail.title: Labor, Investment and Financing Decisions with Diffusion and Jump Ambiguity
detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic real-options model of a firm with market power that incorporates diffusion and jump ambiguity in product-market demand. The model elucidates how ambiguity affects investment timing, labor demand, operating scale, financing policy, and welfare when the firm jointly chooses labor, capital, debt, and default policy. First, ambiguity generates two opposite effects, i.e., the project-value effect, which reduces the robust value of post-investment cash flows, and the option-multiple effect, which decreases the first-passage valuation of waiting. Furthermore, the investment threshold has a non-monotone relationship with ambiguity, which is driven by the two effects. Second, decomposing ambiguity shows that diffusion ambiguity is mainly reflected in the project-value effect, whereas jump ambiguity is mainly reflected in the option-multiple effect. Third, ambiguity reduces operating scale through the joint choice of capital and labor. At the investment threshold, however, capital and labor are governed by the jump-adjusted option multiple rather than by the payoff coefficient alone. Fourth, ambiguity lowers debt capacity and raises credit spreads. Finally, ambiguity widens the private-social wedge: compared with a social planner who internalizes consumer surplus, private levered policies reduces labor and output and delay investment, thereby giving rise to welfare losses.

title: Slice Sampling the Polyak Ravine
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Slice Sampling the Polyak Ravine
detail.abstract: Polyak’s ravine is a deceptively simple global optimization problem: minimize f(x) = min{99 − c ⊤x,(c ⊤x − 99)/398} over the ball ∥x∥ ≤ 100 in R n. A long shallow valley of slope 1/398 leads descent methods to a local minimum of value −1/2, while the global minimum of value −1 hides behind a steep face inside a spherical cap whose relative volume decays geometrically in n. Following Birge and Polson (2012), we recast the problem as sampling the Boltzmann distribution πκ(x) ∝ e −κf(x) with an auxiliary variable slice sampler, and we develop the theory in full. Because f depends on x only through the projection s = c ⊤x, the ideal two block sampler collapses exactly to a one dimensional slice chain, and every question becomes tractable. We prove: a Doeblin minorization giving uniform ergodicity with the explicit rate ∥P g x −πκ∥TV ≤ (1−e −κ ) g ; a sighting bound showing that from the valley interior the chain sees the winning cap at essentially the uniform search rate, so the information theoretic hardness is respected; a refinement theorem showing that, once inside a cap, the optimality gap contracts at the exact rate E[log Dg+1 | Dg = d] ≤ log d− 2 n+1 + 1 κd , so polishing costs O(n log(1/ε)) iterations; and a tunneling theorem giving the exact one step escape probability from the local optimum, whose n → ∞ limit is 1 − e −κ/794 with explicit O(κ/n) finite dimension error, so a temperature of order a thousand suffices at any n. The last result yields a drill and tunnel mechanism, confirmed numerically at n = 50, in which the sampler escapes the local minimum by first descending into it: sharp local minima betray themselves to slice samplers because their shallow level sets grow too slowly to hold the chain against the competing cap. We also prove that the critical temperature at which the winning cap captures half the Boltzmann mass grows as κ ∗ (n) = γ ∗n + β ∗ + o(1) with γ ∗ ≈ 5.8175 the root of an explicit variational equation and β ∗ ≈ 6.11 a second order Laplace constant, and that for n ≥ 6 the cap mass is initially decreasing in κ, so mild tempering helps the wrong minimum first.

title: Automated Tax Decisions: Revisiting Part IVC, The ADJR Act and Taxpayer Rights
affiliations: Curtin University - Curtin Law School

detail.title: Automated Tax Decisions: Revisiting Part IVC, The ADJR Act and Taxpayer Rights
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is expected to play a substantive role in future Australian tax administration by automating aspects of assessments and administrative decision-making. Yet the legal frameworks governing review and accountability remain anchored in assumptions of human deliberation. This article examines the implications of automated tax decisions for taxpayer rights through an analysis of Part IVC of the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (Cth) and the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 (Cth). It argues that both regimes are poorly aligned with technology-driven administrative practices. The article suggests that targeted adjustments—particularly in relation to transparency obligations, evidentiary burdens and the legal status of automated decision letters—are necessary to preserve intelligibility, fairness and meaningful access to review. In turn, such reforms are essential to maintaining public trust in the tax system and supporting the effective operation of Australia’s self-assessment regime.

title: Randomization in Optimization and Simulation: The Russian School Meets Generative Bayesian Computation
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Randomization in Optimization and Simulation: The Russian School Meets Generative Bayesian Computation
detail.abstract: When is a random choice better than a deterministic one? Polyak and Shcherbakov posed this question for robustness, estimation, and optimization and gave a largely cautionary answer: direct Monte Carlo fails exponentially in dimension even for the best convex problems, while carefully structured randomization (random search with smoothing, randomized coordinate descent, random feasibility algorithms, hit-and-run) succeeds. We revisit their program from the standpoint of generative Bayesian computation (GBC) and sequential simulation, and argue that the two schools solve dual problems. The Russian school randomizes the algorithm while treating the objective as a black box; the generative school randomizes the representation, converting optimization into sampling from a tilted measure. A single quantity, the chi-square divergence between the tilted target and the proposal, equals the relative variance of every estimator in the paper and is the common ledger for the comparison. Three case studies make the duality precise. For a linear function on a ball, a Laplace-method argument shows that a von Mises-Fisher tilt collapses Polyak and Shcherbakov's exponential sample size to a dimension-free one, and adaptive multilevel splitting achieves the same in polynomial time without conjugacy. For convex optimization the argument becomes a theorem: the tilt is log-concave, hit-and-run samples it in polynomial dimension, and annealing the temperature yields a polynomial-time optimizer, so the Russian school's own hit-and-run, wrapped in a homotopy of tilts, is the generative solver. For self-avoiding walks the optimal proposal is a Doob transform, and a product bound on the sequential chi-square explains exactly when importance weights degenerate. We are equally precise about the limits: the guarantees are coextensive with log-concavity, weights degenerate exponentially otherwise, and no method escapes the Nemirovskii-Yudin lower bounds on nonconvex targets.

title: THE COST OF ASKING: Investment Chill in the Run-Up to Separation Referendums

detail.title: THE COST OF ASKING: Investment Chill in the Run-Up to Separation Referendums

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial interest in any firm named in this paper, including the firms in the three event-study portfolios listed in Appendix B. The author holds no equity, debt, advisory, board, or consulting relationship with any Alberta or Ontario headquartered firm in the sample, and received no compensation from any party for this work. The author is a Canadian citizen resident in Alberta and British Columbia, and therefore has a personal stake in the outcome of the October 19, 2026 referendum. The analysis is positive rather than normative. The paper does not advocate a vote in either direction, and Section 5 states explicitly that the policy discussion is conditional on federal objectives rather than a recommendation. Generative AI was used for light editorial support, including grammar, consistency, and phrasing, and to assist with brainstorming titles and clarifying wording around the interpretation of statistical results. All analysis, arguments, and substantive contributions are the author's own.
