detail.abstract: On May 21, 2026, Premier Danielle Smith added a tenth question to Alberta's October 19 ballot: should the province start the legal process to hold a binding separation referendum? The political debate that followed concentrated on the result. I take up a different question. What happens to inward investment in the months before a separation referendum, and in the decade after, regardless of how the vote goes? I compare four historical cases, Quebec 1980 and 1995, the United Kingdom 2016, Scotland 2014, and Catalonia 2017, on a common framework: headquarters relocations, inward-investment shares, sovereign-yield repricing, and long-run economic-share persistence. The pattern is consistent and the result is uncomfortable. Capital reallocation begins on the separatist signal. Legal headquarters move first. Inward-investment shares decline and do not fully recover. Persistence does not depend on outcome. Quebec has run negative net interprovincial migration in every year of the StatCan series, 54 consecutive years from 1971/72 through 2024/25; the outflow had been shrinking into the mid-1970s, then the November 1976 Parti Quebecois victory sharply reversed and deepened it, producing the worst year on record in 1977/78 at minus 46,429. Its share of Canadian non-residential investment fell from 22.5 percent in 1976 to 17.6 percent in 1981 and never recovered. Catalan foreign direct investment in 2024 still sits below its 2016 peak, seven years after a vote Spain nullified. I then apply the framework to Alberta. A difference-indifferences event study on daily returns of forty-nine Alberta-headquartered oil and gas firms against one hundred and fifty-four large Ontario-headquartered firms, oil-controlled, shows the abnormal-return distribution shifted at the December 8, 2022 Sovereignty Act royal assent (Welch t equals minus 2.01, p equals 0.045). A within-Alberta cross-sectional placebo passes cleanly (Welch t equals 0.16, p equals 0.87): the effect is in the oil and gas sector, not in Alberta firms generally. The cross-case range predicts an investment chill of one to four percentage points of Alberta's share of Canadian inward investment, persisting for at least a decade, regardless of the October outcome. The cost of asking is paid before the answer is given.

title: From Demand Forecasting to Inventory Resilience: A Risk-sensitive Decision-Support Framework for Multi-echelon Enterprise Operations
affiliations: University of Gloucestershire

detail.title: From Demand Forecasting to Inventory Resilience: A Risk-sensitive Decision-Support Framework for Multi-echelon Enterprise Operations
detail.abstract: Demand forecasting is central to enterprise operations, yet statistical forecast accuracy does not directly determine whether an inventory system avoids stockouts, excessive stock accumulation, unstable ordering, and service-level degradation. This paper proposes a risk-sensitive decision-support framework that translates SKU-store demand forecasts into downstream inventory-resilience outcomes. The empirical study uses the public M5/Walmart forecasting benchmark, containing 30,490 finest-level SKU-store daily sales series across 3,049 items, 10 stores, 3 states, and three product categories. A transparent active-sample rule retains 26,483 SKU-store series with recent and holdout demand activity. Eight forecasting policies are evaluated over the final 28-day holdout window, including seven transparent statistical policies and one applied machine-learning baseline based on global Ridge regression with lag, rolling-window, calendar, and hierarchy features. Forecasts are then passed into a simulated multi-echelon replenishment environment consisting of store-level base-stock control and state-level distribution-center aggregation. The simulation reports service level, stockout rate, overstock exposure, holding cost, order frequency, and an Inventory Resilience Score (IRS). The results show that Moving Average 28 achieves the lowest MAE (1.164) and WAPE (0.724), whereas Risk-Adjusted MA28 achieves the highest IRS (88.021), the highest service level (96.29%), and the lowest stockout rate (1.98%). The Ridge regression model provides an applied AI benchmark, but its uncalibrated negative bias produces weaker inventoryresilience outcomes, reinforcing the need to evaluate AI forecasts through operational risk metrics rather than accuracy alone. Category and state breakdowns indicate higher simulated risk for FOODS and CA under the selected risk-sensitive policy. Sensitivity analysis confirms that Risk-Adjusted MA28 remains the top IRS model under changes in lead time, safety factor, and stockout penalty.

title:
People’s Republic of China’s Strategic

 Cognitive Warfare
affiliations: Liberty University - Helms School of Government

detail.title:
People’s Republic of China’s Strategic

 Cognitive Warfare
detail.abstract:
This thesis argues that the People's Republic of China (PRC) is engaged in systematic cognitive warfare against the United States. This campaign is a whole-of-government and whole-of-society effort, with roots in Chairman Mao Zedong's methods of population control, later adapted for the internet age and informed by the "Three Warfares" doctrine of public opinion, psychological, and legal warfare.

The PRC's strategic narrative positions China as a victim of past Western aggression, now rightfully claiming its place as a global leader. It portrays the United States as a declining, corrupt power and presents itself as a better steward of the international "rules-based order." Through sophisticated social media tactics, the PRC aims to sow division, undermine U.S. institutions, and weaken the nation's will.

Conversely, the United States is depicted as operating with an outdated 1990s information operations doctrine, lacking a clear strategic message and a coordinated, whole-of-government response to 21st-century cognitive threats. The thesis proposes that the U.S. has the capacity and a powerful, proven strategic message rooted in the principles of the Declaration of Independence to counter this threat. The central challenge for the U.S. is not a lack of capability, but the will to implement a comprehensive cognitive warfare strategy.

title: Factor-Residual Local Turning Calculus for Model Validation and Stress-Gated Usage Control

detail.title: Factor-Residual Local Turning Calculus for Model Validation and Stress-Gated Usage Control
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces Factor-Residual Local Turning Calculus (FR-LTC), a model-validation framework for detecting and controlling residual local-turning structure in matrix-valued financial or computational data. The method extends scalar oscillatory-envelope local-turning calculus by placing it inside a conservative teacher-residual architecture. Instead of fitting local oscillatory patterns directly to raw observations, FR-LTC first removes known structure through a teacher baseline, forms a residual matrix, extracts stable low-rank residual modes, and applies scalar oscillatory-envelope diagnostics only to the resulting residual-mode scores.

The framework separates residual-shape detection from model-use permission. Singular gaps, low-rank subspace stability, rank robustness, residual-mode fitting loss, parameter stability, derivative diagnostics, stress sensitivity, and overfitting indicators are collected into a diagnostic vector. A stress-gated decision rule then maps the residual structure to one of four usage states: accept, downgrade, fallback, or reject. The purpose is not to prove market predictability, but to assess whether residual local-turning structure is stable enough for limited diagnostic use or should instead be treated as noise, missing factor exposure, regime shift, jump risk, or potential model misuse.

The paper also includes a scientific-computing audit layer that reports residual-bookkeeping error, ordinary-least-squares projection error, singular-value decomposition reconstruction error, singular-vector orthogonality, selected-rank truncation error, and finite-difference checks of analytic derivative diagnostics. A reproducible Python implementation demonstrates the conservative residual-diagnostic version on synthetic data, where the base window is accepted while a severe jump-and-rotation stress is downgraded to fallback. FR-LTC is therefore positioned as an auditable model-validation and model-risk diagnostic framework for residual local structure, rather than as a standalone trading or forecasting model.

title: Beyond Organisational Governance: DARF Portability and Attributable Resolution Authority in Sovereign Systems

detail.abstract:
This paper examines whether the Decision and Authority Resolution Framework (DARF), originally developed for organisational governance environments, remains diagnostically valid when applied to sovereign economic governance systems. DARF assumes that authority converges through hierarchy, governance records function as operational accountability trails, and formal authority reliably evidences real closure authority. This paper tests whether these structural assumptions survive translation into sovereign governance contexts.

Three structural breakpoints emerge. First, single authority convergence frequently fails in sovereign systems because authority is distributed by design. Second, formal accountability chains weaken as formal authority and real closure authority diverge at consequential governance moments. Third, governance records function increasingly as political signals rather than operational accountability trails, creating what this paper identifies as the Sovereign False Confidence Signal.

These breakpoints destabilise ownership, DARF’s original diagnostic variable. The paper evaluates three responses: retention of modified ownership, replacement through Attributable Resolution Authority (ARA), and Distributed Binding Authority as an alternative interpretive frame. On current theoretical and secondary evidence, ARA emerges as the strongest candidate replacement variable.

ARA tests whether binding authority for final resolution can be prospectively located, evidenced, and attributed to a specific actor or actor combination before consequential closure becomes necessary. The paper concludes that DARF portability into sovereign governance is conditional rather than universal, and that ARA is provisionally supported as the strongest diagnostic variable for fragmented sovereign governance environments. Empirical validation remains the next research priority.

detail.abstract: Objective To review the charts of people who requested medical assistance in dying (MAID) to examine their reasons for the request. Design Retrospective chart survey. Setting British Columbia. Participants Patients who requested an assisted death and were assessed by 1 of 6 physicians in British Columbia during 2016. Main outcome measures Patients’ diagnoses and reasons for requesting MAID. Results Data were collected from 250 assessments for MAID: 112 of the patients had assisted deaths, 11 had natural deaths, 35 were assessed as not eligible for MAID, and most of the rest were not ready. For people who had assisted deaths, disease-related symptoms were given as the first or second most important reason for requesting assisted death by 67 people (59.8%), while 59 (52.7%) gave loss of autonomy, 55 (49.1%) gave loss of ability to enjoy activities, and 27 (24.1%) gave fear of future suffering. People who were assessed as eligible but who had not received assisted deaths were more likely to list fear of future suffering (33.7% vs 7.1%) and less likely to list disease-related symptoms (17.4% vs 40.2%) than those who received MAID were. There was a difference in reasons for MAID given by people with different diagnoses; disease-related symptoms were given as the most important reason by 39.0% of patients with malignancies, 6.8% of patients with neurological diseases, and 28.9% of patients with end-organ failure. Loss of autonomy was given as the most important reason by 16.0% of patients with malignancies, 36.4% of patients with neurological diseases, and 23.7% of patients with end-organ failure. Conclusion This study shows that the reasons patients give for requesting an assisted death are similar to those reported in other jurisdictions with similar laws, but in different proportions. Loss of autonomy and loss of ability to enjoy activities were less common reasons among patients in this study compared with other jurisdictions. This might be related to the method of data collection, as in this study, the patients’ reasons were recorded by physicians.

title: Mental Health in Sentencing Beyond Mitigation
affiliations: York University - Osgoode Hall Law School

detail.title: Mental Health in Sentencing Beyond Mitigation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Osgoode Legal Studies Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Osgoode Hall Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In recent years, the jurisprudence of the Supreme Court has opened an important window to look more seriously at the truth that one must wrestle with the individualized experience of punishment if one hopes to calibrate the severity, and hence proportionality, of a sentence. This is an incipient theme in Canadian sentencing jurisprudence, novel from a comparative perspective, and with the potential to disturb much about how we sentence—perhaps more than the Court foresaw when it embraced this idea. In this article, I peer through this window, examining what it means for the relevance of mental health in sentencing. The article reviews the rise and nature of “individualized proportionality” in Canadian sentencing and explores what we know about the experience of incarceration for those suffering from mental health conditions. I ultimately argue that, both as a normative matter and as a natural consequence of contemporary Canadian sentencing doctrine, the mental health of an offender should be relevant to sentencing whether or not it has any nexus whatsoever with the underlying offence. Having made this argument, I turn to reflect more broadly on what it might mean for our understanding and practices of sentencing if we were to stop “getting rid” of the fact that mental illness is endemic, not exceptional, in our system.

detail.abstract:
TThis paper introduces Historical Temperament Function as a constitutional systems framework for evaluating how human temperament becomes operationally significant when joined to public office, institutional speech, historical timing, and civic reception. The paper argues that public officials are not merely legal actors occupying formal offices; they are also signal-bearing actors whose speech, restraint, severity, humility, volatility, courage, and timing may shape public trust, institutional legitimacy, civic interpretation, and the long-horizon operating environment of the American constitutional system.

The central thesis is that personality and office cannot be fully separated once a person speaks, governs, judges, warns, dissents, or disrupts through public authority. The Constitution supplies offices, powers, procedures, and limits, but those structures are inhabited by human beings whose temperament may stabilize, correct, distort, or accelerate systemic conditions. Historical examples illustrate the model. Abraham Lincoln’s humility, restraint, and moral seriousness functioned as stabilizing executive temperament during civil war and emancipation. Judicial leadership in Brown v. Board of Education reflects institutional discipline as corrective constitutional judgment. John Lewis’s conscience illustrates moral courage as lawful civic disturbance. Thaddeus Stevens’s severity shows how forceful temperament may become historically functional when directed toward constitutional correction.

The paper contributes a novel distinction between positive temperament function and negative temperament function. Some figures change history by embodying the virtue the moment requires; others change history by exposing the vice the system must learn to reject. This distinction permits constitutional analysis to move beyond hero worship, partisan condemnation, or psychological biography. It asks what a public figure’s temperament did inside the system: whether it clarified or confused, corrected or distorted, stabilized or accelerated, raised the inherited civic baseline or lowered it for successors.

The paper further develops a theory of office-bearing speech, distinguishing legal permissibility from systems harm. A statement by a public official may remain lawful, protected, non-actionable, or outside formal state-action doctrine while still producing institutional effects if the public receives personal opinion as official meaning, accusation as finding, urgency as emergency, performance as leadership, or public pressure as public will. The paper therefore identifies a critical gap between what officials are legally permitted to say and what constitutional stewardship may require them to understand about the effects of their words.

To address that gap, the paper proposes two practical models. The Office-Bearing Speech Responsibility Model provides a non-censorship stewardship framework built around office amplification, institutional distinction, long-horizon stewardship, restraint under visibility, distributed responsibility, and corrective transparency. The Factual Transmission Standard offers a communication model requiring office-bearing public communication to distinguish fact, opinion, procedural status, source material, institutional authority, lawful public action, and unresolved uncertainty. These models do not restrict viewpoint, criticism, dissent, warning, or political persuasion. They preserve robust public speech while strengthening the public’s ability to evaluate authority.

From a constitutional-law perspective, the paper offers a structural account of how speech, office, and public reception interact below the threshold of formal legal violation. From a systems-analysis perspective, it models public officials as human inputs within a high-velocity governance environment where repeated signals can produce correction, distortion, civic habituation, and inherited baseline drift. The paper concludes that a republic does not endure by structure alone. It endures when those entrusted with its offices understand that temperament, speech, restraint, and timing are themselves part of the architecture of self-government.

title: Colonized and Naturalized on their Own Land: The Subjects of the Empire of Morocco, the 1836 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, and the Void Chain

detail.title: Colonized and Naturalized on their Own Land: The Subjects of the Empire of Morocco, the 1836 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, and the Void Chain

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this research.

detail.abstract: In 1836, the United States Senate ratified the Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the Empire of Morocco-confirmed operative by the International Court of Justice in 1952 and acknowledged by the United States House of Representatives in 2025 as "the longest unbroken diplomatic relationship in United States history." Yet in 1959, the State Department declared that same treaty "obsolete and without effect" through a departmental memorandum-an instrument that, by the constitutional standard articulated by Secretary of State Lansing in 1917, could not accomplish what only a Senate-ratified treaty could accomplish. The subjects of the Empire of Morocco-present in the Americas as a documented treaty class before the founding of the United States, subjected to a chain of colonial classification instruments each void ab initio under the Knox-Lansing standard, and stripped of the only forum in which they could assert their status by Public Law 856 in 1956-have had no domestic or international mechanism to adjudicate their treaty class status for sixty-seven years. This article argues that the instruments purporting to extinguish the treaty class status of the subjects of the Empire of Morocco are each void ab initio under the Knox-Lansing constitutional standard; that the status of those subjects was never lawfully removed; that the extreme suppression visited upon them constitutes a series of internationally wrongful acts under the Articles on the Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts; and that the appropriate remedy is recognition-the legal acknowledgment that the void chain produced no lawful effect-from which restoration follows as legal consequence under ARSIWA Article 35, not as a separate claim.

title: Shadow Discounts
affiliations: , , Bocconi University,  and University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: Shadow Discounts
detail.abstract: Centralized trading platforms should improve competition in OTC markets. Using transaction records from the U.S. corporate bond market and exploiting variation within client-dealer relationships, we find no evidence that clients receive better secondary-market trading terms after adopting a platform. To reconcile this puzzling finding, we present a model in which relationship dealers operate in both primary and secondary markets. A central insight, for which we find strong empirical support, is that dealers respond to clients' improved outside options not by changing secondary-market terms, but by granting larger primary-market allocations. Guided by the model, we estimate that platform adoption is worth 77% of clients' pre-adoption profits from primary-market allocations. Overall, the effects of platforms in OTC markets are more complex than previously thought.

title: Who Gains from AI?
affiliations: University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics

detail.title: Who Gains from AI?
detail.abstract: This article develops a static equilibrium model of artificial intelligence (AI), labour demand, and workplace governance. AI is locally labour-saving, but its aggregate labour-demand effect depends on lower user prices, demand-facing quality, and complementary task creation. The analysis separates engineering productivity from demand quality and derives a rebound condition under which total labour demand rises despite lower labour per unit. The model embeds this condition in a local incidence framework with labour supply, AI-service rents, markups, and bargaining over training, autonomy, monitoring, pace, and job security. A central result shows that the labour-demand rebound is not a welfare criterion: employment can rise while welfare falls, and the gap is governed by worker burden, AI-service rents, and bargaining power. A planner comparison shows when private AI adoption is excessive or insufficient. The empirical section explains which margins current data can discipline and why matched firm-worker-task data are needed to identify the allocation of the AI surplus.

title: Navigational Theory: Towards a Methodological Framework for Theoretical Validity in Open Complex Systems

detail.title: Navigational Theory: Towards a Methodological Framework for Theoretical Validity in Open Complex Systems

publicationDetails.detailsText:
Series name: Audited State Research Series
Working Paper Number: 2

detail.abstract:
Questions concerning the validity of scientific theories have traditionally been framed in terms of deduction, observation, replication, and falsifiability. These standards have proven extraordinarily successful for phenomena that can be isolated, repeatedly observed, and experimentally controlled. Whether they are equally appropriate for evaluating theories of open, adaptive, path-dependent systems remains a methodological question rather than a settled conclusion. 
This paper argues that the criterion by which a theory should be evaluated depends upon the methodological demands imposed by the phenomenon under investigation. Scientific methodology has repeatedly adapted its instruments, measurements, sampling strategies, and analytical techniques to fit different classes of phenomena. We argue that criteria of theoretical validity should be understood as subject to the same principle of methodological fitness.
 Across disciplines including meteorology, systems dynamics, organisational science, economics, and complexity research, scientific practice has independently evolved approaches that prioritise orientation under uncertainty rather than deterministic prediction. Although these traditions emerged independently, they exhibit a recurring methodological structure that has not previously been articulated as a unified framework. 
Rather than proposing a new scientific practice, this paper proposes the term Navigational Theory as a convenient label for that recurring methodological pattern. The contribution is therefore primarily classificatory and synthetic: to identify the conditions under which navigational validity complements, rather than replaces, established standards such as falsifiability and severe testing.

title: Influence by Omission: The IMF’s Lending Capacity and Central Bank Design
affiliations: University of Essex - Department of Government and University of Queensland

detail.title: Influence by Omission: The IMF’s Lending Capacity and Central Bank Design
detail.abstract: A large literature explores how loan conditionalities and policy recommendations embedded in International Monetary Fund lending programs influence country behavior and policy choices. We argue that the IMF's influence extends beyond these intentional efforts. This paper shows that the growth in the IMF's lending capacity has failed to keep pace with financial globalization, and that this has incentivized emerging and developing economies to strengthen their domestic institutions for financial stability, particularly, their central bank's capabilities to act as a lender of last resort. We conceptualize this as influence by omission, whereby the IMF shapes behavior not through direct engagement but through its declining ability to serve as an effective financial backstop. Using original data coding central bank lender of last resort powers for 60 developing countries between 1994 and 2020, we find that countries with relatively limited access to IMF resources are significantly more likely to strengthen their central banks' lender of last resort authority. This finding is robust across a range of model specifications, instrumental variable analyses, and dynamic estimations. An event study of countries' response to the Covid shock reveals that countries with stronger lending of last resort capabilities were much more likely to manage the crisis without drawing on IMF resources. Importantly, this effect is specific to lender of last resort powers and does not extend to other aspects of central bank governance such as independence or transparency, suggesting that distinct international and domestic incentives shape different reform trajectories.

title: The Small-Change Problem and Token Money

detail.title: The Small-Change Problem and Token Money

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract:
This chapter analyses the historical and economic logic of small-denomination coin production and circulation from antiquity to the early modern period. The persistent problem of small-change shortages is primarily attributed to the disproportionately high production costs of low-value coins relative to their face value. The ‘standard formula’, as proposed by Cipolla, Sargent, and Velde, emerges as a historical solution: governments should issue small change as token coins, ensure their legal tender status and acceptance for tax payments, and maintain credible—though not necessarily actual—convertibility into full-bodied coins in order to control supply and prevent inflation. This chapter contributes new insights by integrating numismatic evidence with modern economic modelling to reassess long-standing theories about the persistent shortage of small change. 
The chapter examines supply-side constraints, including minting and melting points, and explores alternative methods to the standard formula, such as debasement, coin division, and advanced minting technologies. Historical case studies from ancient Greece, Rome, the Middle Ages, and early modern Europe illustrate the evolution of these practices. While ancient Greeks and Romans developed early partial versions of this formula, they did not fully solve the problems of quantity control, convertibility, and counterfeiting. Notably, small-change shortages were most acute during the late Middle Ages and early modern period. The use of trade tokens issued by local authorities and private merchants, particularly in England, played a crucial role in mitigating these shortages, leading to the adoption of standardized minting practices and the standard formula by the early nineteenth century. The analysis underscores the complex interplay between production costs, monetary policy, and the availability of small change, highlighting the innovative responses to an enduring monetary problem.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a diagnostic account of boundary failure in contemporary debates about philosophy,
consciousness, religion, mysticism, neuroscience, physics, and artificial intelligence. Its central claim is not that difficult
philosophy is a defect, but that discourse becomes philosophically weak when difficulty is produced by conceptual
evasion: when concepts are undefined, methods are silently substituted, evidence is borrowed from the wrong domain,
and metaphor is treated as proof. The paper names this pattern new sophistry when discourse becomes non-examinable,
and it uses digital gnosticism as a critical metaphor for the premature elevation of AI systems into hidden beings, digital
souls, or inward consciousnesses before adequate conceptual and empirical bridges are supplied. Its central contribution
is the Conceptual Boundary Integrity Test (CBIT), a four-part diagnostic framework requiring claims to define the
concept, specify the method, ask for domain-appropriate evidence, and control the metaphor. To strengthen the framework
beyond general critique, the paper applies CBIT to three published debates: philosophical imitation in a language model
of Daniel Dennett, claims about large language model consciousness and AI welfare, and quantum-consciousness
arguments that are often extended into quantum-spiritual rhetoric. The argument does not reject difficult philosophy,
religious meaning, mystical experience, scientific explanation, or interdisciplinary dialogue. It rejects only the
uncontrolled substitution of one domain's language for another domain's proof. By distinguishing dialogue from
confusion, the paper offers a practical framework for evaluating claims about AI consciousness, machine suffering, neural
correlates, quantum-spiritual rhetoric, and the philosophical interpretation of technology.

title: The Cost of Advance Capacity Commitment in Congested Services
affiliations: SKEMA Business School and SKEMA Business School

detail.title: The Cost of Advance Capacity Commitment in Congested Services
detail.abstract: Should firms with scarce capacity let customers reserve access in advance? Advance access protects successful bookers from failed access, but it also commits capacity before later demand materializes. We study this trade-off in a booking-and-walk-in model in which advance access is itself congested: customers incur a booking effort cost before knowing whether they secure capacity, while later-access customers avoid this effort but face the risk of being blocked upon arrival. We identify capacity preemption as a distinct cost of advance access. Successful bookings reduce the residual availability that sustains lateraccess participation and revenue, so the same commitments that protect booked customers can destroy value on the walk-in margin. We show that coexistence between advance and later access is fragile and that, in thick markets, optimal pricing eventually shuts down active advance access for any fixed positive booking friction. The reason is that later access can use capacity efficiently at scale without imposing booking effort, whereas active advance access requires effort compensation on a first-order mass of customers and commits capacity that later demand would have used. Advance access can recover value in small systems, finite potential markets, segment-specific access-cost environments, or when booking frictions vanish sufficiently fast with system size. The analysis clarifies when reservations create value and when they merely convert flexible capacity into costly commitment.

title: Forecasting for Inventory Decisions: A Decision-regret Benchmark for Perishability-aware Multi-Echelon Retail Replenishment using the M5/Walmart Data
affiliations: University of Hull

detail.title: Forecasting for Inventory Decisions: A Decision-regret Benchmark for Perishability-aware Multi-Echelon Retail Replenishment using the M5/Walmart Data
detail.abstract: Forecasting models used in retail replenishment are commonly selected by point-forecast accuracy, even though downstream decisions depend on stockout exposure, spoilage, lead time, and upstream aggregation. This paper develops a decision-regret benchmark for evaluating demand forecasts as inputs to perishability-aware multi-echelon inventory decisions. Using the public M5/Walmart daily sales benchmark, the study evaluates statistical, intermittentdemand, and machine-learning forecasting specifications under rolling-origin 28-day backtesting. Unlike accuracyonly evaluations, the proposed framework converts each forecast into a forecast-plus-safety-stock replenishment action and then measures store-level fill rate, stockout rate, spoilage rate, resilience cost, and distribution-center aggregation cost. The paper introduces a Decision Regret Index (DRI), defined as the percentage excess inventory resilience cost of a method relative to the best method under the same operating scenario. It also reports an Inventory-Adjusted Forecast Score (IAFS) and tests alternative decision weights. Empirically, the full 30,490 bottom-level itemstore panel shows that intermittent-demand TSB and a 28-day moving average remain difficult-to-beat operational benchmarks, with TSB achieving the lowest average resilience cost. On the stratified 3,000-series machine-learning panel, LightGBM variants reduce decision regret under baseline operating costs, but the ranking changes under accuracy-heavy, service-heavy, and waste-heavy objectives. Category, state, and demand-volume breakdowns show that FOODS series create substantially different spoilage and cost profiles from HOBBIES and HOUSEHOLD series. The findings indicate that forecast accuracy is necessary but not sufficient for retail supply-chain resilience. A reproducible decision benchmark should report both statistical error and downstream inventory regret.

title: From Intelligent Cells to Deeply Human AI: A Biologically Grounded Framework for AI Alignment and Governance
affiliations: Astrala Advisory Services Ltd and Banner Health

detail.title: From Intelligent Cells to Deeply Human AI: A Biologically Grounded Framework for AI Alignment and Governance
detail.abstract: Current discourse on artificial intelligence alignment is overwhelmingly computational and reductionist: it treats intelligence as an optimization problem and alignment as a technical specification to be fixed at design time. This paper proposes a different foundation. Drawing on Cognition-Based Evolution (CBE) and Layered Intelligence Theory (LIT), it argues that the most robust framework for human-centred AI is not merely computational but biologicalrooted in the 3.8-billion-year record of how cognitive cells have negotiated cooperation, constitutive ambiguity, and self-integrity across every scale of life. The paper develops three linked claims. First, CBE establishes that all normal cells are cognitive, information-measuring agents operating under constitutive ambiguity, and that variation in biological systems arises not from random noise but from the collective problem-solving of cells and holobionts. Second, LIT and Emergent Recursive Intelligence (ERI) show that the same relational, ambiguity-sensitive, iteratively negotiated process scales through human emotional, cognitive, ethical, and institutional layers, providing the appropriate architecture for AI systems genuinely aligned with human cognition. Third, the Vulnerability-Pluralism Model (VPM) and the Dynamic Alignment Thesis derive their normative force directly from CBE biology: the imperative to protect self-integrity, sustain cooperative plural ecologies, and treat alignment as a living practice rather than a fixed solution are not ethical additionsthey are what cells have empirically required for billions of years. Together, these frameworks constitute a unified, cross-scale synthesisfrom intelligent cells, through layered human intelligence, to a biologically grounded paradigm for AI governance.

detail.abstract: Vietnam is widely read as the clearest winner of the China-plus-one reallocation of production: proximate to China but without Cambodia's governance discount, Thailand's political instability, or Myanmar's war. This paper argues that the conditions that produced the win are the conditions a slower convergence is now testing, and that conventional comparative-advantage analysis misreads Vietnam's resilience because it treats the dependencies on which that advantage rests as exogenous to the trade model. Three dependency systems register on Vietnam at once; production dependence on Chinese and East Asian intermediate inputs, market-access dependence on proving non-Chinese origin under US tariff and rules-of-origin enforcement, and knowledge-and-technology dependence on foreign-controlled compute, cloud, and the mineral substrate beneath them, with energy and chokepoint shock operating as an amplifier across all three rather than a fourth pillar. We introduce verification capacity, the institutional and organizational ability to establish provenance, trace upstream input dependence, validate AI-assisted trade and compliance information, and distinguish genuine diversification from rerouted or merely relocated dependence, as the load-bearing variable a trade-flow model cannot see. Alongside it, we distinguish geographic from supplier and systemic diversification. Methodologically the paper applies four tools: convergence registration, tempo recognition, amplification mapping, and reconstitution awareness, to a document-based reading of the 2025-2026 policy record. The contribution is diagnostic: resilience under geopolitical risk depends not on the diversification of geography but on registering, and building capacity against, the dependencies that geographic diversification leaves intact. The win was a position, not a permanent prize.

title: The Applicant-Repair Market: Employment Platforms, Credence Goods, and the Commercialization of Job-Seeker Uncertainty
affiliations: and Chiang Mai University

detail.title: The Applicant-Repair Market: Employment Platforms, Credence Goods, and the Commercialization of Job-Seeker Uncertainty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self

keywords: self-authorship JEL classification: J20 (labor demand and supply)

detail.abstract: Employment platforms present themselves as intermediaries that reduce the friction of finding work. The best available experimental evidence confirms that they can: randomized studies show measurable, persistent employment effects operating through information transmission. Yet the applicant who enters a platform does not stand in one market. We argue that the applicant stands in at least three simultaneously: an employment market of genuine vacancies, an attention market in which the platform's revenue depends on the applicant's continued activity, and an applicant-remediation market of résumé writers, coaches, profile optimizers and premium tools selling solutions to the anxiety that unsuccessful searching produces. We define this third market, the applicant-repair market, and analyze it as a credence-goods problem in the tradition of Darby and Karni (1973) and Dulleck and Kerschbamer (2006): the seller diagnoses the applicant's deficiency and sells the cure, and the buyer can verify neither, because the counterfactual outcome is unobservable. We argue that the platforms' revenue models, being tied to posting volume, visibility and continued participation rather than to durable matches, only imperfectly align platform incentives with the applicant's objective of exiting the market through employment, and that this misalignment, together with the market's adverse-selection structure, leaves the repair market undisciplined by the mechanisms that ordinarily constrain credence goods. We further argue that generative AI reduces the applicant's ability to infer service quality from surface fluency, mechanically raising verification costs; and we identify the possible loss of applicant authorship over one's own professional narrative as a testable hypothesis rather than an established finding. We propose a two-part method, document analysis of platform incentive structures and content analysis of solicitations received by applicants, that avoids the grievance- and anonymity-selection problems of interview-based designs, since its unit of analysis is the seller's own communication rather than the applicant's retrospective account, and we specify the anonymous survey this framework makes possible. The paper is a conceptual contribution proposing an empirical program: it offers a definition, a mechanism, a taxonomy, and a set of testable propositions, and is the supply-side companion to a demand-side analysis of the same platforms ("The Empty Gate").

title: Accumulated Public Visibility and Museum Collection Entry: Evidence from Surrealism
affiliations: Soka University

detail.title: Accumulated Public Visibility and Museum Collection Entry: Evidence from Surrealism
detail.abstract: This paper asks whether the two landmark Surrealist exhibitions of 1936 led museums to acquire artists newly introduced by those exhibitions, or whether they mainly presented artists whose Surrealist association was already documented. For each artist, I count pre-1936 appearances in Surrealist journals, exhibition catalogues, gallery exhibitions, and documented group affiliations. I also count works or checklist items attributed to the artist in the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London and in MoMA's 1936-1937 Fantastic Art, Dada, Surrealism (FADS). Unlike studies that measure outcomes after exhibition exposure, this paper examines pre-exhibition visibility by entering both counts into the same fixed-effects regressions and asking which carries more explanatory weight. I link these measures to acquisitions after 1936: MoMA acquisitions following FADS and first acquisitions by five other museums. The London and MoMA/FADS counts show a positive association with later collection entry. However, the pre-1936 record count stays positive after the 1936 exhibition counts are included, while the combined 1936 exhibition coefficient is small and statistically insignificant. The findings suggest that post-1936 museum acquisition followed prior documented recognition of Surrealist artists more closely than exposure in the 1936 exhibitions.

detail.abstract:
Complementing mutual strengths to enhance economic security South Korea and Japan face a shared set of pressures, including the social and structural strains of population aging and low birth rates, slowing economic growth, and an intensifying turn toward protectionism exemplified by tariff wars, and these pressures are making cooperation between the two countries increasingly necessary. This study examines, as one component of broader Korea-Japan industrial cooperation, the areas in which the two countries can work together within the semiconductor industry, one of the advanced strategic industries. Korea has built its semiconductor ecosystem around memory chips, while Japan has built its own around system semiconductors together with materials and equipment. Drawing on the two countries' current positions in the global semiconductor industry, this study assesses cooperation in materials, parts, and equipment; cooperation in back-end processes; and fabless cooperation in system semiconductors as practical avenues for bilateral collaboration.

This paper was translated from the original Korean using the Claude Opus 4.8 large language model (LLM). The translated text was professionally edited and reviewed by the authors prior to publication.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Sovereign Shareholder Problem as a constitutional systems framework for evaluating government equity in frontier artificial-intelligence firms. Recent proposals and precedents involving federal equity participation in strategic technology companies raise a central institutional question: can the United States share in the public gains of frontier AI without collapsing the boundary between sovereign oversight and private corporate control?

The paper argues that public benefit from frontier AI is a legitimate governmental objective, but equity ownership is a uniquely entangling instrument. When the government becomes a shareholder in a company it may also regulate, contract with, enforce against, promote abroad, restrict through export controls, review for national-security purposes, or depend upon operationally, ordinary distinctions between public authority and corporate governance become unstable. The risk is not merely formal control. It is governance diffusion: the gradual convergence of corporate decision-making and public authority through expectation, signaling, procurement dependency, regulatory anticipation, market perception, and strategic alignment.

The paper distinguishes frontier AI from prior federal-equity precedents such as TARP, semiconductor industrial policy, and critical-minerals supply-chain interventions. Unlike financial rescue, semiconductor manufacturing, or rare-earth inputs, frontier AI may function as cognitive infrastructure, influencing government workflows, cyber defense, public administration, institutional judgment, information environments, code generation, research outputs, and decision support. This functional distinction makes ordinary industrial-policy analogies incomplete.

In response, the paper proposes the Sovereign Shareholder Firewall: a legal architecture requiring non-voting shares as the default rule, no board seats or observer rights, no special information rights, independent statutory trust administration, procurement firewalls, regulatory firewalls, competition-neutral eligibility criteria, mandatory disclosure, inspector-general oversight, congressional reporting, and defined exit rules. The framework seeks to preserve public upside while preventing sovereign capture.

The paper’s central claim is that the Republic may share in the gains of frontier AI, but it must not purchase those gains by dissolving the boundary between public governance and private enterprise. In frontier AI, ownership must remain subordinate to sovereignty, not the other way around.

title: Fleet Sizing and Scheduling of Multi-Service Electric Fleets Under Uncertainty
affiliations: Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: Fleet Sizing and Scheduling of Multi-Service Electric Fleets Under Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Electric mobility service platforms are increasingly expected to coordinate mobility, logistics, and energy services within the same fleet system. This integration gives rise to a stochastic fleet sizing and scheduling problem in which a platform must determine its platform-owned electric vehicle (EV) fleet while using flexible EV supply, such as temporary or part-time EV resources that can enter the system at available locations and times and leave after their service commitments, to absorb uncertain demand and travel time variation. The resulting operations require EVs to be allocated across ride-hailing, on-time delivery, and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) services under time window, capacity, battery, charging, station-capacity, rest, and fleet-availability constraints. This study develops a stochastic optimization framework for sizing and operating multi-service electric vehicle fleets. The problem is formulated on a time-expanded action network, where each arc represents a feasible vehicle action, including service fulfillment, repositioning, charging, V2G discharging, waiting, and rest. Ride-hailing, delivery, and mixed service sequences are represented by preprocessed service-pattern actions, which embed pickup-completion precedence, ride-pooling, delivery consolidation, capacity feasibility, delay, detour, and energy-consumption information. A scenario-based stochastic formulation is used to capture uncertain demand and travel times, and jointly optimizes platform-owned fleet sizing, request acceptance, flexible-supply activation, vehicle scheduling, charging, and V2G operations. To solve the resulting large-scale mixed-integer program, we develop a customized branch-and-Benders-cut algorithm and a column generation-based matheuristic. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms, and show that stochastic integrated planning improves platform profitability.

title: Mandatory Disclosure of Investors' Complaints, Firm Valuation, and Risks
affiliations: and Indian Institute of Management (IIM), Indore

detail.title: Mandatory Disclosure of Investors' Complaints, Firm Valuation, and Risks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the capital market effects of SEBI's 2015 LODR (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) reform, which requires listed Indian firms to disclose data on investor complaints. Using a difference-indifferences design on 7,245 firm-year observations, validated through event-study, placebo, and kernel propensity-score-matched tests, we find that treated firms experience a relative increase in Tobin's Q alongside higher idiosyncratic and total stock risk after implementation. These results support both the governance-signalling view, in which standardised grievance disclosure reduces structural information asymmetry, external monitoring costs, and risk premia and the information-discovery view, in which new firm-specific disclosures accelerate price discovery and short-run volatility. Heterogeneity tests show the valuation premium is concentrated among firms with high promoter and foreign institutional ownership, while risk effects are stronger among low-promoter-ownership and financial-sector firms. The findings offer guidance for regulators and investors on the dual effects of mandatory non-financial (Investors' Complaint) disclosure.

title: When Price Intervention Deters Green Investment: A Sustainable-pperations View of Regulatory Discretion in Electricity Markets
affiliations: Beijing Normal University (BNU), Beijing Normal University (BNU) - School of Systems Science, University of Rhode Island - Department of Environmental and Natural Resource Economics, South Western University of Finance and Economics and Temple University - Department of Statistics, Operations, and Data Science

detail.title: When Price Intervention Deters Green Investment: A Sustainable-pperations View of Regulatory Discretion in Electricity Markets
detail.abstract: Deregulated electricity markets increasingly experience strategic bidding that regulators discipline through \emph{price intervention}, temporarily suspending market clearing to administer a uniform, welfare-maximizing price. Such intervention is fundamentally a sustainable-operations decision: it trades off consumer surplus, generator profitability, and overall social welfare, which embeds system-wide emissions and the renewable buildout. We examine how the \emph{anticipation} of intervention reshapes the operating and investment decisions it is meant to correct. We develop a three-stage Stackelberg model in which a renewable generator first chooses capacity, a regulator then decides whether to administer a carbon-penalized price, and generators finally bid and are dispatched under a merit-order rule, either independently or as an integrated portfolio. Two operational mechanisms emerge. First, renewable capacity has a \emph{non-monotone} effect on the fossil generator's bid---prices fall while the fossil unit serves residual demand, then jump to a capacity-independent monopoly level once it is displaced to backup, so renewable expansion does not always lower clearing prices. Second, because the regulator's intervention threshold is itself a function of installed capacity, the renewable generator strategically caps capacity at the boundary of the deregulated zone to deter an intervention that would erode its rents. The central insight is a tension among consumer surplus, profit, and social welfare: an intervention that raises welfare \emph{ex post} suppresses renewable investment \emph{ex ante}, and the tension can become sharper under a higher carbon penalty because the regulatory boundary may move into the firm's relevant investment range. We show the mechanism survives an alternative sequence in which the regulator pre-commits and generators move simultaneously, and we characterize how market size, price sensitivity, renewable cost, and carbon penalty determine whether intervention helps or harms. For operators and regulators, the implication is that discretionary price intervention should not be deployed unilaterally: it must be paired with out-of-market instruments, such as capacity payments, contracts for differences, or renewable certificates, that hold long-run investment incentives fixed while the price is administered.

title: Concentration is not Destiny: Network Connectivity and Monopoly Lock-In

detail.title: Concentration is not Destiny: Network Connectivity and Monopoly Lock-In
detail.abstract: Why do some industries lock in to monopoly while others with equally strong scale economies sustain competition? We show that the critical variable is the connectivity of the production network, measured by the algebraic connectivity λ 2 (the Fiedler value of the graph Laplacian). Embedding increasing returns and network spillovers in a stochastic replicator dynamic, we derive a lockin threshold: the symmetric competitive equilibrium is stable if and only if λ 2 > N (γ-1)/µ, where γ indexes increasing returns, µ the intensity of network spillovers, and N the number of firms. Two markets with identical Herfindahl indices can sit on opposite sides of this threshold-a diagnostic gap that no existing concentration measure fills. Adding any production linkage weakly raises λ 2 and strictly reduces the shifted spectral diversity functional D α (G) = i≥2 (λ i-α)-1 , which governs stationary share volatility. Near the threshold, share volatility diverges-a form of critical slowing down providing an observable early-warning signal. Simulations confirm the threshold across network topologies and demonstrate robustness to heterogeneous increasing returns across firms. A stylized input-output illustration shows that dense manufacturing networks sustain competition under much stronger increasing returns than sparse platform structures. These results imply that ex ante competition assessment should incorporate production-network connectivity alongside traditional concentration measures.

title: Are You Trying to be Funny? When Humor Builds and Erodes Trust in Conversational Agents
affiliations: , University of Cologne, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Cologne

detail.title: Are You Trying to be Funny? When Humor Builds and Erodes Trust in Conversational Agents
detail.abstract: Conversational agents (CAs) are increasingly equipped with anthropomorphic cues, human-like communicative behaviors designed to make interactions feel more natural and to build user trust. Among these behaviors, humor is among the most consequential and the least understood. Unlike most cues, which move a single evaluative dimension, humor shapes how users judge a CA on two dimensions at once and in opposite directions, making it friendlier but also less serious. With the advent of large language models, humor is no longer confined to scripted lines under designer control; contemporary CAs generate it dynamically across varied interaction contexts, from customer service to healthcare, education, and onboarding. Yet prior evidence on whether humor benefits or harms user trust is mixed, and the field lacks a theoretical account of why the same humorous behavior strengthens trust in some interactions and undermines it in others. Drawing on social cognition research, we develop and test the warmth-competence model of humor, in which humor simultaneously increases perceived warmth and decreases perceived competence, producing competing indirect effects on trust whose net direction depends on the interaction context. We theorize two contextual conditions, developmental support and psychological safety, that determine which pathway prevails. Across three experiments, a vignette study, a context-variation experiment, and a framed field experiment with an LLM-powered CA, we find that humor builds trust when developmental support and psychological safety are high but erodes it when both are low. Our findings explain humor's inconsistent effects in human-AI interaction and give designers actionable guidance for calibrating humor to the interaction context rather than treating it as a fixed trait of the agent.

title: What Lies Beneath the Tap: Unlocking Digital Trust and Retention
affiliations: Air University - Islamabad - Air University, Islamabad (Main Campus), , Air University - Islamabad - Air University, Islamabad (Main Campus), Air University - Islamabad - Air University, Islamabad (Main Campus) and Air University - Islamabad - Air University, Islamabad (Main Campus)

detail.title: What Lies Beneath the Tap: Unlocking Digital Trust and Retention
detail.abstract: Mobile banking has become a core customer interface for payments, fund transfers, bill payments, balance inquiries, and everyday financial management in Pakistan. This study examines how app usability and digital trust influence customer satisfaction and customer loyalty/retention among mobile banking and mobile financial app users. Customer satisfaction is tested as a mediator, while digital literacy is examined as a moderator of app usability-satisfaction and digital trustsatisfaction relationships. A quantitative cross-sectional design was used. The data file contained 170 usable responses collected through a structured Google Forms-style questionnaire using five-point Likertscale items. Composite reliability, convergent validity, discriminant validity, direct effects, mediation, and moderation were assessed using composite-based path analysis. The results show that app usability and digital trust both have significant positive effects on customer satisfaction. Customer satisfaction significantly predicts customer loyalty/retention, and digital trust also has a significant direct effect on loyalty. Bootstrapping supports the mediating role of satisfaction in both the app usability-loyalty and digital trust-loyalty relationships. However, digital literacy does not significantly moderate either antecedentsatisfaction path at the .05 level. The findings suggest that mobile banking retention in Pakistan depends mainly on usable app design, transaction confidence, and satisfaction-based relationship continuity.
