detail.abstract: This article proposes a macrostructural framework for understanding the evolution of the global economic system through the dynamic interaction of three factors: Production (P), Information (I), and Attention (A) — the cognitive resource of human capital, also associated with the growth or contraction of consumption. Historical cycles of capitalism are examined not merely as monetary or production imbalances, but as a sequential shift of systemic deficits within the P/A/I triad, driven by the decisive role of information technologies in resolving crises and shifting technological paradigms throughout the twentieth century and to the present day. The central thesis highlights the observation that, since the 1920s, the structural trigger— paving the way for other anti-crisis measures or significantly bolstering them—has consistently been a new information architecture — radio, television, the personal computer, the internet, the smartphone, generative AI — each of which resolved the prevailing deficit within the triad and thereby unlocked accumulated productive capacity. The article further advances a prognostic thesis: in the 2030s, the systemic deficit shifts to information indexed by Trust (It), opening the prospect of a new economic order in which verifiable humanity becomes the scarcest and most valuable resource across all three factors.

title: The Manufactured Piracy: Server Shutdowns, Revoked Purchases, and the Legal Case for Game Preservation

detail.title: The Manufactured Piracy: Server Shutdowns, Revoked Purchases, and the Legal Case for Game Preservation
detail.abstract: Publishers sell games and digital media with the vocabulary of ownership. Customers click a button labeled buy, pay a one time price, and receive a confirmation that speaks of their purchases and their library. Later, the vocabulary reverses. Servers are switched off and the product stops working. Licensing arrangements change and purchased titles are deleted from customer libraries without refund. And when customers or archivists act to keep what was sold to them running, the industry supplies the label for their conduct: piracy. This Article argues that the label inverts the law. Under the covenant and condition analysis of MDY Industries, LLC v. Blizzard Entertainment, Inc., a customer who breaches terms of use commits a contract violation, not copyright infringement, unless the term breached is a condition on one of the copyright owner's exclusive rights. Under the logic of Davidson & Associates v. Jung, what makes a community server unlawful is circumvention of access controls combined with the enabling of unauthorized copies; a server that authenticates lawful copies and circumvents nothing commits neither wrong. The first sale doctrine and section 117 protect the owner of a copy, and the licensed rather than sold characterization that defeats those protections under Vernor v. Autodesk, Inc. is a drafting choice made by the seller, in an instrument the buyer never negotiates, contradicted by the seller's own marketing vocabulary at the point of sale. The Article makes three contributions. First, it separates the preservation question from the piracy frame, showing that post-shutdown continuation of play maps onto breach of covenant, not infringement, in the ordinary case. Second, it treats the licensed rather than sold characterization as an instrument to be tested against the realities of the transaction and against disclosure statutes such as California Assembly Bill 2426, rather than as a fact about the product. Third, it evaluates the emerging end of life proposals, including the Stop Killing Games initiative and California Assembly Bill 1921, as the modest regulatory completion of promises the sellers themselves made at the point of sale.

title: Timing Selection and Counterfactual Reconstruction in Synthetic Control Designs: A Placebo-in-Time Decomposition
affiliations: and

detail.title: Timing Selection and Counterfactual Reconstruction in Synthetic Control Designs: A Placebo-in-Time Decomposition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects. Ethics approval and informed consent are therefore not applicable. The analysis is based entirely on Monte Carlo simulation using synthetically generated data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Strong pre-treatment fit, the standard credential of a synthetic-control study, cannot rule out a treatment date selected on private information about the future untreated path. We isolate that channel. Given a benchmark timing distribution, the mean untreated reconstruction error under actual timing equals the benchmark mean error plus a covariance term measuring how actual timing reweights candidate-date errors. The split is benchmark-relative-changing the benchmark reallocates the fixed actual-timing error between the two terms-so the decomposition is a disciplined diagnostic accounting that forces the timing benchmark to be stated explicitly. We adapt weighted randomization inference to placebo-in-time diagnostics, state conditions under which the comparisons are interpretable, and give a joint sensitivity analysis for single-event applications. In our baseline simulation, signal-based timing generates bias of about 12 percent of the treatment effect even when pre-treatment fit is, by construction, indistinguishable from that of a clean benchmark case.

title: What Motivates Giving in Dictator Games? Estimating the Role of Social Norms and Preferences
affiliations: National Research Council of Italy, PSB Paris School of Business, National Research Council of Italy and University College London

detail.title: What Motivates Giving in Dictator Games? Estimating the Role of Social Norms and Preferences
detail.abstract: Altruistic cooperation is well documented in laboratory and field settings, yet the motivations that sustain it remain debated. Two leading explanations emphasize outcome-based social preferences and social norms, with the former focusing on distributional outcomes and the latter on compliance with socially appropriate action. We systematically study the relative importance of these competing explanations by conducting structural estimation on a dataset of constructed by combining individual-level data from Dictator Game experiments. Additionally, we study the role of social norm strength-the extent to which social norms are clearly defined and widely shared-in translating what should be done into action. We find that generosity in Dictator Games is jointly determined by outcome-based social preferences and social norms, and that the influence of social norms on behaviour is strongly associated with their strength.

title: A Gaussian Recency Score for Detecting Breaks in Central-Bank Policy-rate Inertia
affiliations: Middle East Technical University

detail.title: A Gaussian Recency Score for Detecting Breaks in Central-Bank Policy-rate Inertia
detail.abstract: Policy rates change rarely; the practical question for a rate-watcher is whether the next break out of a stay is predictable from the bank's own recent history. We propose the Gaussian Policy Index (GPI), weighting recent rate moves by a Gaussian kernel in the lag, and a hybrid (GPIH) adding a country-specific stay-streak hazard, both tuned only on each country's training data. On monthly BIS policy rates for 48 economies (3,658 test months, 768 breaks), GPIH attains the best F 1 (0.430) and κ (0.204) under a 10,000-draw country-cluster bootstrap. Under class imbalance the always-stay rule is most accurate yet detects no breaks, and several machinelearning models on the same information set collapse toward the same silence; GPI significantly outperforms them on F 1. Breaks cluster after recent activity, not long pauses.

title: Short-Selling Constraints and Multiple Asset Markets
affiliations: University of Southampton

detail.title: Short-Selling Constraints and Multiple Asset Markets
detail.abstract: We study two interacting asset markets where investors are heterogeneous and shortselling of risky securities is prohibited. We provide conditions on expectations such that short-selling constraints are active or slack in equilibrium for an arbitrary number of investors. More importantly, we present two cases of economic interest in which our active-slack analytics make it tractable to find a solution, such that the consequences of short-selling constraints can be studied absent the usual curse of dimensionality.

title: Does Holding Anti-Democratic Leaders Accountable Backfire? Evidence from Bolsonaro's Arrest in Brazil

detail.title: Does Holding Anti-Democratic Leaders Accountable Backfire? Evidence from Bolsonaro's Arrest in Brazil

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest, financial or otherwise, that could have influenced the research reported in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Prior to data collection, the study received approval from the relevant Institutional Review Board (IRB Approval No. 2025-S-1) at the author’s institution.
declarations.funderStatement: Financial support for this research was provided by a British Academy/Leverhulme Small Research Grant and the University of Reading Tyler Prize. Particular gratitude is extended to the Tyler family for their generous support of early-career researchers and for continuing Professor Cyril Tyler's legacy of fostering innovative research.

detail.abstract: Whether holding anti-democratic leaders accountable strengthens or weakens democracy remains one of the unresolved questions in contemporary debates about democratic backsliding. Sceptics argue that prosecuting elected leaders who challenge democratic institutions may deepen affective polarisation, erode trust in democratic institutions, and ultimately undermine democratic legitimacy. Yet there is little evidence on whether these concerns materialise in practice. I address this question by examining public reactions to the enforcement of legal accountability following Jair Bolsonaro's arrest during fieldwork for a nationally representative survey in Brazil. Exploiting this unexpected event to compare respondents interviewed immediately before and after the event, I estimate the immediate political consequences of a highly salient act of democratic accountability. Contrary to widespread concerns, I find no evidence that accountability increased affective polarisation, reduced support for democracy, or diminished trust in democratic institutions. These findings challenge the widespread assumption that democratic accountability necessarily carries substantial political costs.

title: Generative Creativity, the Incentive Function of Copyright, and European Technological Sovereignty
affiliations: University of Salerno

detail.title: Generative Creativity, the Incentive Function of Copyright, and European Technological Sovereignty
detail.abstract: This paper examines the tension between generative artificial intelligence and copyright law, arguing that the current crisis concerns neither the aesthetic quality of works produced by AI systems nor the protection of style, both historically extraneous to copyright doctrine, but rather the economic incentive function of copyright. It is argued that automatically protecting AI-generated works would create industrial-scale enclosures benefiting the few actors who control computational infrastructure, with no connection whatsoever to the creative effort that the authorial system is historically meant to remunerate. The analysis closes with a reflection on the geopolitical implications of European dependence on US-based AI providers, in light of the most recent regulatory developments and public enforcement actions.

title: The Geometry of the Regime Space: How the Strategic-Inattention Boundary Bifurcates at a Cusp

detail.title: The Geometry of the Regime Space: How the Strategic-Inattention Boundary Bifurcates at a Cusp
detail.abstract: The many models of this programme are one payoff, and the boundary that sorts them into strategic-inattention and active regimes is not a single surface: past a cusp in the production response it bifurcates into a hysteretic band, and it is inside that band-on the productive substrate, at high stakes-that the programme's dynamic traps live. An atlas (Claim A, the stage) places every model-the foundational observability-gradient equilibrium, the vertical cascade, the rotation dynamic, the single-monitor composition, the observation portfolio, its rotation and coupled extensions-as a point or region in one regime space with coordinates (g, δ, α 0 , ∆, Φ, ψ) under one of two gate substrates, sharing one local boundary δ * (g, ψ); each placement is verified against a direct global-optimum solve. The mechanical result (Claim B) is that δ * is a single clean boundary only for production response g below a cusp curve g cusp (δ); above it the boundary splits into three sheets-a lower spinodal (which is δ * itself), a Maxwell global switch, and an upper spinodal-with hysteresis, and a single δ * mispredicts the global regime by a gap that grows with g and δ. What separates the model families is not which side of a boundary they fall on but the width of the band at their operating stakes: at the weak-production corner (δ = 0) the band is a razor-thin, lowstakes sliver that the programme's static models-operating far above it-never feel, so they are effectively single-regime; on the productive substrate (δ > 0) the band is wide and rises to the operating stakes, which is exactly where the dynamic (rotation) models sit. The fold is organized like a cusp-one behaviour variable (attention) folding as two controls vary, the production response g and the stake ψ, with the production value δ sliding the pinch-but the pinch is boundary-constrained rather than a textbook interior cusp, so the catastrophe language is used as an analogy (§5). Its policy corollary is sharp: inside the band, recovery from the inattention trap requires crossing the lower spinodal, not the Maxwell point-the band's width is the size of the over-correction a regime redesign must fund.

title: Constitutional Amendment Bill No. 3 and Zimbabwe's Vision 2030: A Legal Assessment of The Business Case for Extended Political Tenure

detail.title: Constitutional Amendment Bill No. 3 and Zimbabwe's Vision 2030: A Legal Assessment of The Business Case for Extended Political Tenure
detail.abstract: Constitutional Amendment Bill No. 3 has renewed debate in Zimbabwe over the relationship between constitutional reform, political tenure, governance stability and the attainment of Vision 2030. The Bill is advanced partly on the premise that extended political tenure can promote policy continuity, reduce governance uncertainty, improve long-term planning and strengthen investor confidence. This article critically examines whether that business case provides a constitutionally defensible basis for altering political-tenure arrangements under the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 20) Act, 2013. It employs qualitative doctrinal legal research, supported by comparative constitutional analysis and law-and-economics scholarship, to assess the Bill's implications for constitutional supremacy, democratic accountability, separation of powers, judicial independence, the rule of law and sustainable economic development. The article analyses the proposition that political continuity can facilitate implementation of long-term national development programmes, including industrialisation, infrastructure development, institutional reform and inclusive growth envisaged under Vision 2030. It argues, however, that policy continuity alone cannot establish a credible investment environment or guarantee sustainable development. Investor confidence and effective economic governance depend equally, and often more fundamentally, on constitutional certainty, predictable regulation, protection of property and contractual rights, transparent public administration, institutional integrity and independent courts. Drawing comparative lessons from Rwanda, Uganda, Botswana and South Africa, the article demonstrates that there is no automatic relationship between prolonged political tenure and developmental success. While continuity may support administrative coordination, constitutional reforms that diminish periodic electoral accountability or are perceived to consolidate political power may weaken public trust, institutional legitimacy and governance credibility. The article concludes that the developmental objectives associated with Vision 2030 are legitimate, but they must be pursued through constitutionally faithful means.

title: CAPM-X: Domestic Funding Exposure and the Equity Premium Puzzle

detail.title: CAPM-X: Domestic Funding Exposure and the Equity Premium Puzzle

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This theoretical study does not involve human participants, personal data, animals, or clinical material.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The Capital Asset Pricing Model prices systematic risk through a single source, the covariance of asset returns with the market portfolio, and treats the risk-free rate as a common investment alternative available to all investors. This is the correct benchmark for discounting risky payos against a safe asset. The model does not separately identify how the domestic funding environment is transmitted into rms' marginal nancing costs, renancing risk, distress risk, and equity valuation. We develop a conditional two-factor extension in which rms with equal market beta can require dierent expected returns because they carry dierent loadings on a priced domestic funding-stress factor. The extension keeps the investor's risk-free rate as a common intercept and adds a priced funding-factor loading to expected excess returns. We distinguish the raw domestic funding-stress state, S t+1 , from the factormimicking return used in pricing tests, F t+1 , and from the pass-through of funding conditions into rms' marginal debt cost, ϕ i , which is an economic mechanism and not itself the equity-return loading γ i,F,t. Under a linear conditional stochastic discount factor representation, equal-beta rms with dierent funding loadings have dierent expected returns whenever the funding factor is priced. We propose this channel as a potential, not demonstrated, decomposition of the equity premium: if the market portfolio carries positive loading on the priced funding factor, part of the aggregate premium that appears excessive under a one-factor CAPM may compensate investors for bearing domestic funding risk that market beta does not separately identify. Monetary and credit aggregates remain economically relevant as informational precursors of the funding-stress state, not as the priced object itself. Whether they help identify a priced funding-stress state, and whether the implied compensation is quantitatively material, are empirical questions that the subsequent papers in this program address directly.

title: Testing for Bubbles: What Variable to Use in Recursive Right-Tailed Unit Root Tests?
affiliations: CREATES, Aarhus University, Aarhus University, University of Aarhus - CREATES and Aarhus University - CREATES

detail.title: Testing for Bubbles: What Variable to Use in Recursive Right-Tailed Unit Root Tests?
detail.abstract: Right-tailed unit root tests assume the testing variable follows a martingale in the absence of a bubble under the null. However, neither the stock price nor the price-dividend ratio satisfies this condition. We address this implementation challenge by showing how to scale the stock price to induce martingale behavior. Simulations show that the adjusted price gives correctly sized right-tailed unit root tests, whereas tests are oversized when using the stock price and under-or oversized when using the price-dividend ratio. The adjusted price and the price-dividend ratio display similar power, while log-transforming the testing variable reduces the power substantially.

title: The Population Myth: The Real Factors Behind Where Elite Athletes Come From
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Population Myth: The Real Factors Behind Where Elite Athletes Come From
detail.abstract:
The 2026 World Cup, now underway across the United States, Canada, and Mexico, opens on a fact that should embarrass the most common theory of athletic talent: the two most populous nations on Earth are not in it. China and India, home to roughly 2.8 billion people, thirty-five percent of humanity, could not claim two of forty-eight places in the most expanded field in World Cup history, and China missed despite a decade of state-directed investment in academies, facilities, and national-team development explicitly designed to make it a contender. Meanwhile the question that has followed the United States for decades is back in its usual form: how can a country this large, this wealthy, and this devoted to youth sports have spent so long losing to nations a fraction of its size? It is not an idle complaint. FiveThirtyEight has built data features around it, and in Soccernomics the economist Stefan Szymanski and journalist Simon Kuper show, with a formal model, that a nation’s population and wealth are surprisingly weak predictors of its soccer success. This paper argues that the same faulty assumption drives a more familiar American debate, the one that runs every draft season about which states produce the most professional athletes. The athletes in question are the ones those debates are really about: the players who reach the five major North American men’s leagues (the NFL, NBA, NHL, MLB, and MLS) and the U.S. Olympic team, where the country’s best ultimately compete. The belief that bigger places should produce more of them is intuitive, endlessly repeated, and largely wrong. Population predicts raw volume, not efficiency: once you adjust for the size of the youth population a place draws from, the rankings scramble, and the states and countries that overperform are explained not by how many people they have but by the structure of the athletic ecosystem those people grow up in. Population, this paper argues, is only one of four or five structural forces that determine where elite athletes come from, and far from the most interesting.
The paper’s central mechanism is opportunity cost. Every child has finite time; every community has finite fields, coaches, and public dollars. A place that offers a dozen organized sports spreads its talent across all of them; a place that offers two concentrates its talent into those two. That single economic idea explains a puzzle that population cannot: why the United States, with enormous youth-soccer participation, has historically underperformed much smaller nations in men’s international soccer, and why some American states feed the five major men’s professional leagues at far higher per-capita rates than others. Diversity of athletic opportunity is, for any single sport’s pipeline, a tax. The same breadth that enriches a population’s overall athletic life thins the funnel into any one sport.
Around that spine, the paper develops four structural drivers (climate, public and private investment, culture and political economy, and media-driven capital allocation) and one behavioral mechanism, early specialization versus multi-sport sampling, through which those structures shape individual athletes. It scopes its evidence deliberately to men’s major-league and Olympic pathways, tests the framework against the U.S. soccer case and a contrasting case, and closes with the conditions under which the argument would be proven wrong

title: On The Optimal Precision of Central Bank Communication
affiliations: Wake Forest University - Department of Economics, Wake Forest University - Department of Economics and Yonsei University

detail.title: On The Optimal Precision of Central Bank Communication
detail.abstract: How precisely should central banks communicate about the future policy rate path? We study this question in an incomplete information model where the central bank chooses the precision of its communication. The key feature is an endogenous cost of precision: clearer communication makes financial markets respond more strongly to policy path news. A simple overlapping generations framework links this financial market volatility to volatility in the real economy that central banks care about. The benefit of precision is that it helps agents make more informed decisions, and we show how the central bank optimally balances the two. High-frequency monetary policy announcement data provide evidence consistent with the model's amplification mechanism.

title:
The Agentic Shelf 
A Structural Framework for Brand Decision Architecture in Multi-Turn AI Recommendation Systems
affiliations: Independent and

detail.title:
The Agentic Shelf 
A Structural Framework for Brand Decision Architecture in Multi-Turn AI Recommendation Systems
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Agentic Shelf as a formal structural framework describing the displacement of purchase-decision authority from the human consumer to the AI model in multi-turn commerce conversations. Building on the empirical findings of the Linkage Gap (Sheals and de Rosen, 2026, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20761232), which documented 87.3% brand-level displacement across 1,427 brand probes, this paper situates that finding within the broader academic literature on long-context degradation, multi-turn reliability, and brand bias in large language model outputs. We formalize the distinction between the Linkage Gap, a retrieval and activation failure addressable through structured evidence infrastructure, and the Reasoning Gap, a structural model judgment not addressable through evidence alone. We argue that existing generative engine optimization (GEO) and AI-visibility measurement approaches address only the first of three necessary layers, possession, mention, and decision-stage activation, and that decision-stage activation is both commercially determinative and presently unmeasured by the tooling available to most brands.

title: Adaptive Antitrust Agency Enforcement and the Use of AI: Legal and Policy Implications
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), USC Gould School of Law and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) - Lally School of Management

detail.title: Adaptive Antitrust Agency Enforcement and the Use of AI: Legal and Policy Implications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: There was no funding of this paper.

detail.abstract: Antitrust enforcement increasingly targets markets where pricing, product visibility and consumer interaction are mediated by adaptive AI systems. This Article argues that the core enforcement challenge is not complexity but continuous redesign: firms use algorithmic tools to alter the technical manifestation of harmful conduct while preserving supracompetitive prices, collusion or exclusionary effects. We distinguish detection from recognition, and show that enforcement effectiveness depends on how quickly agencies learn new patterns of conduct. When recognition is slow, firms can engage in persistent “cat-and-mouse” redesign, creating an arms race between agency and firm AI capabilities. We develop a framework in which AI investments by agencies reduce harm only if they cross a deterrence threshold; sub‑threshold, partial adoption can worsen congestion and increase workload without diminishing aggregate harm. Although elaborated in an antitrust setting, the recognition‑redesign dynamic generalizes to consumer protection domains such as phishing, robocalls and investment scams, where legality is clearer and adaptive evasion is pervasive. The Article concludes that frustration with case‑by‑case antitrust enforcement should not automatically justify broad ex ante regulation; instead, existing institutions must become more adaptive in their use of AI or risk declining relevance.

title: The Structural Evolution of Higher Education Governance: A Comparative Review of the Dhaka Central University Ordinance 2026 and the Dhaka University Order 1973
affiliations: Dhaka College

detail.title: The Structural Evolution of Higher Education Governance: A Comparative Review of the Dhaka Central University Ordinance 2026 and the Dhaka University Order 1973
detail.abstract:
This study provides a comparative legislative analysis of the Dhaka University Order of 1973 and the Dhaka Central University Ordinance of 2026 to evaluate their structural alignment with modern higher education standards. The university system traces its evolutionary lineage back to 859 CE, when Fatima al-Fihri founded the University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco (Esposito, 2011). European institutions later adapted this traditional residential madrasa framework into scholastic corporations, establishing the foundational principles of institutional autonomy and structured academic governance (Makdisi, 1981; Ruegg, 1992). 
In Bangladesh, public university management now features two contrasting legislative approaches. The 1973 Order establishes a centralized, democratic campus framework that concentrates all administrative, examining, and disciplinary burdens onto a single academic core (Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, 1973). This legacy model faces operational strain and systemic delays when managing mass student populations across expanded networks. Conversely, the 2026 Ordinance introduces a federal, networked cluster model designed to govern seven large metropolitan public colleges under a unified central management layer. 
This comprehensive review examines specific statutory provisions regarding institutional scale, executive authority, research decentralization, and quality control systems. The findings indicate that the 2026 Ordinance provides a superior framework for modern mass higher education by incorporating permanent quality assurance cells, streamlined executive decision-making paths, and localized postgraduate research pipelines. This structural design effectively separates large-scale undergraduate logistics from primary research hubs, balancing academic accountability with operational efficiency to meet global accreditation standards.

title: Finite-Horizon Optimal Switching for Mean-Reverting Asset Trading via Double Obstacles and PINNs
affiliations: Konkuk University, Kyung Hee University - Department of Applied Mathematics  and Kongju National University

detail.title: Finite-Horizon Optimal Switching for Mean-Reverting Asset Trading via Double Obstacles and PINNs
detail.abstract: We study a finite-horizon optimal switching problem for trading a mean-reverting asset with proportional transaction costs. The investor switches between two regimes, being flat and holding one share, while any remaining long position is liquidated at the terminal date. Using the dynamic programming principle, we derive a coupled system of quasivariational inequalities for the flat-state and long-state value functions. By introducing the value-difference function, we reduce this coupled system to a scalar parabolic double obstacle problem. We establish the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of a strong solution, analyze the associated buying, waiting, and selling regions, and characterize the optimal trading rule through two time-dependent free boundaries. We further reconstruct the original switching value functions from the double obstacle solution and prove a verification theorem showing that the resulting free-boundary strategy is optimal. For numerical computation, we propose a hard-constrained physics-informed neural network formulation in which the two-sided obstacle constraint is satisfied exactly by construction. The remaining variational inequalities are enforced through an active-set-dependent residual loss. Numerical experiments show that the proposed method accurately captures the free boundaries and illustrates their dependence on transaction costs and volatility.

title: Sequential Search and Oligopoly Competition: A Counter-Example to Equilibrium Existence
affiliations: Shandong University

detail.abstract: This paper revisits the consumer search and price competition model of Wolinsky (1986). When the market has a finite number of firms, I provide a counterexample to show that equilibrium may not exist.

title: Guided by Norms, Seen Through Stereotypes: Muslim Women's Labor Market Expectations
affiliations: University of Technology Sydney, , University of Technology Sydney (UTS) and University of Technology Sydney

detail.title: Guided by Norms, Seen Through Stereotypes: Muslim Women's Labor Market Expectations
detail.abstract: This paper studies how minority women's labor-market expectations are shaped by community norms and external stereotypes. We use a relational belief-elicitation design that holds fixed the attitude being guessed and varies the respondent's relation to the target group. Beliefs about a reference group measure perceived norms; beliefs about a group outside the respondent's reference network measure stereotypes; beliefs about what an external audience believes about one's own group measure anticipated stereotypes. We implement the design in surveys of Muslim students, working professionals, and general students in Australia, eliciting own attitudes and higher-order beliefs about women's freedom to work and maternal employment. Among Muslim women, expected labor supply with a preschoolaged child is strongly associated with own views and perceived in-group norms about maternal employment. External stereotypes concentrate instead on women's freedom to work: Muslim men's actual support is high, yet professionals and general students substantially underestimate it, and Muslim women anticipate this underestimation. These anticipated stereotypes are associated with Muslim women's expected labor supply even after conditioning on the corresponding in-group norm. The paper contributes a framework for measuring norms, stereotypes, and anticipated stereotypes jointly, and suggests that community norms and external stereotypes are distinct but potentially reinforcing belief layers.

title: Do Tolerance-Based Operational Frameworks Exist for Net-Zero Buildings? A Scoping Review of Current Standards and Practices
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Do Tolerance-Based Operational Frameworks Exist for Net-Zero Buildings? A Scoping Review of Current Standards and Practices
detail.abstract: The credibility of net-zero building claims increasingly depends on operational performance rather than design intent. While existing standards, frameworks, and certification schemes acknowledge the importance of in-use performance, it remains unclear whether mechanisms exist to verify net-zero performance under realistic operational conditions characterized by human behaviour and climatic variability. This study investigates whether tolerance-based operational verification frameworks currently exist for net-zero buildings. A scoping review methodology was adopted to map and analyze internationally recognized standards, frameworks, and certification schemes relevant to building energy and carbon performance. Practice-based documents were treated as primary evidence and evaluated against four analytical criteria: operational (in-use) evaluation, explicit tolerance bands, time-based performance rules, and decision/action logic. Academic journal literature was synthesized thematically to provide contextual understanding and support interpretation. The results demonstrate that no reviewed standard or framework integrates all components required for tolerance-based operational verification. While elements such as post-occupancy evaluation, measurement and verification protocols, and annual performance disclosure are present, these approaches remain partial, descriptive, or process oriented. Explicit tolerance thresholds, persistence criteria for underperformance, and formal decision/action mechanisms are consistently absent. The findings indicate that the primary limitation of current net-zero practice lies not in the availability of performance data, but in the absence of governance frameworks capable of judging operational performance under real-world variability. By clarifying this gap, the study provides a foundation for future doctoral research on tolerance-based approaches to operational performance verification in net-zero buildings.

title: An Exploratory Study of Adolescent ACG Consumption and Commercial Activity in Beijing
affiliations: International School Suva

detail.title: An Exploratory Study of Adolescent ACG Consumption and Commercial Activity in Beijing
detail.abstract: In recent years, under Beijing's "Internet Plus" environment(L.Wang, 2017), ACG culture has become one of the city's emerging cultural industries and has remained active within its cultural market. Adolescents have gradually become one of the major consumer groups within this sector. From the perspective of regional economics, this study explores how the consumption behaviors of adolescents toward ACG-related products may influence the development of Beijing's cultural and entertainment economy. This research combines questionnaire surveys and field observation. A questionnaire distributed through the Wenjuanxing platform collected 23 valid responses from adolescents in several districts of Beijing. In addition, field observations were conducted at the iJOY Expo held at the China National Convention Center and at several ACG-related retail stores between July and December 2025. The findings suggest that adolescent ACG consumption in Beijing is generally characterized by relatively small but frequent spending, diverse information channels, and strong preferences for shopping mall-based retail spaces and visually appealing products. At the same time, the study observes that Beijing's ACG-related retail industry presents differentiated spatial distribution patterns across districts, reflecting local commercial conditions, industrial clustering effects, and differences in consumer concentration. The case of Beitou Shopping Park further suggests that ACG-related commercial activities may contribute to the revitalization of retail spaces and surrounding consumption activities. Although limited by its small sample size and exploratory scope, this study provides a localized perspective for understanding the interaction between youth cultural consumption and urban commercial development in Beijing.

title: Encouraging Experimentation: Persuading Individuals to Experiment Through Explanation
affiliations: Illinois Institute of Technology - Stuart School of Business, IIT and Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School

detail.title: Encouraging Experimentation: Persuading Individuals to Experiment Through Explanation
detail.abstract: We analyze whether explaining the benefits of the information generated from experimentation can encourage individuals to experiment with an unknown option. In an experiment, subjects repeatedly face a two-decision one-armed bandit problem. At the start of the first bandit, subjects receive one of four possible messages regarding the bandit's two options. Two messages encourage initially experimenting with the unknown option and two messages encourage initially selecting the known option. After the first bandit, subjects repeatedly face this same bandit and receive this same message. We find that subjects who repeatedly receive the message explaining the informational benefits of experimentation consistently experiment at the highest rate across bandits. Importantly, this message leads to more experimentation than a control message that suggests experimentation without explaining its informational benefits. Our results suggest that it is possible to encourage experimentation when an individual faces a single bandit and that repeated messaging can lead to a durably higher experimentation rate across bandits. We also find that providing this explanation in one bandit environment can lead to more experimentation in a different bandit environment.

title: Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond

keywords: Credit Card Spending JEL Codes: D12

detail.abstract: We introduce a novel monthly county-level consumption dataset constructed from spending data on over 350 million credit cards in the Federal Reserve's Y-14M reports, covering over 3,000 U.S. counties since 2014. We first show that the data closely approximate traditional consumption measures, explaining 92 percent of the variation in monthly adjusted personal consumption expenditures (PCE) growth at the national level and capturing meaningful cross-sectional variation in annual adjusted PCE growth at the state level. As a proof of concept, we use the county-month panel to estimate heterogeneous consumption responses to monetary policy shocks across the county-level income distribution, an analysis infeasible with traditional consumption data. We find that low-income counties exhibit larger spending declines than high-income counties, consistent with heterogeneous agent New Keynesian models. Finally, we provide practical guidance for researchers working with similar data, discussing coverage, sample composition, and the approximation of credit card spending from credit bureau data.

title: Autopsy of a Myth: Dissecting the Fallacy of Anatocism in Amortization Systems
affiliations: University of São Paulo (USP) - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Autopsy of a Myth: Dissecting the Fallacy of Anatocism in Amortization Systems

contentType.other: English version of a paper originally written in Portuguese and accepted for publication.

detail.abstract: Compound capitalization-or anatocism-in loans is prohibited by law in Brazil, although it is widely practiced. Judicial decisions often require that such products be evaluated under simple capitalization. This article demonstrates, through four original alternative arguments, that anatocism exists in a family of amortization systems called the General Amortization System-SGA, in which interest is the product of its rate and the previous outstanding balance. This includes the Constant Amortization System (or Hamburg system)-SAC, the Price (or French) system, and the American system. In addition, the article develops an original and economically grounded model to construct Simple-Capitalization Amortization Systems-SACS, for infinitely many payment or amortization configurations, extensible to multiple and simultaneous focal dates. The elegance of the model lies in its direct analogy with the case of compound capitalization, which makes its implementation immediate and allows it to function as the natural counterfactual.

title: The Architecture of Restraint: Capacity-Backed Money, War Finance, and Sovereign Credibility
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Architecture of Restraint: Capacity-Backed Money, War Finance, and Sovereign Credibility
detail.abstract: This article argues that monetary architecture is not neutral with respect to war. Existing fiat systems often allow states to defer, conceal, and socialize the costs of aggression, while sanctions and credit downgrades typically operate only after political bargaining has already delayed the consequence. The article develops the Providence Value Unit (PVU) as a capacity-backed monetary blueprint. It is an institutional-design proposal, not an operational regime. Its central claim is that sovereign credibility can be anchored in three auditable reserve families: human capital, institutional reliability, and productive continuity. The article specifies four linked instruments: a Composite Capacity Index (CCI), Sovereign Capacity-Indexed Bonds (SCIB), an Automatic Degradation Protocol (ADP), and a Global Value Unit (GVU). Together, these instruments would make aggression financially visible earlier and progressively more costly than existing monetary architectures allow. It identifies five mechanisms of restraint: war destroys the value anchor; automatic degradation narrows the war-finance escape route; peace is monetized through lower capacity-linked borrowing costs; public scoring reduces the information asymmetry on which manufactured consent depends; and responsible governance of frontier AI and the postquantum transition becomes part of sovereign credibility. The article does not claim that monetary design can abolish war. Its claim is limited but testable. A capacity-backed architecture could make aggression harder to hide financially, less institutionally costless, less technologically deniable, and harder to sustain. The article also specifies the measurement, adoption, and attribution constraints under which that claim could be tested.

title: HAICO-SLR Guide: Conducting and Reporting Human-AI Collaboration in Systematic Literature Reviews
affiliations: , Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul - UFRGS, Universidade Federal de Ciências da Saúde de Porto Alegre (UFCSPA), Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS),  and Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre (HCPA)

detail.title: HAICO-SLR Guide: Conducting and Reporting Human-AI Collaboration in Systematic Literature Reviews
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in scientific research, yet its role in systematic literature reviews (SLRs) remains methodologically underdeveloped. This study maps how generative AI has been utilized across SLR stages, identifying its benefits, risks, and ethical implications through a systematic review of 124 papers retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed, analyzed via qualitative content analysis. The mapping reveals a fragmented and unstandardized landscape along three dimensions: (i) usage, with AI most often applied to screening and summarization, rarely involved in methodological decision-making, and unreliable in database searching; (ii) benefits of AI adoption; and (iii) risks and ethical concerns, for which we identified mitigation practices. From these findings, we propose the HAICO-SLR Guide (Human-AI Collaboration in Systematic Literature Reviews Guide). This framework represents a methodological advancement by formally classifying each review stage as exclusively human, automatable, or hybrid, shifting the focus from addressing AI in isolation to defining explicit operational boundaries within human-AI collaboration. The guide also outlines how to report AI use in SLRs and the role of the researcher who guided it. Designed as a flexible, structured tool, HAICO-SLR can be seamlessly coupled with existing review protocols (e.g., PRISMA). This adaptability allows researchers across diverse fields, including the social sciences, health sciences, and engineering, to standardize procedural reproducibility and mitigate risk when conducting SLRs. The framework positions AI as a co-intelligence agent within a human-in-the-loop paradigm, enforcing a dual-reporting mechanism that elevates transparency to shared methodological co-responsibility.

title: Skill-Selective Settlement Barriers: Spatial Misallocation and the Incidence of Hukou Reform
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Skill-Selective Settlement Barriers: Spatial Misallocation and the Incidence of Hukou Reform
detail.abstract: China's remaining internal migration barrier is skill-selective: settlement rules bind on less-educated migrants while waiving requirements for the college-educated. We cast this barrier as a skill-specific destination wedge in a quantitative spatial equilibrium, recover it from the channel structure of settlement policy across 227 cities, and find it equivalent to as much as a 72 percent consumption tax on low-skill entry into the most restrictive cities. Identification comes from period matching: the migrant stock responds to the policy vintage under which it accumulated, current flows to the current vintage, and each is unrelated to the other's. Removing the wedge raises aggregate output by 4.3 percent and welfare by 1.9 percent, almost entirely through the spatial reallocation of low-skill labor. The incidence inverts the politics of reform: the largest winners are the high-skill residents of restrictive cities, whose wages the inflow of complementary labor restores, while the only losers are their registered low-skill incumbents-a narrow, compensable constituency. The counterfactual is the generalequilibrium endpoint of the services-by-residence path Chinese policy adopted in May 2026.

title: Neuroanthropological Economics: Theory and Foundations

detail.title: Neuroanthropological Economics: Theory and Foundations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: This working paper summarises the theoretical architecture of Neuroanthropological Economics (NAE)-a new discipline proposed by the author that integrates neuroscience, anthropology, developmental psychology, trauma studies, and institutional economics into a unified framework for understanding economic behaviour in contexts of chronic poverty, institutional distrust, and historical dispossession. NAE advances three foundational arguments: that economic agents are neurobiologically constituted rather than abstractly rational; that economic behaviour is culturally embedded rather than universally uniform; and that economic agency is historically shaped by intergenerational trauma in ways that neither mainstream nor heterodox economics currently theorises with adequate precision. The paper introduces the NAE paradigm agent-Homo Neuroculturalis-as the formal replacement for Homo Economicus, operationalised through two complementary personas: the Contextual Agent (universal diagnostic) and the Ubuntu Agent (African-context prescriptive). It presents a thirteen-index NAE measurement architecture, introduces the Neuro-Anthropological Leadership Model (NALM) as NAE's applied delivery vehicle, and situates NAE within the broader history of economic thought as a paradigm-level challenge to its ontological foundations, not a revision of them.

title: Gold and Bitcoin: A Quantitative Comparative Analysis
affiliations: and Holy Spirit University of Kaslik (USEK)

detail.title: Gold and Bitcoin: A Quantitative Comparative Analysis
detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between two of the most important assets in the modern market, Bitcoin and gold. While gold has historically been considered a safe-haven asset, Bitcoin has emerged as a new digital alternative to gold. Using daily data from 2014 to 2025, the study applies a purely quantitative comprehensive mathematical framework that includes risk and return analysis, correlation analysis, regression models, granger causality tests, cointegration analysis, vector autoregression and impulse response functions. The results indicate that Bitcoin is a poor alternative to gold for central banks and hedgers, and a successful substitute for gold for speculators and investors, providing higher returns at a higher risk. Furthermore, even though correlation is low, investors may achieve substantial return by focusing on short term market shocks. One of the important results also include that a significant change in Bitcoin price may influence the price of Gold, but changes in the latter do not impact the former. In conclusion, the study recommends the use of Bitcoin and Gold as complements, not as substitutes.

title: Outcomes: Worldwide Evidence from Government Expenditure Strategies

detail.title: Outcomes: Worldwide Evidence from Government Expenditure Strategies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest to be declared.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The corresponding lead author has all proper rights reserved for the manuscript with associated replication packages.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding received.

detail.abstract: Employing global coverage of economies across income groups, the study examines the impacts of global geopolitical risk (GPR) on green growth outcomes through government spending decisions. Under global geopolitical uncertainty, governments are likely to depress innovation investment expenditures on research and development (R&D). The depressed innovation investments have been driven by national incentives to prioritize military expenditure for crossborder security forces due to heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Such investment expenditure incentives lead to shrinking total reserves, for which economies may have to decrease overall government expenses and increase short-term debt financing. Depressed innovation investments with GPR-induced precautionary motives lead to unfavorable green growth outcomes, including carbon efficiency levels, renewable energy consumption, and green electricity output. The global impacts of global geopolitical uncertainty have been heterogeneous across income groups, with high sensitivity to low-income countries. The public expenditure strategies and green growth outcomes follow the aggregate multidimensional developments of financial institutions and markets as well as the stages of growth. Our global study offers insightful empirical evidence on the consequential outcomes of geopolitical uncertainties on the delayed green transition efforts of economies worldwide. Even though the impacts of GPR remain uneven across income groups and regions, mitigated geopolitical risks are critical to green growth targets globally for the Sustainable Development Goals.

title: Constructing a Two-country Input-output Model for Türkiye and Iraq: Structural Path Evidence from the Development Road Project

detail.title: Constructing a Two-country Input-output Model for Türkiye and Iraq: Structural Path Evidence from the Development Road Project
detail.abstract: This study constructs a two-country input-output model for Türkiye and Iraq to evaluate the production transmission channels of the Development Road Project. The analysis focuses on the 2025 benchmark year and models the project as a USD 37 billion final investment demand shock, consisting of USD 20 billion in Türkiye and USD 17 billion in Iraq. Previous Iraq-focused matrix studies include input-output tables for 2000 and 2009 and a 2011 social accounting matrix. Building on this limited literature, the paper constructs a new, updated, and publicly documented 2025 benchmark input-output table for Iraq from national accounts data and integrates it with Türkiye's aggregated and RAS-updated table. Given the constraints of Iraqi sectoral statistics, both economies are harmonised under a common 9-sector classification. Bilateral Türkiye-Iraq trade flows are internalised through a Chenery-Moses-type trade-share approach. Structural path analysis is then used to trace how the shock propagates across sectors and borders. The results show that the shock generates USD 73.1 billion in total production effects, with an aggregate multiplier of 1.97. Türkiye accounts for USD 46.3 billion and Iraq for USD 26.8 billion.

title: How Sensitive are Synthetic LLM Participants to Experimenter-demand Effects?
affiliations: University of Zaragoza - Deparment of Management and Strategy and University of Zaragoza

detail.title: How Sensitive are Synthetic LLM Participants to Experimenter-demand Effects?
detail.abstract: Are inferences based on synthetic samples from large language models (LLMs) robust to experimenter demand effects? We bound demand effects across eight LLMs from three providers and nine canonical economic tasks, benchmarking our estimates against a human sample of 7,517 participants. Our results are consistent with large demand effects in LLM samples. Making the researcher's expectation explicit—weak demand treatment-shifts—responses by 1.223 standard deviations for LLMs, compared with 0.157 among humans. Making the researcher's request explicit—strong-demand treatment—shifts responses by 1.714 standard deviations for LLMs and 0.571 among humans. On a common unit-interval scale, demand wording shifts average LLM choices by 22.3% of the feasible action range under weak demand and 48.1% under strong demand, compared with 3.8% and 15.2% in the human benchmark. The magnitude of these effects varies across tasks, providers, and individual models, but no provider or model family approaches the relatively low level of demand responsiveness observed in the human sample. These findings suggest that LLM agents may be useful for some experimental applications, but inferences based on synthetic samples should explicitly assess and bound potential demand effects.

title: Privacy, Testing, and Sanov Duality
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Privacy, Testing, and Sanov Duality
detail.abstract: We develop a unified mathematical framework connecting three central but apparently distinct problems in statistical science: differential privacy (Wasserman and Zhou, 2010), nonparametric goodness-of-fit testing via the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) statistic, and pre-Bayes risk calibration (Rubin and Sethuraman, 1965). The thread linking them is the empirical cumulative distribution functio, which serves simultaneously as the de Finetti sufficient statistic under exchangeability, the object whose large deviations are governed by Sanov's theorem, and the natural domain on which privacy-preserving mechanisms operate. We establish that all three frameworks inhabit a single asymptotic scale hierarchy-the CLT scale (fixed-α testing), the large-deviation (LDP) scale (Chernoff-Stein, hypothesis testing under pure differential privacy), and the moderate-deviation (MDP) scale at which Bayes risk is optimally calibrated. The canonical exponential tilting the information-geometric I-projection of Q onto a moment constraint set-emerges as the universal answer to four seemingly different questions: the optimal privacy mechanism (McSherry-Talwar exponential mechanism), the Bayesian posterior under an exponentialfamily prior (de Finetti), the mixed Nash equilibrium in the Cover-Thomas football game (von Neumann minimax), and the Rubin-Sethuraman Bayes-risk-optimal test (MDP calibration). The MDP threshold √ log n on the scaled statistic corresponds to a natural privacy budget of ε = log n nats and to the log-pole singularity of the horseshoe prior that makes it the canonical Bayes-risk-efficient prior for KS-type testing.

title: Trade Openness, Foreign Direct Investment and Industrial Growth: Evidence from Selected ECOWAS Countries
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria, Abuja, , Central Bank of Nigeria and Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: Trade Openness, Foreign Direct Investment and Industrial Growth: Evidence from Selected ECOWAS Countries
detail.abstract: This study examined the impact of trade openness and foreign direct investment (FDI) on industrial growth in selected ECOWAS countries. Motivated by the mixed evidence on the effectiveness of openness-led development strategies in Sub-Saharan Africa, the paper investigated whether increased integration into global markets and foreign capital inflows have translated into meaningful industrial expansion in the region. The empirical analysis employed panel data techniques, beginning with pooled Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimation, followed by Fixed Effects (FE) and Random Effects (RE) models to account for unobserved country-specific heterogeneity. The results indicated that trade openness exerts a positive and statistically significant impact on industrial growth, particularly in the long run, suggesting that greater participation in international trade enhances industrial performance through market expansion and efficiency gains. In contrast, FDI did not appear to support industrialization and had a negative effect under dynamic specifications, reflecting its concentration in extractive sectors with limited linkages to domestic manufacturing. The study therefore recommended a strategic reorientation of FDI toward manufacturing and value-adding sectors, enhancement of domestic linkages, and improved institutional and infrastructural frameworks to ensure that both trade and investment contribute to sustainable industrial transformation in the region.

title:
Back to Solana Beach Days: 
Kaypro and the Human-Cognition Standard Before the Predictive LLM Machine

detail.title:
Back to Solana Beach Days: 
Kaypro and the Human-Cognition Standard Before the Predictive LLM Machine

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: This essay ranges across many scenes of writing, but its argument turns on two of them, set side by side. In the first, dated to the early 1980s, a writer composes book-length prose on a Kaypro portable computer running CP/M and WordStar: the human supplies every word, while the machine registers keystrokes and drives a printer without contributing content of its own. In the second, dated to 2026, a writer issues a prompt and a hyperscale datacenter returns prose, figures, and calculations whose epistemic status the writer is often poorly positioned to confirm. I argue that the difference between these scenes is not primarily a matter of efficiency, nostalgia, or deskilling, but of where formal causation sits and, more decisively, of whether the human can still vouch for—can warrant—what reaches the page. The Kaypro produced zero semantic surplus: nothing in its output supplied wording or substance the writer had not authored. The predictive model produces such surplus by design, and the cost it imposes is a verification premium that, when left unpaid, lets unwarranted content enter the record as settled knowledge. Drawing on my own experience coauthoring two TAB Books manuals on the Kaypro, on the documentary record of the machine preserved at the Smithsonian, and on a contemporaneous writer’s account of the Kaypro as a liberating instrument, I frame the early personal computer as the limiting case of a transparent, pass-through tool and the predictive model as its structural opposite. The Kaypro workflow becomes a benchmark—a human-cognition standard against which the modern human–machine relation can be measured and, where appropriate, found wanting. The standard it names is not that the machine must never supply wording, but that the human must remain the warrant of the result, whether by authoring it or by auditing it. As the disciplined heir to the Kaypro I set the bounded instrument—a small, source-bound language model the scholar runs locally over a curated corpus, here the Maestro–Stradivarius Language Model (MSLM). Opaque in mechanism but bounded in provenance, it admits machine-supplied wording only on terms the human can audit, and so carries the Kaypro’s standard into 2026 by discipline rather than by incapacity. Appendix A sets out, verified against primary sources and cited, a practical path by which a reader may build one. Appendix B then carries that instrument into use, walking one revision cycle in which machine-supplied surplus is audited against an admitted corpus and only what traces to it is kept. That instrument, however, is reached for only at need. Appendix C measures the choice by the scale of the corpus: where the sources can be read in full, an unaided scholar—online search to find, hand and judgment to digest, citation to bind—keeps the standard whole with no language model at all, and is the default; the bounded instrument is warranted only where the corpus outgrows what one reader can hold, and the opaque frontier model at no scale. Appendix C sets out that scale schema and a step-by-step build for the case that warrants it. That landscape is itself the endpoint of a documented drift: Appendix D samples a single national computing-magazine spine from 1980 to 2015 and traces, issue by issue, the migration of warrant off the scholar’s desk—and with it a measurable slide along the theoria–techne gradient, from technique that serves the scholar’s thinking toward technique that performs it.

title: Bayesian World Models
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Bayesian World Models
detail.abstract: A world model learns a compressed, predictive representation of an environment and lets an agent plan by "dreaming"-rolling the model forward in latent space rather than in the costly real world (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018). We argue that such a model, if it is to be rolled forward and optimized against, must be Bayesian. A world model is a family of one-step predictive kernels, and the only family that composes coherently into a joint law over trajectories is a σadditive posterior predictive, which under exchangeability is Bayesian updating on an unknown mechanism (de Finetti). Three consequences follow. First, large language models already are Bayesian world models: next-token prediction is an amortized Dirichlet-multinomial posterior predictive whose noninformative limit is a Bayesian bootstrap over corpus continuations, with temperature as tempering and in-context learning as posterior updating (Dalal and Misra, 2024; Rubin, 1981; Newton et al., 2021). Second, conformal prediction gives finite-sample marginal coverage for a single step but cannot serve as the belief state: by the separations of Datta et al. (2025), per-step coverage does not compose across a rollout, and a controller planning in a rankreduced dream is provably deficient. Third, "cheating the world model" (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018) is off-support misspecification, curable only by epistemic uncertainty that widens where data are scarce-exactly the mechanism that safe model-based agents such as LAMBDA (As et al., 2022) use, and which lets us prove that a multi-step safety constraint is a path-space functional requiring the coherent kernel. The design principle is one line: carry a σ-additive predictive kernel as the state; attach conformal wrappers only as terminal guardrails.

title:
What is Truth?

Sam and Nel’s Round Trip: A Bit’s Journey from a Brooklyn Café to a Hyperscale Datacenter and Back, and the Errors It Cannot See

detail.title:
What is Truth?

Sam and Nel’s Round Trip: A Bit’s Journey from a Brooklyn Café to a Hyperscale Datacenter and Back, and the Errors It Cannot See

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: This essay traces two bits of a three-word query — “What is Truth?” — from a Brooklyn café to a hyperscale datacenter and back, keeping a single error ledger across the round trip. The journey divides into transport and computation. In transport — Wi-Fi, glass fiber, the long-haul backbone — every fault the bits can suffer is one the system is built to detect and repair, and the ledger runs green. Inside the datacenter the character of error inverts: runtime arithmetic admits silent corruption no error-correcting code guards; the training corpus admits faithfully-wrong “knowledge” no validation at scale can certify; and fluent prediction admits confabulation, the confident falsehood produced even when hardware and corpus are sound. The essay’s thesis is a distinction between two activities a computing system performs — transporting symbols, which modern infrastructure guards with magnificent fidelity, and certifying that they are true, for which a bare predictive model stands in no position, a limit tool-augmented systems relocate rather than remove. Two instruments make this measurable: the running ledger and the Epistemic Richter Scale, on which each escaping error is rated by order of magnitude. Read through them, one figure recurs at every scale — transport guarded, certification withheld — a self-similarity the essay calls Mandelbrotian. Two appendices test the thesis from opposite directions: Appendix A turns a panel of six frontier systems outward onto a single loaded question and finds them enacting the prediction rather than being merely described by it; Appendix B turns five systems inward to rebuild the essay’s own instruments blind, and finds them reproducing the argument’s shape while missing its hidden rule and over-certifying the result. The essay closes at the café counter, where a human’s grounded inexactitude proves truer than the machine’s bit-perfect groundlessness, and argues that truth is earned by labor and a shared world, not delivered stamped and certified. What the single journey exposes is general: every large language model inherits its world model from a corpus that is epistemically unsound and largely unverifiable — only a small fraction of it ever validated by knowledgeable and otherwise qualified human validation teams — so a flawed world model is the structural inheritance of them all, not the defect of any one system.

title: The Platform-Property Paradox
affiliations: University of Houston Law Center

detail.title: The Platform-Property Paradox
detail.abstract:
In digital markets, the essential functions of property turn against each other. Common law property divides the world into mine, yours, and others’ by excluding non-owners. This exclusion strategy generally serves three essential functions in economic ordering: internalizing externalities by channeling positive and negative effects on third parties back to the owner; creating modularity by dividing the world into manageable chunks; and promoting liberty by enabling private control over resources. These functions usually work in harmony. As this Article shows, not so in the digital platform economy.

Digital networks create enormous value by facilitating communication, transactions, and knowledge production—value that grows exponentially as more people participate. Through property-like entitlements, law enables platforms like Amazon, Google, and Facebook to exclude others from these networks and thereby capture that exponential value. This legal architecture encloses digital networks just as law once enclosed common meadows. The resulting control over digital networks disproportionately benefits incumbents. Paradoxically, this Article argues, property's internalization function captures value so effectively that it fuels industrial concentration. Rather than creating modularity, this concentration amplifies systemic complexity and interdependence; instead of promoting liberty, it entrenches economic dependence, centralizes control, and breeds oligarchy.

This Article reveals property design as a central and underappreciated driver of platform dominance, one amenable to legal correction. While scholarly and policy responses to economic concentration have largely emphasized antitrust enforcement and sector-specific regulation, this Article foregrounds the upstream design of property entitlements. The Article challenges the classical prescription that property should maximize internalization of externalities. When platforms internalize network effects under that logic, the result is industrial concentration with deep structural harms to modularity and liberty. Reconciling property’s essential functions thus requires curtailing property-like entitlements, expanding the digital commons, and recalibrating the remaining protections.

title:
The Applewood Estates Evidence-generating Operational Research Constitution 
Governing Principles for an Evidence-generating Operational Research Program
affiliations: Liberty University

detail.title:
The Applewood Estates Evidence-generating Operational Research Constitution 
Governing Principles for an Evidence-generating Operational Research Program

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author served as a compensated technology and organizational modernization consultant for Applewood Estates during the operational activities described in this paper. This relationship is disclosed in the interest of transparency. The conceptual framework, analysis, interpretations, and conclusions presented are the independent scholarly work of the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This manuscript presents a conceptual and methodological framework and does not report research involving human participants, identifiable personal data, or regulated human-subjects research. Institutional ethics approval was therefore not required. Future empirical studies under the Applewood Estates Evidence-Generating Operational Research Program will obtain all required institutional approvals before collecting human-participant data.
