The operational modernization activities described were conducted as part of a professional consulting engagement through EWTECHNERD LLC. No sponsor influenced the conceptual development, analysis, interpretation, or preparation of this manuscript.

detail.abstract: Small organizations frequently undertake modernization initiatives involving technology, facilities, financial systems, governance, and workforce development. While these initiatives often improve operational performance, they rarely produce systematic organizational evidence that can support executive decision-making, institutional learning, or scholarly research. This paper introduces the Applewood Estates Evidence-Generating Operational Research Program (AE-EGORP), a constitutional framework that integrates operational modernization with continuous evidence generation. Rather than treating consulting and research as separate activities, the framework embeds documentation, evidence validation, organizational learning, and publication directly into implementation activities. The paper presents six original conceptual contributions: the Evidence-Generating Operational Research Framework (EGORP), Evidence Architecture, the Operational Evidence Lifecycle (OEL), the Evidence Maturity Model (EMM), the Applewood Operational Modernization Index (AOMI), and a Dual Workstream Architecture integrating IT and Facilities Modernization with Financial Evidence Architecture. Together these constructs establish a governance model through which modernization activities simultaneously improve organizational performance and generate transferable organizational knowledge. Although developed within a small property management organization, the framework is designed for adaptation across nonprofit, governmental, educational, healthcare, faith-based, and commercial organizations. This constitutional working paper serves as the methodological foundation for a broader research program that will empirically evaluate and refine the proposed constructs through future implementation studies.

title: Contextual Trust in AI-driven Financial Services: A Systematic Review of How user Type, Decision Risk, and Individual Characteristics Shape Trust in Algorithmic Decision-making

detail.title: Contextual Trust in AI-driven Financial Services: A Systematic Review of How user Type, Decision Risk, and Individual Characteristics Shape Trust in Algorithmic Decision-making
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence now mediates consequential decisions across financial services, yet adoption has outpaced the value institutions realise, and user trust is widely identified as the binding constraint. This systematic review reconceptualises trust in AI-driven financial services as a contextual, calibration-worthy state rather than a stable, monolithic trait. It maps how trust is formed, calibrated, and broken across two user populations, customers and employees, operating at three decision-risk levels. Following PRISMA 2020 and a preregistered OSF protocol, it synthesises 60 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2018 and 2026. Each study is coded along the Ability-Benevolence-Integrity (ABI) dimensions of the Mayer, Davis and Schoorman trust model, adapted for human-AI interaction, by user type and decision-risk level, and by dominant failure mode. Three findings stand out. First, an "empty cell": no study examines trust in employee-facing AI used in routine, lowstakes back-office workflows, precisely where automated decision-making is densest. Second, a stark asymmetry: algorithm aversion is documented in 28 studies but automation bias in only one. Third, a synthesised gradient in which the salience of the three ABI dimensions shifts with decision risk, with ability dominating at low stakes and procedural integrity and benevolence becoming jointly necessary at high stakes. From this evidence the review develops the Contextual Trust Calibration Framework (CTCF), a five-layer model that reorients the field from maximising trust to calibrating it, and derives six testable propositions, including a falsifiable prediction about the empty cell.

title: When AI Talks Back: Behavioral Consequences of AI-Generated Social Interaction on Platforms
affiliations: Tsinghua University and

detail.title: When AI Talks Back: Behavioral Consequences of AI-Generated Social Interaction on Platforms
detail.abstract: Social media platforms have begun deploying generative-AI social bots that comment on ordinary users' posts, uninvited, in the same public streams where humans interact. We argue that such bots create hollow ties: interactions that supply the social presence of being responded to while carrying none of the relationship investment a human comment signals. Using a 34-month panel of 20,134 Weibo users and 22.1 million comments around the platform's deployment of its Comment Robot, we combine propensity-score matching with a doubly robust staggered difference-indifferences design to trace what routine bot exposure does to users' participation and to their human ties. AI comments activate participation where human attention is scarce: low-popularity users post 16% more and receive 41% more human comments. The activation, however, is relationally hollow: the extra reply effort that costly human comments normally command flattens, high-popularity users withdraw in an ordered cascade that begins with their own replying, and human ties formed deeper into exposure are progressively less likely to persist (-5.8 to-12.8 percentage points). Aggregated with equal weight, the bot looks beneficial; weighted by where audience-bearing content is produced, platform-level human interaction turns negative in the long run. The spillover weakens when AI comments are distinguishable from human ones, and it runs through the bot's informational rather than emotional content. Engagement volume is thus an incomplete metric for governing social bots; preserving the legibility of human attention is the operative design lever.

title: Life-Cycle Effects of Taxation and Social Safety Net Pensions on Labor Supply, Savings, and Human Capital
affiliations: University of Chittagong

detail.title: Life-Cycle Effects of Taxation and Social Safety Net Pensions on Labor Supply, Savings, and Human Capital
detail.abstract: This paper structurally estimates a dynamic life-cycle model of consumption, savings, labor supply, human capital accumulation, and retirement using data from the Bangladesh Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES 2016-2022) and the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics Labour Force Survey. We evaluate the effects of the personal income tax schedule and the Old-Age Allowance (OAA), Widow Allowance, and voluntary contributory pension programmes on household behaviour over the life cycle. The model incorporates learning-by-doing human capital, uninsurable wage risk, credit constraints, discrete hours choices, and non-absorbing retirement. Counterfactual simulations show that the current means-tested OAA is poorly targeted: expanding coverage and eliminating the implicit 100% tax at the eligibility threshold yields a consumption-equivalent welfare gain of 3.1% while raising female labour supply by 6.4%. A revenueneutral shift to a universal social pension dominates the status quo on both efficiency and distributional grounds. Results are robust to alternative assumptions on the Frisch elasticity and the intertemporal elasticity of substitution.

title: Economic-Aware Agentic Private Networks
affiliations: , Celona Inc., Chongqing University and NIT, Warangal

detail.title: Economic-Aware Agentic Private Networks
detail.abstract: Private wireless networks are increasingly becoming operational infrastructure for factories, ports, airports, logistics campuses, hospitals, mines, and energy facilities. In these environments, connectivity decisions affect production continuity, safety, quality control, logistics flow, operating cost, and return on investment. However, most autonomous network-control frameworks still optimize technical key performance indicators such as latency, throughput, reliability, coverage, and spectral efficiency, rather than the enterprise value created by those improvements. This paper introduces Economic-Aware Agentic Private Networks, a framework in which bounded autonomous or semi-autonomous agents reason over technical state, spectrum state, application criticality, business-economic state, governance rules, and historical evidence to select or recommend private-network actions. The proposed framework treats spectrum, edge compute, slice capacity, energy, redundancy, and operational attention as economic assets. It combines business-intent interpretation, service-level specifications, digital-twin validation, supervisorspecialist agent orchestration, economic scoring, and governance-constrained actuation. The paper formalizes economic-aware private-network control as a constrained enterprise-utility maximization problem and presents a reference architecture, data model, closed-loop workflow, illustrative enterprise use cases, scenario-based numerical validation, and a sensitivity analysis across workload, criticality, cost, energy, and SLS-penalty assumptions. The numerical results compare economic-aware control with KPI-only, static-priority, and cost-minimizing baselines and show that economic-aware control provides the strongest utility-cost tradeoff while preserving critical SLSs.

title: Cooperation is Not a Safety Property: A Position on Adversarial-Resistant Agent Identity

detail.title: Cooperation is Not a Safety Property: A Position on Adversarial-Resistant Agent Identity
detail.abstract: Recent technical-governance proposals for AIagent identity-provider-side schemes, signed agent cards, decentralized-identifier registries, multi-stakeholder frameworks-defend an honest issuer against external forgery, spoofing, and theft. They share an architectural assumption: identity is issued or attested by an entity willing to cooperate. We invert the threat model. The party that issues identity is often the party a safety case must hold accountable, so cooperation is itself the vulnerability, and it fails in four structural cases: open-source models with no provider, partial-cooperation labs with variable transparency, adversarial providers with incentives to evade attribution, and jurisdictional asymmetries beyond regulator reach. The governance regimes that depend on identity-attribution, liability, audit, deterrence-fail when they are most needed. We propose adversarial-resistance as a design requirement, derive four conditions it entails, and argue that the structurally non-cooperative cases are where agent-identity safety research is most needed.

title:
The Body Cannot Consent 
Inferred Mental States, Consumer Spatial Computing, and the Triple Gap Between Data Protection, the AI Act, and Neurorights
affiliations: University of London

detail.title:
The Body Cannot Consent 
Inferred Mental States, Consumer Spatial Computing, and the Triple Gap Between Data Protection, the AI Act, and Neurorights
detail.abstract: Consumer spatial-computing headsets such as Apple Vision Pro depend on continuous physiological sensing-gaze, fixation, pupil dilation and fine motor behaviourfrom which systems can infer attention, arousal, intent and sensitive traits. The argument here does not depend on proving present third-party access to raw gaze data; its concern is the legal status of mental-state inference from bodily interaction signals and their proxies. Such inference, the paper argues, occupies a triple gap: data-protection law is built around consent and declared data, not involuntary signals; the EU AI Act prohibits emotion recognition only in the workplace and education, leaving consumer settings insufficiently prohibited rather than unregulated; and neurorights frameworks are anchored to neural signals these devices never record. Building on the established notions of mental data (Ienca & Malgieri) and cognitive biometrics (Magee, Ienca & Farahany), the contribution is not the concept but its legal operationalisation: a doctrinal account of the AI Act's consumer-venue gap, a comparative reading of Chile's Emotiv ruling extended from neural signal to inference, an operational test and a model clause, and a signal-agnostic per-se rule for consumer spatial computing. The analysis is conceptual and doctrinal; it relies on no human-subjects data.

title: Personalized Bayesian Causal Inference: The Probability of Individual Effect
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, George Mason University and

detail.title: Personalized Bayesian Causal Inference: The Probability of Individual Effect
detail.abstract: The average treatment effect (ATE) is an accounting identity: a population average whose value depends on the reference population, not on the underlying mechanism. We argue the correct estimand for individual decisions is the probability of benefit. We give four results. (i) A positive ATE is compatible with harm to a majority of units, illustrated with the 1930 Lanarkshire milk experiment and the RECOVERY dexamethasone trial. (ii) A hierarchical Bayesian model with a horseshoe prior on sparse effect heterogeneity, fit via Generative Bayesian Computation (GBC) after Neyman-orthogonal residualization, achieves the sparse minimax rate O(s log p/n) and circumvents Ritov et al.'s (2014) curse-of-dimensionalityappropriate ("CODA") critique of high-dimensional Bayesian inference by orthogonalizing the nuisance functions before the Bayesian step. (iii) A Bayesian difference-indifferences estimator with individual random effects  on the treatment indicator delivers  exactly; across 200 replications a panel simulation shows about a fourfold smaller individual-effect RMSE and near-oracle signdecision accuracy relative to two-way fixed effects (TWFE), which, giving one number for all units, is near chance. (iv) The excess decision regret of double machine learning (DML) relative to the personalized Bayes rule is non-negative, a weak-dominance result, with three identifiable sources: uncertainty, heterogeneity, and sparsity.

title: Navigating Artificial Intelligence in Education: Pathways to Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion
affiliations: , University of Groningen, University of Groningen, University of Groningen, University of Groningen, University of Groningen and University of Groningen

detail.title: Navigating Artificial Intelligence in Education: Pathways to Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion
detail.abstract:
The recent ranking of 28th in The World's Most International Universities 2025 demonstrates the University of Groningen's (UG) reputation for its high-quality, inclusive education serving diverse student populations and its commitment to fostering diversity and student success. However, recent developments threaten this progress through budget cuts that may lead to fewer educational opportunities, limited investment possibilities and reduced individual student support. Simultaneously, educators and students increasingly rely on Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools as convenient solutions amid limited resources, creating a critical intersection between digital technology adoption and Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) principles.
This white paper emerges from collaborative work between two Communities of Practice at the UG —one focused on DEI in teaching and learning, another on AI in Education. The paper's objective is to promote ethical selection, development, and use of digital tools grounded in DEI principles that support educational practice at the UG. It aims to guide broader community discussion on ethical AI integration while representing educator concerns and offering practical strategies.
Presented in the paper are three main calls for action. The first promotes ethical selection and use of digital tools through criteria for inclusivity, accessibility, and sustainability. Also proposed is exploring educational applications for AI literacy via transparency, responsive professional development, and aligned policies. The third recommendation is to involve the UG community in ethical AI integration discussions within a structure of educators and policymakers. These recommendations aim to address the urgent need to ensure that the necessary digital systems serve diverse populations equitably.

title: Generative AI and Venture Scaling
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Management Department and Fundación Instituto de Empresa, S.L. - IE Business School

detail.title: Generative AI and Venture Scaling

declarations.funderStatement: We acknowledge support from the Spanish Ministerio de Ciencia, Innovación y Universidades and the Wharton AI & Analytics Initiative.

detail.abstract: A central challenge in venture scaling is that growing external output typically demands a corresponding increase in human and financial resources. This study investigates how the adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reshapes this relationship. Using a panel of U.S. software startups in 2018-2024 and a difference-in-differences design centered on ChatGPT’s release, we find that GenAI adoption does not significantly affect overall hiring or venture funding. Instead, GenAI-adopting startups experience greater adoption of complementary technologies and significant output growth, as reflected in increased website traffic and faster commercialization outcomes. While total headcount remains unchanged, GenAI adoption induces a compositional shift away from junior roles toward senior-level positions. This organizational change is reflected in an increase in internal promotions, suggesting that GenAI enhances the value of labor by accelerating upskilling and internal career advancement. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that GenAI allows nascent firms to accelerate scaling without a proportional expansion in headcount.

title: Low-Tech Sector, High-Complexity Innovation: Firm-Level Patent Specialisation in Türkiye's Dairy Industry

detail.title: Low-Tech Sector, High-Complexity Innovation: Firm-Level Patent Specialisation in Türkiye's Dairy Industry
detail.abstract: This article examines whether firms operating in conventionally low-technology sectors can develop measurable technological specialisation through production-system innovation. Focusing on Türkiye's dairy industry, the study analyses the patent and utility model portfolio of SÜTAŞ, one of the country's largest integrated dairy firms, for the period 2016-2024. Rather than treating patents as simple counts of inventive output, the article constructs a firm-level patent landscape by combining International Patent Classification codes, WIPO 35 technology fields, NACE sectoral correspondences, technology-intensity classifications, concentration indicators, diversity measures, portfolio similarity coefficients and relative technological specialisation indices. The analysis asks whether SÜTAŞ's patent portfolio reflects a narrow product-based food technology profile or a broader and more complex production-system architecture. The findings show that the firm's technological profile is not confined to dairy products or food chemistry. Instead, it is structured around a dual core of dairy product technologies and production-system engineering, including packaging, filling, transport, special machinery, heat treatment, hygiene, process control and resource-efficiency technologies. SÜTAŞ accounts for a substantial share of dairy-related patent and utility model applications in Türkiye and displays strong relative specialisation in A01J, A23C, B65B and B67C technology classes. The article contributes to low-tech innovation, firm-level innovation systems and patent landscape literatures by showing that low-technology sectoral classifications may conceal complex, cumulative and patentable technological capabilities at the firm level. The results also suggest that patent data can support technology mapping and industrial policy design in agrifood manufacturing.

title: Spectral-Gap-Protected Non-Abelian Quantum Memory: Certified Exponential Lifetime via a Constructive Yang–Mills Mass Gap
affiliations: Universal Standard Axiom Corp

detail.title: Spectral-Gap-Protected Non-Abelian Quantum Memory: Certified Exponential Lifetime via a Constructive Yang–Mills Mass Gap
detail.abstract: We propose and analyze the Spectral-Gap-Protected Non-Abelian Quantum Memory (SGP-NQM), a cryogenic, large-scale quantum memory whose logical qubits are encoded in non-local Wilson-loop sectors of a three-dimensional lattice Yang–Mills (YM) simulator with gauge group SU(2) or SU(3). The central theoretical obstacle to certifying exponential memory lifetime has been the absence of a nonperturbative, constructive proof that the four-dimensional YM mass gap ∆YM > 0 is strictly positive with computable bounds. We demonstrate that a constructive solution to the Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap Millennium Prize Problem, supplied by the QASL-P framework, removes this obstacle in its entirety. Given constructive bounds ∆YM ≥ cG ΛMS (with cG explicitly computed for SU(2), SU(3)), we derive a rigorous continuum-to-lattice mapping guaranteeing a simulator spectral gap ∆eff ≥ f(∆YM), which implies: (i) exponential suppression of thermally activated error strings at Top ≪ Tc = ∆eff /kB; (ii) exponential scaling of logical lifetime τ (L, T) ≥ τ0 exp(γL) with system linear size L; and (iii) deterministic, specification-level reliability certification derived from first-principles QFT. We present two physical implementation routes (cold-atom Rydberg/alkalineearth optical lattices; superconducting Josephson-junction arrays), a five-criterion Compton-Class Safety certification (CCS-RH), and a concrete falsifiability protocol specifying experimental refutation conditions. The SGP-NQM constitutes the first quantum memory architecture whose reliability guarantee is anchored to a solved Millennium Prize problem.

title:
The Anticipatory Economy and Ambient Commerce 
AI, Geospatial Intelligence, and the Architecture of Presence-Triggered Trade
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
The Anticipatory Economy and Ambient Commerce 
AI, Geospatial Intelligence, and the Architecture of Presence-Triggered Trade
detail.abstract: A new coordination logic is forming across retail, logistics, and consumer services: economic activity organized around predicted demand rather than confirmed orders. This paper names and traces that logic as the anticipatory economy and introduces ambient commerce as its consumerfacing expression. In ambient commerce, the act of signalling intent to go somewhere, entering a destination into a navigation application, triggers the entire service chain ahead of arrival. A grocery store sees the customer coming, confirms inventory, stages the order, and reserves a curbside slot before the car leaves the driveway. A restaurant receives arrival time, requests a menu decision, and has the order placed before the customer walks in. Every transaction is just in time. Every service is pre-positioned. The physical visit becomes the final step in a transaction already substantially complete. We trace the verified evidence base for this emerging system. Walmart's hurricane-stocking program, running continuously since 2004, established that demand correlation can drive supply decisions without causal explanation. The more consequential development is the agentic commerce infrastructure built between September 2025 and early 2026, when OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Stripe, PayPal, Visa, and Mastercard (Mastercard, 2026) launched competing transaction protocols allowing AI agents to discover, negotiate, and pay on a consumer's behalf in real time. McKinsey projects this channel will redirect 3 to 5 trillion dollars in global retail spending by 2030 (Roberts, 2025). We connect this evidence to classical economic theory (Hayek, Coase, North, Granovetter) and examine the implications for competition policy, data governance, and the participation of developing economies in standards-setting processes now underway.

title: Network-Varying Coefficient Ridge Regression
affiliations: University of Turku and University of Turku - Department of Mathematics and Statistics
